title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago

Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.

title: Multi-scale Biological Adaptation to Environmental Variability
description:
More information - https://www.nitmb.org/multiscale-biological-adaptation-to-environmental-variability
 Understanding how complex, multi-scale biological systems operate in a constantly changing environment is a challenging scientific problem. One important issue is that the relevant scales span separate fields of research, such as genetics, cellular biology, physiology, neurobiology, and ecology—disciplines that use largely different methods and experimental models. This is an important limitation because biological systems are inherently multi-scale and involve complex coordination across scales. Moreover, we currently lack the theoretical and experimental framework to understand the impact of an unpredictable environment on organismal and supra-organismal responses.
 Mathematical approaches will play a critical role in modeling and predicting the complex, often multifaceted effects of environmental variability on biology across scales. Adapting existing mathematical models and developing new methods to capture the multi-scale effects of environmental variability is not a trivial task, especially when we are only beginning to document its impact on biological systems across scales.
 This workshop will bring together 75 scientists working across the fields of experimental biology, mathematics, theoretical biology, and experts in complex systems to discuss the effects of photoperiod, temperature, seasonality, and other types of environmental variability on the function of the nervous system, on organismal physiology, and on super-organismal responses, such as those that occur at the level of ecology and population dynamics.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Pierre Bismuth: Love Bless America
location: Neubauer Collegium for Culture and Society
description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. The film traces the magic and workaday practice of “inspiration,” taking the traditions of religious music as a point of departure for a multi-layered reflection on love, music, and the divine. In addition to this new film, Bismuth will present a series of digital images resembling American flags emblazoned with lyrics from the hymn.
 Curated by Dieter Roelstraete.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is free and open to the public. Gallery hours: M–F, 9–4.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is supported by the Neubauer Family Foundation and the Brenda Mulmed Shapiro Fund. Additional support for this exhibition was provided by Bernard Friedman, the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, and the France Chicago Center at the University of Chicago.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: Veterans Day Commemoration Ceremony
address: 1410 S. Museum Campus Dr., Chicago, IL, 60605
description:
Veterans Day is set aside to thank and honor living veterans who have served honorably in the military in wartime and peacetime. Originally known as Armistice Day and so declared by President Woodrow Wilson, it was created to mark the signing of the Armistice which ended World War I. Following World War II, it was declared a day to honor all veterans and in 1954, renamed Veterans Day by Congress.
The City of Chicago will host its annual Veterans Day Commemoration Ceremony on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, at 11 a.m. at Soldier Field in the first-floor United Club (1410 S. Special Olympics Drive). The annual ceremony brings together veterans, military families, elected officials and community members to honor the courage, sacrifice and dedication of the men and women who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces. Doors open at 10 a.m., with entry at Gate 0.
Walidah G. Bennett, founder and chief executive officer of the Multi-Faith Veterans Initiative (MFVI) at DePaul University, will serve as the keynote speaker. With more than two decades of nonprofit leadership experience, Bennett has dedicated her career to strengthening community networks that connect veterans and military families with critical resources, education and opportunities for leadership and belonging.
Bennett's commitment to veterans is deeply personal. Her father served as a Montford Point Marine and became a dedicated advocate for veterans and active-duty service members following his military service. Inspired by her father’s legacy and the loss of her veteran son, Bennett established the Multi-Faith Veterans Initiative to address challenges facing veterans and their families, including social isolation, moral injury and the transition to civilian life. Through partnerships with faith communities, educational institutions and veteran-serving organizations, her work emphasizes community connections, healing and long-term support.
Bennett has also contributed to the City of Chicago's veterans advisory efforts and participates in the Illinois Governor's Challenge to Prevent Veteran Suicide. Her work continues to advance a vision in which veterans are recognized not only for their military service but also as leaders and valued members of their communities.
The ceremony will feature musical performances by the U.S. Navy Band Great Lakes and will be emceed by retired U.S. Army Master Sgt. Adam Shaw. Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th Ward), a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, will deliver welcoming remarks, while retired U.S. Navy Seabee Chief Petty Officer Leonardo Alicea will lead the invocation and benediction.
Remarks will be delivered by Mayor Brandon Johnson and Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle. The program will include a wreath laying and recognition of distinguished veterans and military representatives, including Ald. William "Bill" Conway (34th Ward), a U.S. Navy Lieutenant (O-4); Sgt. Maj. Janet Sandoval of the U.S. Marine Corps Recruiting Station Chicago; U.S. Navy veteran Rocio Varela; and U.S. Army National Guard veteran Lourdes Fernando. Benediction will be given by Seabee Chief Petty Offi­cer Leonardo Alicea Chaplain, United States Navy, Retired. Chicago Park District General Superintendent and CEO Carlos Ramirez-Rosa will also be in attendance to join in honoring the service, sacrifice and dedication of our nation’s veterans.
A resource fair featuring local veterans’ organizations and City offices will take place from 10 a.m. to noon, providing veterans and their families with access to information and resources. Participating organizations include the Mayor’s Office of Veterans Affairs, Jesse Brown Department of Veterans Affairs, Chicago Veterans, and the Cook County Clerk’s Office.
Veterans and their families are especially encouraged to attend as Chicago comes together to recognize their service, celebrate their contributions and reaffirm the city's commitment to supporting the veteran community.
Business attire or service dress uniform is requested. Admission is free and open to the public. Complimentary parking is available at the Waldron Deck parking structure. Attendees are encouraged to arrive by 10:30 a.m. to allow time for security screening and seating.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Graduate Reading Group – Meeting 3
description:
Join us in Autumn 2026 to discuss James Lang’s 2020 book Distracted: Why Students Can’t Focus and What You Can Do About It.
 Why is it so hard for students – and for us – to pay attention? We know that distraction isn’t good for learning, but it can be hard to resist other demands on our attention. With regard to learning, distraction is widely seen to be an impediment, something to avoid at all costs. But recent research reveals that our brains aren’t designed for intense focus all the time, and distraction can sometimes even help us. Although we often want our classrooms to be distraction-free zones, Lang points out that in requiring focus all the time, we’re working against our brains’ natural function. Lang offers ways for us to think about the classroom not as a ‘distraction-free zone’ but rather as a place that nurtures students’ attention.
 Reading Group meetings are informal and provide an opportunity to share reactions, questions, and thoughts about implementation and practice, however, for planning purposes, we ask that those interested in participating only register if they plan to attend all three sessions.
 Books will be available to pick up in advance of our first meeting. Registration is limited to 25.
 For the reading schedule, please see the CCTL website.

title: Interdisciplinary Archaeology Workshop
description:
The IAW was founded as the primary point of substantive intellectual connection between archaeologists in the divisions of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Chicago. The workshop allows for graduate students, faculty members and special guests to present their work as well as research plans to a community which could provide a deeply grounded and theoretically informed set of responses and feedback.
 Historically, archaeological research has itself been divided amongst different academic disciplines, with corresponding variations in intellectual traditions and approaches. It has always been the primary object of the IAW to bridge these divisions and to foster a healthy, informed dialogue on the aspects of method and theory that cut across the field’s diverse disciplinary locations. The workshop brings together faculty and students from Anthropology and Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, forging an archaeological community that is more than the sum of its parts. In addition, the workshop has succeeded in its ambition to draw on members of other interested departments and committees such as Classics, African Studies, History, East Asian and South Asian Studies, as well as Geographical Studies.
 In casting archaeology into discussions that move broadly across the Social Sciences and the Humanities, we hope to reaffirm the interdisciplinary perspective that lies at the heart of archaeological research.

FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: Voices of Our Common Life
description:
In this talk, musician and author Stephen Wade explores his new book, Our Common Life: Folksong from the Front Porch to the Concert Hall (University of Illinois Press, 2026). The book, its research drawn in part from the Newberry’s modern manuscripts collections, begins in Bughouse Square with its leather lunged orators and their artfully overheated rhetoric. That soapbox forum, and others like it that once dotted the city, before nighttime television and indoor air conditioning dissipated listeners out for a summer’s evening, summons an imaginative counterpart in the playful and extravagant speech found in early American stage plays and comic literature. Among the radiations of this tall talk tradition, much embraced in Chicago by locally-based scholars and collectors, Stephen Wade created Banjo Dancing which opened in May 1979 at the Body Politic, the city’s first off-Loop theater. The show built on this verbal foundation, coupled with traditional Southern music.
Such sources fill this book. Kentucky-born musician Doc Hopkins, and his Chicago-based student, Fleming Brown, who learned the five-string banjo over coffee and rolls before Doc’s early morning WLS broadcasts in the late 1940s, leads to other musicians and talkers. These include writer Jack Conroy, Chicago Daily News editor Lloyd Lewis, Grand Ole Opry performer Uncle Dave Macon and his accompanists, blues artists David “Honeyboy” Edwards and Jim Schwall, rural banjoists Thaddeus Willingham and Omer Forster, and Mississippi storyteller Helen Marie Rowe. Rowe, a mother of sixteen, twelve of whom survived, found in the antebellum tales she learned from her grandmother, a way of putting her brood to sleep. In doing so, she offered a domestic entertainment no less expressive than the soapboxers who populated the hobohemias of Chicago. As Will Keys, another of the musicians featured here once told the author about his way of playing, it’s “AWYC, Any Way You Can.” These individuals and their stories speak to a resourcefulness of our common life, a creative freedom that echoes just outside this library’s grand entrance.
View a trailer for Our Common Life on YouTube.
A book signing follows the program (which includes live music).
Native Chicagoan Stephen Wade, a past Newberry fellow and contributor to the Encyclopedia of Chicago, is a Grammy-nominated musician and writer. He is the author of the award-winning book The Beautiful Music All Around Us: Field Recordings and the American Experience (University of Illinois Press, 2012). A recipient of Chicago’s Joseph Jefferson award, his Banjo Dancing became in its day one of the five longest running, off-Broadway shows in the United States.
Colloquium is a weekly series of talks featuring staff, fellows, and scholars who are working with the library’s vast collections. These events bring together experts from various fields to share their research on a wide range of topics, followed by an opportunity for the audience to ask questions and engage in conversation.
Colloquium is open to the public and offers a chance to explore fascinating ideas and new discoveries. No advance registration is required.
Call us at (312) 255-3602 or send us an email.

2002, North Little Rock, Arkansas. Besties Minnie and Callie are getting ready for their high school senior year. Charismatic Callie, a singer and performer, is the town’s golden child, while the more awkward Minnie has grown up in her protective shadow. When their friendship is suddenly upended by a tragic accident, Minnie is left rudderless. Struggling to find herself and looking for companionship, Minnie forms a complicated relationship with Callie’s mother, who is also seeking solace from her grief (Sophie Okonedo).
With their latest gem, Chicago-based filmmaking duo Alex Thompson and Kelly O'Sullivan (Ghostlight, Saint Francis), deliver another deeply authentic and bittersweet drama about people coming of age and reckoning with who they are and their relationships with the people closest to them. Anchored by powerful performances from Okonedo, as well as Ghostlight stars Katherine Mallen-Kupferer and her real-life mother Tara Mallen, it is a superbly told, cathartic story filled with warmth and emotion.

Presented by Campfire Repertory Theatre Directed by Campfire Rep Associate Artist, Gina Cioffi
What happens when accountability becomes a business? In Steph Del Rosso’s sharp, darkly funny satire, men accused of sexual misconduct enter a futuristic rehabilitation center designed to reform them. When idealistic new employee Tess joins the organization, she quickly discovers that redemption becomes complicated when good intentions collide with technology, corporate ambition, and profit. The Gradient challenges audiences to examine power, forgiveness, and who gets to decide when someone has truly changed.

title: Finding Meaning in Work in the Age of AI
description:
AI can draft memos, generate and debug code, brainstorm research ideas, and even solve complex math problems; but how does this impact our relationship with our work and learning?
 Join the Chicago Forum for a student discussion on the meaning of work in the age of AI. As AI is transforming entry-level tasks across finance, academia, law, tech, research, and startups, come share your experiences from internships, research, and other work this past summer and beyond, and hear how peers across different fields are witnessing and navigating these changes.
 Does AI free us from grunt work to focus on “more meaningful” work, or distance us from the process that makes work meaningful? What does genuine “co-intelligence” with AI look like, or does that erode a sense of agency and ownership over what we create?
 No AI or technical expertise required. Just bring your experiences, disagreements, and questions.

title: Fat Notes: a fairytale cabaret
description:
Come join Fat Theatre Project performers as they bring to life songs from your favorite princesses, villains, and beyond!
FEATURING:
Joel Caballero
Aira Lheiz Aquino
Rachel H. Maloney
Kristin Schmitz
Lou McNaughton
Melody DeRogatis
& Femme De Violette
Doors at 6pm and our show begins at 7pm.
Tickets are $12 in advance and $17 at the door.
Dorothy is 21+ and requires physical or mobile ID for all to enter. Dorothy is ADA accessible with elevator access on Campbell Ave. If you are a guest who requires elevator access, please wait by the black door with our logo in the window and call our staff to assist: 773-770-3799
Please note: refund requests are only available until 24h before the show (11/10, 7pm). No other refund requests will be honored.
-----------
ABOUT THE PERFORMERS
Joel Caballero is a queer, nonbinary, luxury size entertainer performing burlesque as Wilde. Joel believes that there is no honor in making yourself small. Stand up and take space! Joel can be seen performing around Chicago with their clothes on with the Windy City Performing Arts Choir and otherwise at The Newport Theater 
Aira Lheiz Aquino is a Chicago-based extrovert, creative connector, and lifelong lover of a good story. Born in the Philippines and raised between languages and cultures, she is happiest bringing people together, whether that means gathering friends around a karaoke mic, discovering a new NPR Tiny Desk Concert, or enjoying a matcha latte. She is also the concierge friend who always has a restaurant recommendation, knows where to find the good stuff around Chicago, and will absolutely stop to take a tourist’s picture.
By day, Aira is a Social Impact and Fundraising Strategist who helps creative ideas find the people, resources, and support they need to flourish. Outside of work, she sings, plays ukulele, travels whenever she can, and collects songs that make life feel a little more magical. For her first live performance, Aira is dedicating “How Far I’ll Go” from Moana to her fellow island princesses. She loves Moana’s open-mindedness to what lies beyond the reef, her connection to her ancestors, and her trust in the ocean even when she doesn’t yet know how to navigate it. Moana reminds her that not knowing the way is not a reason to stay put: si no puedes parar las olas, las surfeas. And you can meet the waves with courage without giving up your softness, joy, or femininity along the way.
Rachel H Maloney is a Chicago-based performer and fat liberation activist, and she is thrilled to be a part of this rendition of Fat Notes! Much of Rachel’s work is rooted in her experience as a fat queer person, and she is so excited to get to be a part of this event celebrating fat people and their talent. She would like to shout out her best friend Cas and her former professor Dr. John Elson Williams for always being in her corner when things were rough. @rachelhmaloney
Kristin Schmitz (she/her) is honored to be a part of the Fat Theatre Project collective! Originally from the Bay Area, Kristin now resides in Chicago where she is a performer, improviser, singer, and sign language interpreter. She is also a writer, singer, and voice actor for the Signal Award winning Dorktales Storytime podcast.
Voted least likely to Need A Sensitivity Course by Forbes Magazine Lou McNaughton started pursuing theatre in their 30s to fill a void their inner theatre kid was feeling. Last seen In Gender Fucked Productions “transcribe” and The Terror Cottas Production of “the Ostrich”. They are a proud member of the Fat theatre Project as our volunteer coordinator. In their free time they enjoy reading, writing poetry and meeting people’s cats.
Melody DeRogatis is a lifelong Chicagoan director, producer, actor, teaching artist, and playwright. Melody holds her BFA in Musical Theatre/BA in Writing from Drake University in Des Moines, IA. Melody directed two readings for Fat Theatre Project’s inaugural event “Fat Tuesdays” in 2024, as well as directed mainstage production The Interplays, and co-produced/directed for “Fat Tuesdays” in 2025. Outside of the Fat Theatre Project, Melody is the Performing Arts Supervisor for Northbrook Park District and Artistic Director/Founder of Possibilities Theatre Company. Additional recent directing credits include: Newsies, The Crucible (Beverly Arts Center), Failure: A Love Story (Triton College), and Head Over Heels (High School Edition), School of Rock, A Christmas Story, Chicago: Teen Edition (Northbrook Theatre).
Femme De Violette is the busty Broadway broad who got off the bus just a liiiittle too late, and is making sense of this modern world around her while trying to keep her divas alive. She’s a hostess, producer, showstopper, and maven of the stage. She is also a proud associate collective member for fat theatre project, and believes wholeheartedly in the beauty and dignity of fat bodies onstage. You can find her all over this beautiful Windy City bringing her larger than life personality everywhere- can’t believe it fits in a suitcase!

When Alex Stephens (A.K.A. Strawberry Guy) self-released his debut single in 2018, he was merely doing it out of a love for songwriting. What he wasnt expecting was millions of streams and an avid worldwide fanbase.
A one-man impressionist, painting majestic soundscapes, Strawberry Guy blends truthful lyrics with lush arrangements to conjure new emotive worlds. Inspired by composers of the Romantic period, or Debussy, Ravel, and other classical artists of the 1800s, his wonderland moves like a Monet painting where arpeggios dance between meadows of dazzling dynamics and dramatic key changes.
Imitating natures effect on emotion, like 70s songwriters, or the fantastical soundtracks accompanying vibrant scenes in the Japanese animated Studio Ghibli films and video games, landscape is brought to the fore. Monets picturesque Meadow at Giverny features as the albums accompanying artwork perhaps a reminder of the rural Welsh countryside views through his childhood homes window.

How does change really happen? What is revolutionary change? Are there relationships between political revolution, social revolution and musical revolution?
Revolutions 1 explores these questions through the music and politics of 1796, in the aftermath of the French Revolution. In fact, post-revolutionary Paris was also home to a revolutionary time in the development of the bow. Violinist and violin expert Stefan Hersh will explain how changes in bow design led to changes in music that helped to usher in the heightened emotional range of the Romantic era that followed.
A program of selected works by Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven will bring these revolutionary changes to life.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756-1791): Sonata for Violin and Piano in E minor, K. 304
Joseph Haydn (1732-1809): Piano Trio No. 35 in C major, Hoboken XV:21

title: FRANK CATALANO Celebrates Eddie Harris!
description:
FITZGERALDS NIGHTCLUB PRESENTS:
Frank Catalano Celebrates Eddie Harris!
"Swiss Movement, Cold Duck Time, Exodus To Jazz, Freedom Jazz Dance"
$25 General Admission SEAT / Reserved Tables Available
Legendary saxman Frank Catalano consistently headlines world-class festivals and sells-out venues throughout the USA, Europe, and Japan. Thanks to his signature sound and renowned reputation, Catalano averages 150 concerts a year with his jazz quartet.
As a coveted guest artist, Frank often lends his sax stylings to high-profile rock groups. Recent highlights include playing a 7-minute improvised sax solo at The Hollywood Bowl with The Smashing Pumpkins, closing out the Chicago Blues Festival with Los Lobos, and performing with Les Claypool, Sean Lennon, and the Violent Femmes. He also teamed up on a unique version of the Jane’s Addiction hit “Jane Says” with Perry Farrell, Billy Corgan, and Jimmy Chamberlin, Frank’s longtime friend and collaborator.
Eddie Harris was born October 20, 1934 in Chicago, Illinois. He began his career as a singer in various Baptist churches throughout Chicago. Around the age of 3, Eddie’s cousin, Bernice Benson, who played piano at Eddie’s mother’s church, began teaching him how to play the piano where he learned to play by ear and eventually learned to read music.
Eddie learned to play the clarinet, vibraphone, and saxophone while attending DuSable High School in Chicago, Illinois under the guidance of a well-known and influential musical director, Captain Walter Dyett. Captain Dyett was responsible for the development of several Jazz musicians who came out of Chicago from the 1940’s to the early 1960’s. Eddie always wanted to play the saxophone simply because he admired the way it looked, however in order to play saxophone for Captain Dyett one had to play the clarinet first, so Eddie’s first wind instrument was the clarinet.

title: Rockin’ in the Park
description:
Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.
Concerts run from 7–10 PM. Admission is free. Outside food and coolers are prohibited. Parking is available at the Parkway Bank Park parking garage and is free with validation from any Parkway Bank Park venue.
2026 Lineup
Thursday, July 9: New World Men*
A powerful tribute to Rush, bringing the spirit, precision, and intensity of the legendary band’s live shows to the stage.
Thursday, July 16: Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press*
Beloved Chicago party band Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press delivers huge harmonies, sharp musicianship, and a wildly fun setlist built for singing, dancing, and staying out later than planned.

title: Concerts of Dance: Kara Hunsinger
description:
Kara Hunsinger presents a solo variation of her new work entitled Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation. We congratulate a friend on an achievement, then repost footage of state violence. We take in news of war, genocide, and climate collapse while presenting images of perfection, productivity, and belonging. Hunsinger’s work interrogates the normalization of such digital behavior and considers the cost of performing stability while everything feels fractured. Tracing an arc from disconnection to reconnection, Return to Us questions how easily we surrender agency to the rectangle in our hands.
Open Rehearsals
Wednesday, November 11 | 12-4 pm
Thursday, November 12 | 12-1 pm
Kara Hunsinger hosts an open rehearsal of new work Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation.
Free; Walk-ins Welcome.
—
Movement for Anyone Workshop
Wednesday, November 11 | 5:30-6:30 pm
Movement for Anyone is a guided improvisational class designed for non-dancers. Through simple movement prompts and sensory exploration, participants develop awareness, attention, and connection with themselves and others. Drawing from principles of movement meditation, the session supports physical mobility, nervous system regulation, and emotional well-being. Participants experience how movement, like conversation, can foster presence, release stress, and create meaningful human connection.
This workshop is intended for non-dancers.
Free; Registration Required.
—
Performance of Return to Us
Friday, November 13 | 1-2 pm
Experience Kara Hunsinger’s new work, Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation.
Free; Registration Recommended.
—
Live Filming of Return to Us
Friday, November 13 | 2-4 pm
Kara Hunsinger conducts a live filming of Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation.
—
About the Artist
Kara Hunsinger is a Chicago-based dance artist whose movement lives at the intersection of athleticism, emotional depth, and storytelling. Her work is rooted in presence, curiosity, and the belief that the body holds both memory and meaning. She received her BFA in Dance from the University of Arizona School of Dance, where she deepened her understanding of the body as both instrument and narrator. Her training has taken her across the U.S. and internationally, including time with Hubbard Street Dance Chicago, Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Ate9 Dance Company, SALT Contemporary Dance, San Francisco Conservatory of Dance, and Share Dance Intensive Berlin. Hunsinger is currently a company member with Boykin Dance Project and has previously performed with multiple Chicago based dance companies. Her performance repertoire spans contemporary and ballet-based works by Helene Simoneau, Noelle Kayser, Mike Tyus, Robert Battle, James Gregg, Nacho Duato, Christopher Wheeldon, Alexei Ratmansky, and Ohad Naharin. In addition to performing, Kara is an emerging choreographic voice. She served as Choreographic Assistant with Boykin Dance Project from 2022–2024, contributing to works such as Nonsense! and Smart Mouth. Her own choreography, including Can You Hear Me Now? and Let The River Answer, reflects her interest in physical storytelling, human connection, and the emotional undercurrents that shape modern life. This is her third collaboration with Brendan Fernandes, following his installation Skin in the Game (2024), and the immersive performance 72 Seasons (2021) at Lurie Garden.
About the Performer
Josephine (Josie) Starr, born and raised in Marshall Missouri, began her training as a competition dancer. She has sense graduated with a B.F.A. in Dance and departmental honors from Webster University. She has had the privilege of training with companies across the United States, some of them including Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Complexions Contemporary Ballet, Inaside Dance Chicago and Visceral Dance Chicago. She continues her dance practice post college, performing professionally with Little Fire Dance Project and Boykin Dance Project.

title: Min Yé
description:
Souleymane Cissé · 135m · DCP
 Originally conceived as a series, Souleymane Cissé’s Min Yé draws on the style of Malian television serials to tell a story of adultery within a polygamous marriage. Cissé, educated at Moscow’s VGIK in the 60s alongside fellow pioneers of African cinema Ousmane Sembène and Sarah Maldoror, reflects on the realities of Malian media production, where television is state subsidized and soap opera remains a vital vernacular. An indictment of the contradictions of the Mailian bourgeoisie, civic and social organizations become implicated in this high-pitched domestic drama.

title: Great Lake Swimmers w. Colleen Brown
description:
Capturing light is not easy: ask any outdoor photographer. In order to capture the perfect shot, one has to be ready for fragmentary shifts in illumination. In that spirit, Caught Light is Great Lake Swimmers’ ninth album, and perhaps their most nimble: be prepared, don’t overthink, act fast.
Founder Tony Dekker has always been akin to a wildlife photographer, often choosing to make records in unique surroundings with a connection to Ontario history. This time, he holed up in the Ganaraska Forest, between Peterborough and Port Hope, with producer Darcy Yates (Bahamas) and engineer Jimmy Bowskill (Blue Rodeo). Their goal was to tap the warmth of early ’70s folk/pop/rock, whether it be the cozy sonic sweater of Gordon Lightfoot’s classic work, or the gentleness of underrated American songwriter Dory Previn. Dekker made everyone listen to John Martyn’s 1971 album Bless the Weather before the session.
For the first time, Dekker ceded control to a producer, albeit one who had once been the bassist in Great Lake Swimmers (2007-08). Yates chose the studio and the backing band, which included veteran drummer Gary Craig (Bruce Cockburn, Jann Arden), who Dekker calls “the Jim Keltner of Canada.” Tracking was completed in three days, Nashville-style, with only two days of overdubs, including Colleen Brown’s backing vocals. Compare that with 2023’s Uncertain Country, which took three pandemic-stricken years to make.
Caught Light was captured in the shortest amount of time Dekker had ever spent making a record, and it’s likely to be the one with perhaps the longest impact. That’s because Caught Light is not just the most fully realized Great Lake Swimmers album in years, but it also leads off with two of Dekker’s strongest singles.
“One More Dance Around the Sun” is an open-window, summer-driving song to accompany a golden-hour trip through the backroads of your childhood hometown. Dekker himself moved back to the Niagara area during the pandemic, with his partner and two young children. “I spent the first half of my life trying to get out of the small town where I was born and raised, and I’m spending the second half getting back there,” says the songwriter who lived in Toronto his entire adult life until now. “It’s an ode to the familiarity and the joy in that and the repetition of seeing the same faces and places, knowing all of that very well. It’s also important to feel grounded in community, to feel the power of that in a specific place, keeping one’s moral compass fixed in the right direction.”

title: The Animeros, Fachoso
description:
With musical notes that span well beyond genres like bolero, psychedelic, and cumbia, The Animeros not only make their audience hit the dance floor, but they also invite their listeners and tastemakers alike to a glimpse of their rich cultural upbringing.
The group who is made up of Nick Tozzo (drummer and percussionist), Nicolas Sanchez (bassist), and Mauro Lopez (guitarist) craft a genre-blending sound that drifts between the lush jungles of Colombia, the palm-lined streets of 1960s coastal Mexico, and the dusty cantinas of West Texas.
Sanchez’s Colombian roots, growing up listening to his parents’ beloved salsa and cumbia; Lopez’s parents’ Mexican and American discography, which spanned from traditional Tejano to improvised jazz; and Tozzo’s love for jazz and salsa music, the latter stemming from his college years, leading him to study and live in Colombia to experience music greats first-handedly. All of this, paired with their undeniable chemistry and meshed with their now hometown Austin’s innovative creative sounds has led them to create the unique sonic movement that is The Animeros, a name inspired by Colombian shamans who would usher lost souls to their peace.
Their journey took an unexpected turn when their music reached the ears of Dan Auerbach, the Grammy Award winning producer, songwriter, and frontman of The Black Keys. Auerbach first heard them by chance, music floating from an open hotel window that stopped him in his tracks. Captivated, he made a note to track them down, and within a year, that chance encounter led to something bigger. Now signed to Auerbach’s Easy Eye Sound label, The Animeros are preparing to release their debut album next year, produced exclusively by Auerbach himself.
“I feel like it’s only a matter of time for these guys and for the music that they play. All they have to do is be themselves,” Auerbach said about the trio. “They’re playing the kind of music that they can play forever until they’re 100 years old because it’s rooted in history, but it’s very much in the present.”
“When we first talked, one of the things was our love for the nuance in Latin music,” Lopez shared. “That’s what initially drew ourselves to each other That’s like a language among musicians.” Tozzo also talked about their shared musical bond: “What makes our chemistry special is that even if one of us has just a glimpse of an idea, together we can take that and really create something out of it.” “That encyclopedia of [music] knowledge everyone bringsThat’s what’s really appealing about this project. It’s not just surface level. Everybody’s going pretty deep on it,” Sanchez added.
The Animeros are on the cusp of reaching new audiences all over the globe. More singles are coming with a new album on the way in 2026 via Easy Eye Sound.

title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.
Hayward is made possible by a special gift from Show Sponsor, The Michael and Mona Heath Fund.
The Gift Theatre Company’s 2026 Homecoming Season is made possible, in part, by generous contributions from The Arts Work Fund · The Copernicus Foundation · Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events · The Gaylord and Dorothy Donnelley Foundation · The Illinois Arts Council · Melissa Thornley Consulting · The Paul Angell Foundation · The Rabb Family Foundation · The Saints · The Service Club of Chicago · The Shubert Foundation, Inc.

title: Mother Soki
description:
**Mother Soki** is among a generation of new artists forging their paths and creating music that attracts fans seeking a soul connection. That creativity led her to sign with independent label Mom+Pop early in 2025.
A bit farther back in her trajectory, Mother Soki wasn't even clear about how to pursue music. Carving her way through adolescence with a fierce artistic drive, though, the Minneapolis-based musician discovered her passion for making music while attending college in Chicago.
Attempting to pursue other forms of art and avoiding what was her true calling, Mother Soki says, “I realized it was far more fulfilling than any art medium I had tried (and I’ve tried a lot), from beginning to end, and even after. Something about the process of music felt so natural to me, even when I did not know how I was doing it, I was just doing it.”
Now immersed in her passion for music, Mother Soki gravitates toward the dreamy textures of Dream Pop and the sonic nostalgia of the ’90s. Drawing daily inspiration from her surroundings, she channels her creativity through classic influences: The Sundays, Imogen Heap, and Cocteau Twins.
Her sound blends modern interpretations of vintage synths with heavy guitars and airy, spacious vocals—creating contrasts that shouldn't work, but somehow do. Mother Soki makes the unexpected feel seamless.

title: Jason Bonham’S Led Zeppelin Evening
address: 105 East Main Street, Saint Charles, IL, 60174
description:
Jason Bonham always finds himself at home behind the drumkit. From this spot, he has anchored the tempo for a myriad of the most legendary artists of all-time. It’s the place where he initially realized his destiny as a kid. It’s a tried-and-true safe harbor for the expression of his purest emotions. It’s a direct conduit to his late father and Led Zeppelin drummer John Bonham. Following stints with Airrace and Virginia Wolf, he handled drums on Jimmy Page’s gold-certified Outrider. During 1988, he notably accompanied Page, John Paul Jones, and Robert Plant behind the kit for Led Zeppelin at the Atlantic Records 40th Anniversary Celebration Concert. Beyond helming solo projects such as Bonham and The Jason Bonham Band, he appeared in Rock Star with Mark Wahlberg and Jennifer Anniston. Plus, he lent his talents to Foreigner, Little Steven, Joe Bonamassa, and Paul Rodgers. He held down the drums for Led Zeppelin’s 2007 reunion at the Ahmet Ertegun Tribute Concert—which set the Guinness World Record® for “Highest Demand for Tickets for One Music Concert.” The evening spawned the Celebration Day concert film and multiplatinum album, debuting Top 10 on the Billboard 200, selling three million-plus copies, and garnering a GRAMMY®. Other notable projects have included Black Country Communion (Bonamassa, Glenn Hughes, and Derek Sherinian) and California Breed (Hughes and producer and guitarist Andrew Watt). He joined Sammy Hagar and the Circle with Van Halen’s Michael Anthony and Joe Satriani. In 2010, he introduced Jason Bonham’s Led Zeppelin Evening (JBLZE), packing venues coast-to-coast and supporting everyone from Heart to Kid Rock. A spectacle of top-flight musicianship, arresting visuals, mind-blowing lighting, and emotionally charged storytelling, Rolling Stone hailed its “set of Led Zep gems that were strikingly faithful to the originals,” while Billy Joel handpicked JBLZE to open up a handful of dates. Ultimately, Jason remains forever at home on the drums.

title: An Evening w/ Kate Nash (GA Standing Room Only Ticket)
description:
London born singer-songwriter Kate Nash is coming to Martyrs' Wednesday, November 11th, 2026.
Kate Nash is a platinum selling recording artist, musician and actress from London. Kate started her career on myspace uploading her demos to the platform and playing in and around London in 2006. In 2007 her debut album, Made of Bricks, went to number one in the UK charts and she was crowned ‘Best Female Artist’ at the 2008 BRIT Awards. Her hit song, Foundations, stormed the charts and remains in radio rotation. In the wake of Kate’s second album, My Best Friend Is You, Kate set about using her influence to shift gender perceptions and inspire a new generation of female musicians, launching the Rock ‘N’ Roll for Girls After School Music Club. She released her third album 'Girl Talk' independently, and notoriously opened London Fashion Week’s Felder Felder show for the spring/summer 2013 season, marking a significant change in direction for Kate.
Her fourth album 'Yesterday was Forever' was 222% funded on Kickstarter and she's been touring globally for 18 years to fans who have come to expect the unexpected. In 2024, Kate released her latest album ‘9 Sad symphonies,’ her first signed to the legendary Kill Rock Stars label. She spent the year selling out shows in the UK, Europe and North America, and playing festivals including Glastonbury. The tour culminated in a triumphant headline show at London’s Kentish Town Forum, broken foot and all!
Summer 2025 also saw Kate debut her powerful new song GERM live alongside reinterpretations of her beloved catalogue with the Royal Philharmonic Concert Orchestra at a special performance at Mighty Hoopla festival. She is currently shining a light on the crisis in live music touring through her campaign Butts for Tour Buses, and works closely with the Music Venue Trust, for whom she is an artist patron.
Alongside her music career, Kate is also an acclaimed actress and producer. Kate was approached by legendary Hamilton choreographer, Andy Blankenbuehler, to write and develop a Broadway musical using her original songs. Kate starred in the production ‘Only Gold’ in 2022 in New York at the MCC theatre. Nash is also well known for her performance as Rhonda Richardson on Netflix's Emmy nominated original, 'GLOW', produced by Jenji Kohan, and for playing Boudica in the BAFTA nominated 'Horrible Histories'. A raw and honest documentary following her career "Underestimate the Girl" was picked for the BBC's notorious Storyville and has screened at festivals across the world.

Having evolved from their understated slowcore beginnings in Austin, Texas, theyre now seasoned veterans of the scene. Across their first five studio albums, the duo established their trademark sound of twangy indie rock, 2000s-inspired pop-country, and emotional acoustic ballads with strong pop sensibilities. description: Tyler Ballgame was born from the concept of radical presence in expression—the idea that each live performance is an opportunity to transcend the ordinary digital world, and surrender to the magic of a truly human experience. Now, he's gearing up to release his debut full-length album, “For The First Time, Again,” produced by longtime collaborators Jonathan Rado and Ryan Pollie. title: "Normal Dreams”
description: Normal Dreams 'Normal Dreams' is a new performance by dancer Liana Zhen-Ai and musician Astrid Sonne. First presented as a part of the Pairings series at La Mama Experimental Theatre Club in New York, curated and produced by Cameron Sczempka, now brought to London via Club Cheek and Qu Junktions. Expect never heard before songs, movement, noise, props and a video call from the big apple. About Liana Zhen-Ai Liana Zhen-ai is a Brooklyn/London-based dancer and interdisciplinary artist from Los Angeles. She has performed as a soloist with choreographers Holly Blakey, Andrea Miller, and Akira Uchida. Her dancing has been featured in Vogue US, NOWNESS, and Face Magazine, and in venues including MoMA, Lincoln Center, Southbank Centre, and Théâtre Chaillot de Nationale. Liana's work uses the lenses of new materialism and object-oriented ontology to interrogate shame, nature, and narrative. Her choreographic practice sits at the intersection of dance, dramaturgy, and scholarship, and her work has been presented at Prototype Festival, Amant, Center for Performance Research, and Green-Wood Cemetery in collaboration with the New York Philharmonic. About Astrid Sonne Astrid Sonne is a Danish, London based composer and viola player. Throughout her acclaimed discography, Astrid Sonne has been carefully crafting different moods through electronic and acoustic instrumental endeavours. On her most recent album Great Doubt (January 2024) this skill is refined, now with the distinct addition of the composer's own vocal in the fore. The tone of each track is unmistakably Sonne's, structured around contrasts through an impeccable sense of timing. Lyrics on the album are sparse, merely highlighting different scenes or emotional states of being, leaving the music to fill in the blanks. Yet they also form a pattern of ambiguity, consolidated through the album title, searching for answers through looking at how and what you are asking, questions for the world, questions of love.

title: 2nd Set With Charles Heath
description:
Originating from Chicago, IL, Charles “Rick” Heath IV is a versatile and renowned musician from local to international levels. Playing anything from Jazz and Blues to Gospel and Latin music, his signature sound is prominent in the recording studios, concert settings, live Broadway theater platforms, and as the drummer for late pianist and jazz legend Ramsey Lewis. Some of his proudest accolades include works with Donald Byrd, McCoy Tyner, and Slide Hampton. He also served as the resident drummer with the national tour of Oprah Winfrey and Quincy Jones’ theater production of “The Color Purple.” He is often rotating hats of composer, band leader, recording artist, musical director, producer and teacher and simply inspires and outreaches to his surrounding communities at all times.
Heath’s prominent sound can be heard on recordings with Ramsey Lewis, Robert “Babe” Irving III, Bobby Broom, Zvonimir Tot, Larry Gray, Sergio Perez, Ken Chaney and the Roger Harris Trio. He proudly launched his first independent recording project entitled “Conversations” encompassing the sound of his very own Charles Heath Quartet.

title: Black Harvest Film Festival: ABOUT HIM
description: ABOUT HIM offers an expansive portrait of Black manhood grounded not in dominance or performance, but in care. Across documentary and narrative cinema, these films illuminate the responsibilities Black men carry as fathers, sons, mentors, artists, laborers, friends, and community leaders. Whether navigating grief, preserving cultural traditions, creating spaces of refuge, confronting injustice, or defending collective dignity, the protagonists reveal masculinity as a practice of stewardship, vulnerability, courage, and collective responsibility. Together, these works challenge reductive narratives and affirm the richness, complexity, and humanity of Black men's lives across generations and across the African diaspora.

title: Marci
description:
$18 Adv + Fees | 21+
When we last heard from Marci aka Marta Cikojevic, she was dancing the pain away on 2022’s Marci. A longtime member of Montreal soft-rock group TOPS, Marci established Cikojevic as a solo artist with an intuitive understanding of pop as a vehicle for emotional catharsis. Four years later, Cikojevic returns with Mask Lady and Late Night Girl, a record of party girl anthems for when the party is over, delivered with love and compassion for the good times and great memories.
Collaborating again with TOPS bandmate David Carriere, Mask Lady has elements drawn from both the Y2k-era messy pop girlies like Uffie and Kesha and Cikojevic’s love of 80s power balladeers like White Snake and Def Leppard, along with the vintage synths that gave Marci a warmly futuristic aesthetic. Album opener “Stars Are Fake” calls back to funk-inflected synthwave with a tight drum pattern and a juicy synth line. “Butterfly Sticker” pulses with a melodic rhythm reminiscent of 90s classics like Savage Garden’s “I Want You.” Glam metal influences come to the fore on “Chaotic Princess,” written and produced with Mike Silver (CFCF), an over-the-top guitar-driven banger about a crazy night out on which Cikojevic begs an officer not to take her to jail—Eddie Van Halen riding shotgun in a car with Britney at the wheel. Of course, this is a Marci album, so there’s plenty of pure pop sugar, as on “99 Dimensional,” a bubbly Janet Jackson-esque dance track about a telepathic connection that lasts forever.
With a balance of bittersweet and breezy sentiments, Mask Lady and Late Night Girl explores the dualities that define our lives: rock and pop, past and future, happiness and sadness. We all have both a masked woman and a late night girl inside—sometimes we live as if the sun will never rise, sometimes we hide our true face from the world. “It’s anybody and nobody,” Cikojevic says. “It’s you”.

title: BTS Express w/ Laretha Weathersby
description:
Two 
calibers of singers exist in today’s music industry. There are vocalists and 
then there are entertainers. Laretha Weathersby is both. Her dynamic, effervescent stage presence 
is unparalleled and her sultry, wispy vibrato makes her a Blues natural.
Voted 
2009-2010’s “Chicago Blues Diva of the Year,” she belts out traditional Blues 
classics with passion and poise and delivers riveting renditions of timeless 
R&B, Soul and Top 40 tunes, all while captivating crowds with her jovial 
disposition and dynamic dancing. Known for her rousing stage presence, crowd members rarely 
blink when Laretha hits the stage, fearing they will miss one of her signature 
dance moves or the chance to chant along with the charismatic chanteuse.
Reigning 
from the Southside of Chicago, Laretha’s mother, a former Gospel soloist, 
detected her daughter’s singing abilities and enrolled the toddler in piano classes 
and encouraged her as a teenager to be an active member of the choir at the 
family’s place of worship. But it was not until the 1990s that Laretha began to 
cultivate a personal relationship with Blues music.
Emerging 
as one of the premiere female Blues vocalists in the City of Chicago in the 
late 1990s, Laretha has performed at such legendary Blues hotspots as The 
Kingston Mines, BLUES on Halsted and since 2010 is a spectacular presence here 
at BLUE CHICAGO.
Her 
debut album – Dance the Blues Away – is an eclectic mix of traditional Blues 
infused with remnants of contemporary R&B and Soul. The album reveals 
Laretha’s reverence for conventional Blues music while flaunting her fluent 
transition into contemporary R & B and Soul.
According 
to Ms. Weathersby, “the power of Blues music lies in its ability to relate to 
each and every member of the human race. People of all different backgrounds 
can connect with the universal concepts of love, triumph and tribulation, which 
are the very elements upon which Blues music is based. I consider it an honor 
and joy to incorporate that human element into my live performances and it is 
with passion and humility that I accept the honor and challenge of preserving 
Blues music for future generations.”
www.LarethaWeathersby.com

Stefan played in several gospel, funk, rock, and R&B groups in southern California before he relocated to Chicago, IL in pursuit of a full-time career as a blues musician. The blues has always been at the heart of Stefan’s passion for music - Chicago provided the ideal scene for him to grow as a blues artist and learn from the best and most authentic sources. Stefan is best known for his slide guitar playing, soulful vocals, and dynamic live performances. Being considered an "old soul", Stefan's main inspirations are Elmore James, Howlin' Wolf, and Albert King.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: ISAC Exhibit: Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC) Museum
description:
Seven years ago, Hartapu was little more than a name. Then, in 2019, an inscribed stone pulled from an irrigation canal in central Türkiye introduced the world to a king who claimed to have conquered Phrygia—one of the most powerful kingdoms of the ancient world. Suddenly, a ruler and a kingdom largely unknown to history demanded a place on the map of Iron Age Anatolia. The stone was found at Türkmen-Karahöyük, a massive tell rising 35 meters above the Konya Plain, that must have been Hartapu’s capital. Though the site had gone largely unnoticed by archaeologists, it is one of the largest Iron Age sites in Anatolia—and excavations launched in 2024 by ISAC and Bilkent University (Ankara, Türkiye) are only beginning to reveal the city’s historical development.
 Hartapu ruled in the eighth century BCE, during a period of intense rivalry between great powers—Phrygia to the west, the Neo-Assyrian Empire to the east—and his kingdom sat squarely between them. The exhibition tells his story through ancient inscriptions, archaeological finds, and new technologies, including 3D printing and advanced imaging, that are transforming how scholars study the past. Contemporary works by artist SaraNoa Mark offer a counterpoint, reflecting on landscape, memory, and the labor and care of preserving the past.
 The ISAC Museum special exhibition Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia is on view from September 17, 2026 through March 14, 2027. It is accessible with museum admission during museum hours.

title: Multi-scale Biological Adaptation to Environmental Variability
description:
More information - https://www.nitmb.org/multiscale-biological-adaptation-to-environmental-variability
 Understanding how complex, multi-scale biological systems operate in a constantly changing environment is a challenging scientific problem. One important issue is that the relevant scales span separate fields of research, such as genetics, cellular biology, physiology, neurobiology, and ecology—disciplines that use largely different methods and experimental models. This is an important limitation because biological systems are inherently multi-scale and involve complex coordination across scales. Moreover, we currently lack the theoretical and experimental framework to understand the impact of an unpredictable environment on organismal and supra-organismal responses.
 Mathematical approaches will play a critical role in modeling and predicting the complex, often multifaceted effects of environmental variability on biology across scales. Adapting existing mathematical models and developing new methods to capture the multi-scale effects of environmental variability is not a trivial task, especially when we are only beginning to document its impact on biological systems across scales.
 This workshop will bring together 75 scientists working across the fields of experimental biology, mathematics, theoretical biology, and experts in complex systems to discuss the effects of photoperiod, temperature, seasonality, and other types of environmental variability on the function of the nervous system, on organismal physiology, and on super-organismal responses, such as those that occur at the level of ecology and population dynamics.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Implementation Science to Advance HIV Prevention in France
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
Open to the public, but registration is required due to limited space. 
 Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a medication that is highly effective in preventing HIV. In France, PrEP use has steadily increased among certain populations. However, there are other populations, such as migrant women, who are disproportionately affected by HIV yet underrepresented among PrEP users in France. Consequently, there is a clear gap in PrEP use that needs to be addressed in order for HIV prevention efforts in France to be successful. Investigators at the University of Chicago and Paris Cité University have established a partnership to address the multilevel complexity of HIV prevention. Using implementation science research methodology, we aim to identify the barriers and facilitators to HIV prevention in France. We will conduct focus groups and surveys among providers and patients. Using these results, we will develop tailored implementation strategies to address the specific challenges facing certain populations (e.g., migrant women) at family planning centers throughout Paris and Seine-Saint-Denis. Throughout this process, we will engage relevant stakeholders (e.g., community-based organizations and patients) to define the content of these interventions, which may include educational and training videos and other resources. We hope that our work will help to improve HIV prevention efforts in France, such as reducing disparities in PrEP use, and also serve as a foundation for similar projects in the near future.
