title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Workshop - Shared Pasts: Collaborative Archaeology in Mesoamerica and the Andes
description:
This workshop equips participants with the tools and perspectives needed for public engagement in interpreting and preserving Mesoamerican and Andean archaeological heritage. Participants will engage in interactive activities to explore the ethics and inclusivity of storytelling and outreach. A forum discussion is planned to present diverse perspectives from the multiple publics involved in archaeological research, with Dr. Luis Muro, assistant curator of South American Anthropology at the Field Museum, participating and drawing on his experience working at sites in Peru. Public archaeology has transformed the relationship among archaeologists, communities, and heritage in Mesoamerica and South America. Public archaeology should be considered when designing research that requires a participatory component involving diverse publics. By the end of the workshop, students will be able to: understand the principles of public archaeology, compare experiences from Mesoamerica and South America, analyze real-world heritage conflicts, design participatory strategies, and communicate archaeological findings to diverse audiences. Below is the tentative schedule for the workshop:
 12:00 to 12:30 PM - Lunch
 12:30 to 2:00 PM - Forum
 2:00 to 2:30 PM - Break
 2:30 to 4:00 PM - Hands-on activity
 4:00 to 5:00 PM - Reception
 Bárbara Arroyo is a research associate at the Museo Popol Vuh of Universidad Francisco Marroquín in Guatemala. For the last fifteen years, she has led the Kaminaljuyu Archaeological Project, overseeing fieldwork, training programs, and initiatives to protect its delicate earthen architecture. She obtained her B.A. in Archaeology from Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala and her Ph.D. in Anthropology from Vanderbilt University. title: CEGU Colloquium: Reed McConnell
description:
The Epistemological Wild West: Suspicion, Speculation, and Environmental Knowledge in California’s Colorado Desert
 Reed McConnell, PhD Candidate in Anthropology
 In this ethnographic dissertation chapter, I explore how all sorts of stakeholders - environmental justice activists, corporate farmers, residents, state bureaucrats, and entrepreneurs - use different kinds of speculation as a tool in battles over environmental knowledge in California’s Imperial Valley. Imperial Valley is a desert region in southeastern California facing a looming air quality crisis from an enormous evaporating toxic lake called the Salton Sea, as well as a simultaneous rush of investment in lithium extraction at the Sea’s southern end. I particularly focus on the way that speculation is used to both shore up and unsettle authority with regard to Salton Sea and lithium extraction - often in the form of conspiracy theory - and how this speculation both generates and results from senses of suspicion.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

title: The Future of Energy Access - with T. Patrick Walsh, CEO of Sun King
description:
T. Patrick Walsh is Co-Founder and CEO of Sun King, a social business that designs, distributes, and finances solar energy kits for off-grid homes and businesses in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The company today powers the homes of 58 million people. It employs 4,300 staff and 45,000 field agents who install and service solar kits in 13 countries.
 The company’s roots trace back to Patrick’s undergraduate years at the University of Illinois, where he studied physics and economics. In 2005, he traveled to rural northern India with the university’s Engineers Without Borders chapter. Shortly after, he designed the company’s first solar lantern to replace the kerosene lamps families relied on for light.
 Two decades later, two-thirds of Sun King customers are getting electricity for the first time via solar, having previously relied on candles and kerosene for lighting, while often walking long distances to charge their phones. Sun King has committed to extending clean energy access to 200 million people by 2030.
 A Chicago native, Patrick splits his time between Chicago and Nairobi. He’ll talk with students about turning a student project into a global company and the future of energy access.
 Presented by Global Studies and CEGU (Committee on Environment, Geography and Urbanization)

title: Kara Hunsinger: "Return to Us"
description:
Kara Hunsinger presents a solo variation of her new work, Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation. We congratulate a friend on an achievement, then repost footage of state violence. We take in news of war, genocide, and climate collapse while presenting images of perfection, productivity, and belonging. Hunsinger’s work interrogates the normalization of such digital behavior and considers the cost of performing stability while everything feels fractured. Tracing an arc from disconnection to reconnection, Return to Us questions how easily we surrender agency to the rectangle in our hands.
About the Artist
Kara Hunsinger is a Chicago-based dance artist whose movement lives at the intersection of athleticism, emotional depth, and storytelling. Her work is rooted in presence, curiosity, and the belief that the body holds both memory and meaning. She received her BFA in Dance from the University of Arizona School of Dance, where she deepened her understanding of the body as both instrument and narrator. Her training has taken her across the U.S. and internationally, including time with Hubbard Street Dance Chicago, Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Ate9 Dance Company, SALT Contemporary Dance, San Francisco Conservatory of Dance, and Share Dance Intensive Berlin. Hunsinger is currently a company member with Boykin Dance Project and has previously performed with multiple Chicago based dance companies. Her performance repertoire spans contemporary and ballet-based works by Helene Simoneau, Noelle Kayser, Mike Tyus, Robert Battle, James Gregg, Nacho Duato, Christopher Wheeldon, Alexei Ratmansky, and Ohad Naharin. In addition to performing, Kara is an emerging choreographic voice. She served as Choreographic Assistant with Boykin Dance Project from 2022–2024, contributing to works such as Nonsense! and Smart Mouth. Her own choreography, including Can You Hear Me Now? and Let The River Answer, reflects her interest in physical storytelling, human connection, and the emotional undercurrents that shape modern life. This is her third collaboration with Brendan Fernandes, following his installation Skin in the Game (2024), and the immersive performance 72 Seasons (2021) at Lurie Garden.
About the Performer
Josephine (Josie) Starr, born and raised in Marshall Missouri, began her training as a competition dancer. She has sense graduated with a B.F.A. in Dance and departmental honors from Webster University. She has had the privilege of training with companies across the United States, some of them including Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Complexions Contemporary Ballet, Inaside Dance Chicago and Visceral Dance Chicago. She continues her dance practice post college, performing professionally with Little Fire Dance Project and Boykin Dance Project.

title: Geo. Sci. Seminar: Patrick Rafter, University of South Florida
description:
Title: North American / North Atlantic Wind And Sea Level Pressure Alongside Global Climate Change
 Abstract: The easterly trade winds crossing Central America through mountain gaps (“Gap Winds”) are major freshwater conduits from the Atlantic to the Pacific (Zaucker & Broecker, 1992) with variability driven by changes in regional sea level pressure (SLP). Considering the importance of North Atlantic salinity for global ocean overturning (Broecker, 1989), Gap Wind variability could be an important ocean-climate feedback (Latif et al., 2000). Here, using radiocarbon (14C/C) measurements of marine microfossils and terrestrial wood, we reconstruct the strength of the northernmost Gap Wind—the “Tehuano Wind” (Müller‐Karger & Fuentes‐Yaco, 2000)—which principally responds to SLP variability over the Gulf of Mexico, North America, and subtropical North Atlantic (Barton et al., 1993; Karnauskas, 2014). We find that the Tehuano Winds were much stronger than today during the later Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), implying a larger freshwater loss from (and salinity gain to) the North Atlantic at that time. New model experiments suggest a higher SLP anomaly over the Gulf of Mexico (caused by regional landmass exposure at lower sea level) is one driver of the much stronger LGM Tehuano Wind. Stronger Tehuano Winds plus widespread high SLP are consistent collectively explain evidence for dry atmospheric conditions (Grimm et al., 1993; Manabe & Broccoli, 1985; Wharton et al., 2026) and provide a coherent mechanism to increase LGM North Atlantic salinity—this mechanism is consistent with previously hypothesized ocean-atmosphere feedback on North Atlantic Deep Water formation (Broecker, 1989; Broecker et al., 1990; Leduc et al., 2007). As Earth warms through the deglaciation, the Tehuano Winds weaken and eventually recover, which is a sequence consistent with the large-scale change in atmospheric dynamics from North American icesheet meltwater flux the North Atlantic (Conroy et al., 2025) and later icesheet shrinkage (Löfverström & Lora, 2017).
 Host: B.B. Cael

title: Waleed Qaisar (Toronto): Isomonodromy, higher Lie theory, and $\pi_2$ in algebraic geometry [AG seminar]
description:
Given a family of complex algebraic varieties, we can deform a flat connection from one fibre to another while keeping the underlying monodromy representation constant. Viewing the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence (including with ramification) as an instance of higher Lie theory, we will upgrade this operation of isomonodromic deformation to give parallel transport functors between categories of flat connections with logarithmic singularities. As a result we will encode higher homotopical information at level 2, and produce a 2-local system valued in geometric analytic stacks (rather than valued in a linear category), from which the classical notion of isomonodromy can be recovered by passing to categories of principal bundles on the stacks.
We will give an example which shows that applying this construction to the trivial case of parallel transport along the constant path recovers an enriched version of the degree 2 connecting homomorphism of a fibration. 
Time permitting, we will use this to formulate a question about upgrading (Betti) geometric Langlands from an equivalence of categories to an equivalence of local systems of categories by finding the Langlands dual of isomonodromy and matching the mapping class group actions on the automorphic and Galois sides. We will outline how this reduces to constructing the Betti spectral action in families.

title: Beyond the Ice: A Conversation with Dominik Hašek on Sports, Ukraine, and Speaking Up
description:
What responsibility do athletes and public figures have when democracy, freedom, and human rights are under threat? Can sports really remain separate from politics?
 Join legendary Czech hockey goaltender Dominik Hašek for a conversation about his extraordinary career, his outspoken support for Ukraine, and his belief that staying silent in the face of injustice is not an option.
 From Olympic gold and Stanley Cup victories to his advocacy against Russia’s aggression, Hašek brings a unique perspective on the intersection of sports, politics, and personal responsibility.
 The conversation will explore why he chose to speak out, what solidarity with Ukraine means today, and how individuals — whether athletes, students, or ordinary citizens — can use their voices to make a difference. The event will include an opportunity for audience questions.
 Dominik Hašek is one of the greatest goaltenders in ice hockey history. A two-time Stanley Cup champion, Olympic gold medalist with the Czech national team, and member of the Hockey Hall of Fame, he is widely known as “The Dominator.” In recent years, Hašek has also become a passionate and outspoken advocate for Ukraine, using his public platform to condemn Russia’s aggression and defend democratic values. He believes that sports cannot be separated from questions of human rights, freedom, and responsibility. He is also an ambassador for People in Need USA.
 People in Need is an international humanitarian and human rights organization founded in the Czech Republic in 1992. Working in countries affected by conflict, disasters, poverty, and repression, the organization provides emergency assistance, supports long-term recovery, and promotes human rights and democratic values. PIN has been active in Ukraine since 2014 and significantly expanded its humanitarian response following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, helping millions of people affected by the war.
 People in Need USA is the organization’s growing presence in the United States, established to build partnerships, engage American communities, and strengthen international solidarity with people affected by crises and human rights violations around the world. Dominik Hašek supports this mission as an ambassador, helping bring attention to the importance of standing up for Ukraine and defending democratic values.
 This event is free and open to the public and is sponsored by the Masaryk Club and the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures, with the gracious support of the Otto V. Čapek Fund.

title: Colloquium - Lena Borise
description:
How strictly verb-final languages become less so
 Lena Borise 
 (joint work with Erika Asztalos, Katalin Gugán, Nikolett Mus, Andreas Pregla, and Balázs Surányi)
 Verb-final languages, despite what their name suggests, often allow for postverbal constituents (PVCs). It has also been observed that rigidly verb-final languages can become more tolerant of PVCs throughout their history. In this paper, we show that prosodic/information-structural factors play an important role in determining the availability of PVCs in languages that seem to be undergoing a change from more to less rigid verb-finality. The starting point for this approach is the generalization that given/backgrounded PVCs tend to appear in this type of languages first, followed by new/focused PVCs at a later time, which has been shown to hold for some Uralic languages (É. Kiss 2014; Asztalos, Gugán & Mus 2017).
 We bring in additional empirical support for the given>new generalization and further show that the progression of change in different languages may distinguish subtypes of given and new. Specifically, among new PVCs, narrow foci become available earlier than PVCs that are part of broad focus, and among narrow foci, contrastive foci become available post-verbally earlier than new-information foci. We derive these generalizations from the prosodic/information-structural properties of the postverbal domain in verb-final languages, offer an Optimality Theoretical account of the process, and illustrate it with data from a variety of languages.

title: How Not to be an American Catholic | Writing About Religion at the End of American Empire
description:
Old questions about religion and politics have taken on a new urgency, and few of our institutions seem wholly equipped to address them. How strange, then, that the Roman Catholic Church should reemerge as an important moral force—and that the Pope should emerge as a pointed critic of governments, corporations, and even religion itself, including his own. What are we to make of this new development? What can the Church’s renewed public role tell us about the political and moral uncertainties of our moment? And how might the study of religion help us see these questions in a different light?
 Join writer and scholar of religion Jack Hanson of Columbia University for a talk on the Catholic Church’s renewed public role and the larger questions it raises about religion, politics, and the search for a common good. The talk will be followed by an informal conversation with Professor Ryan Coyne.

title: Colloquium: Yonin Malin
description:
Yonatan Malin, Associate Professor, University of Colorado Boulder
 “Gurevich’s Dobriden and the Language of Klezmer Music”
 Yonatan Malin is Associate Professor in the College of Music and Program in Jewish Studies at the University of Colorado Boulder. His areas of research include the German Lied, theories of rhythm and meter, klezmer music, schema theory, relations between ethnography and analysis, corpus studies, and performance timing. His book Songs in Motion: Rhythm and Meter in the German Lied was published by Oxford University Press in 2010; recent work includes articles on klezmer in the Journal of Music Theory, MTO, and Analytical Approaches to World Music. Malin also collaborated with Daniel Shanahan to produce a searchable website with modal analyses of 249 tunes from Jewish Instrumental Folk Music by Moshe Beregovski. Malin was editor of MTO from 2010 to 2014, and he is currently Chair of the Publications Committee for the Society for Music Theory. He has very fond memories of roaming the Goodspeed Halls and Hyde Park as a graduate student in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and he is honored to be invited back for this colloquium series.

FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: Lloyd Sachs, "Bill Forsyth: Interviews"
description:
About the Book:
One of the most beloved filmmakers of his time, Bill Forsyth (b. 1946) has--with one exception--not directed a feature in more than thirty years. This long silence is all the more remarkable given his meteoric rise: between 1979 and 1983, the Glasgow native crafted four comic gems that helped put Scottish cinema on the map. How did the director of such enduring classics as Gregory's Girl and Local Hero seemingly vanish from the film world?
It's tempting to blame his retreat on the painful fallout from Being Human, the troubled Hollywood production starring Robin Williams. But even before that big-budget flop, the deeply reserved Forsyth wrestled with the discomfort he felt directing--and with audiences who often overlooked the serious themes beneath his offbeat comedies. "I've always had a much darker side than most people have perceived," he confided to British critic John Brown.
Through interviews with leading critics and film authorities, Bill Forsyth: Interviews offers a revealing look at the filmmaker's personal approach to his art, shaped by early encounters with the French New Wave and a youthful stint making industrial films about forestry, fishing, and factories. Forsyth reflects on his debt to auteurs like Francois Truffaut, Preston Sturges, Jean Renoir, and Jacques Tati, and offers candid insights into his process. These conversations highlight his methods and the underappreciated dimensions of his work, including what Scottish critic Jonathan Murray calls their "comic ingenuity, idiosyncratic narrative structures, and tonal complexity."
About the Author:
Lloyd Sachs is author of the critical biography, T Bone Burnett: A Life in Pursuit. He was a film and jazz columnist and editorial writer for the Chicago Sun-Times; podcast host of Sachs and the Cinema (and the Chicago radio segment of the same name), crime fiction columnist for the Chicago Tribune, senior editor at No Depression, and media columnist for the Chicago Reader. His work has appeared in such publications as Kirkus Reviews, Rolling Stone, the Village Voice, DownBeat, the Los Angeles Times, the Washington Post, and JazzTimes.

title: Charlene Kluegel - Beyond Fifths
description:
Join Grammy-nominated violinist Charlene Kluegel for the contemporary world-premiere performance of ***Beyond Fifths***, a radical solo violin program exploring unchartered acoustic worlds through deliberate mistuning. Drawing exclusively on music composed within the last four decades, this immersive recital abandons traditional fingerboard geometry in favor of raw, vibrating overtones, microtonal friction, and hidden sonic resonances.
The evening charts a daring course through eight distinct acoustic landscapes, featuring pioneering European complexitism alongside vibrant new commissioning voices and virtuosic masterworks:
- **Edu Haubensak** — *Vier Saiten* (1987)
- **Manfred Stahnke** — *Capra* I (1987)
- **Peter Eötvös** — *para Paloma* (2015)
- **Katherine Balch** — *Iaspis* (2013)
- **Hannah Selin** — *Meditation on 2/5* (2021)
- **Sepehr Pirasteh** — *Simple* (2021)
- **Ramin Akhavijou** — *probable* (2020)
- **John Corigliano** — *STOMP* (2011)
Culminating in the high-octane, vernacular-infused release of Corigliano’s *STOMP*, *Beyond Fifths* challenges the limits of the instrument and redefines what a solo recital can be. Experience an uncompromising sonic journey curated and executed by an artist operating at the absolute cutting edge of contemporary performance.
Presented by The CheckOut.

title: JAY WEBB w/ KALEB SANDERS
description:
Country artist Jay Webb writes songs that hit like a gut punch. He grew up bouncing between the backroads of North Alabama and the city in South Alabama, using music to make sense of the chaos around him. What started as a way to process a turbulent childhood quickly became his purpose –- gritty storytelling layered over genre-blurring beats, delivered with zero filter. He began recording demos in high school and never let up, releasing track after track on his own and building a following from the ground up. His lyrics cut deep, his voice carries the scars and his sound refuses to stay in one lane. Webb doesn’t try to clean up the mess – he leans into it, and has a good time doing it.M
The genre-blurring artist pulls from a wide range of influences, pairing the weight of Johnny Cash and Hank Williams with the edge of Juice WRLD and Post Malone. It’s not traditional country, and he doesn’t want it to be. He calls it “music for real people with real problems” and his fans know exactly what that means. In 2022, a viral TikTok launched his music to a wider audience. Since then, he’s released standout tracks like “Down Here,” “Bury Me With Bourbon” and “Broken,” racking up more than 415M streams and a growing legion of fans over 2M strong.

title: Tom Kenny & The Hi Seas, Expo’76
description:
TOM KENNY & THE HI-SEAS
Tom Kenny & the Hi-Seas is a high energy 12 piece band “RocknSoul” party band.
Performing songs from artist such as Chuck Berry, Sam Cooke,The Shangri-Las, The Righteous Brothers, Gary US Bonds, the band has gained a reputation for raucous live performances in venues from Los Angeles to Atlanta to Tijuana, Mexico.
EXPO’76
After more than a dozen years as an entity, Expo’76 rolls on — impossibly fresh in each performance, their reputation as the Chicago area’s most reliably potent and unpredictable cover band firmly established. Their secret all along has simply been remaining true to themselves, playing the music they want to play. Their set list is a far-flung assortment of hits, forgotten classics and deep cuts, that careens effortlessly across all genres and politely sidesteps old warhorses.
When singer/guitarist Dag Juhlin (Poi Dog Pondering, Sunshine Boys) put out a call to his longtime friends, keyboardist Kenny Goodman (The Service, New Duncan Imperials) drummer John Carpender (Outronaut, The Real Pretenders) and bassist Ralph Baumel (The Real Pretenders) in 2009, his only guideline was that the band just focused on being great, and that the rest would take care of itself. It worked. Expo’76 began their monthly residency at Simon’s Tavern in Chicago in early 2010, and within a few months the room was packed out and they were on the cover of The Chicago Sun Times arts section.
Along the way, they’ve played hundreds of gigs beyond that residency: street fairs, dances, weddings, private parties, swanky fundraisers and more, in every possible setting. They’ve been joined onstage by notable singers and assorted show folk like Robert Cornelius, Kelly Hogan, Joel Murray, Syd Straw, Frank Orrall, Michael McDermott, Jack McGee, and an up and coming singer from Evanston named Eddie Vedder.
Being bolstered by the ferocious and rightly in-demand Total Pro Horns means the Expo’76 catalog has even more depth and power, and the Pros wholly share the band’s irreverent but musically razor-sharp approach to performance.
A night of Expo’76 is an unforgettable experience: songs that unlock memories or invite further exploration, performances that dazzle, and overflowing good vibes, delivered with a generous serving of world class banter. There’s no one else like them.

title: Them Coulee Boys Final Tour
description:
FITZGERALDS NIGHTCLUB PRESENTS:
THEM COULEE BOYS seen HERE
$30 General Admission // $40/seat reserved tables
Soren Staff and Beau Janke – co-founders of folk/rock/Americana outfit Them Coulee Boys – met as camp counselors in northern Wisconsin in 2011. Their weekend workshopping of Avett Brothers and classic country tunes led to original songs and adding Soren’s brother Jens on mandolin. As the years grew, the band turned into a more rollicking outfit, adding Neil Krause on electric bass and Stas Hable on drums. The band’s name is a nod to the glacial melt-carved river valleys they call home, known by early French fur trappers as coulees. Known for wild swings of emotion during sets, it is not unusual to see fans in tears and minutes later dancing with abandon. The honesty and ability to talk and sing about the feelings and emotions that shape them has endeared them to a growing group of fans and friends.
With four full-length albums and an EP behind them, including 2019’s Die Happy (produced byTrampled By Turtles’ Dave Simonett on Lo-Hi Records) and 2021’s Namesake (produced by Grammy winner Brian Joseph), the band has garnered international attention and earned press in American Songwriter, Ditty TV, Folk Alley, and The Bluegrass Situation, as well as tours with Trampled By Turtles, Los Lobos, Old Crow Medicine Show and a spot on the songwriter’s Cayamo Cruise.
2021’s Namesake found the band following a new trajectory, combining their signature take on folk-grass and Americana with comfort on electric instruments and playing rock and roll. The record lives and breathes. It’s both intimate and bombastic. It’s the sweet aunt who makes delicious pies and the wiley uncle who’s not afraid to hit a bit of the bottle. At the bottom is the acceptance that comes with family and old friends; none of us are perfect, but there’s enough love out there to make up for it.
In 2020, they were named Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Band to Watch. In 2021, they won Bluegrass/Americana Band of the Year by the Wisconsin Area Music Industry. For all things Them Coulee Boys, please visit themcouleeboys.com.

title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
description:
DIRECTED BY
David Greaves,
Liani Greaves,
William Greaves
WRITTEN BY
William Greaves
STARRING
Romare Bearden,
Arna Bontemps,
Ida Mae Cullen
A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

title: Concerts of Dance: Kara Hunsinger
description:
Kara Hunsinger presents a solo variation of her new work entitled Return to Us, a live performance examining the psychic and social dissonance of contemporary life under constant digital mediation. We congratulate a friend on an achievement, then repost footage of state violence. We take in news of war, genocide, and climate collapse while presenting images of perfection, productivity, and belonging. Hunsinger’s work interrogates the normalization of such digital behavior and considers the cost of performing stability while everything feels fractured. Tracing an arc from disconnection to reconnection, Return to Us questions how easily we surrender agency to the rectangle in our hands.

Movement for Anyone is a guided improvisational class designed for non-dancers. Through simple movement prompts and sensory exploration, participants develop awareness, attention, and connection with themselves and others. Drawing from principles of movement meditation, the session supports physical mobility, nervous system regulation, and emotional well-being. Participants experience how movement, like conversation, can foster presence, release stress, and create meaningful human connection.
This workshop is intended for non-dancers.

About the Artist
Kara Hunsinger is a Chicago-based dance artist whose movement lives at the intersection of athleticism, emotional depth, and storytelling. Her work is rooted in presence, curiosity, and the belief that the body holds both memory and meaning. She received her BFA in Dance from the University of Arizona School of Dance, where she deepened her understanding of the body as both instrument and narrator. Her training has taken her across the U.S. and internationally, including time with Hubbard Street Dance Chicago, Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Ate9 Dance Company, SALT Contemporary Dance, San Francisco Conservatory of Dance, and Share Dance Intensive Berlin. Hunsinger is currently a company member with Boykin Dance Project and has previously performed with multiple Chicago based dance companies. Her performance repertoire spans contemporary and ballet-based works by Helene Simoneau, Noelle Kayser, Mike Tyus, Robert Battle, James Gregg, Nacho Duato, Christopher Wheeldon, Alexei Ratmansky, and Ohad Naharin. In addition to performing, Kara is an emerging choreographic voice. She served as Choreographic Assistant with Boykin Dance Project from 2022–2024, contributing to works such as Nonsense! and Smart Mouth. Her own choreography, including Can You Hear Me Now? and Let The River Answer, reflects her interest in physical storytelling, human connection, and the emotional undercurrents that shape modern life. This is her third collaboration with Brendan Fernandes, following his installation Skin in the Game (2024), and the immersive performance 72 Seasons (2021) at Lurie Garden.
About the Performer
Josephine (Josie) Starr, born and raised in Marshall Missouri, began her training as a competition dancer. She has sense graduated with a B.F.A. in Dance and departmental honors from Webster University. She has had the privilege of training with companies across the United States, some of them including Alonzo King LINES Ballet, Complexions Contemporary Ballet, Inaside Dance Chicago and Visceral Dance Chicago. She continues her dance practice post college, performing professionally with Little Fire Dance Project and Boykin Dance Project.

title: Early Modern Trans Archives 2.0
description:
What does it look like to do trans studies in premodern archives? How might early modern trans studies be more archival? What tools would we need or might we make to help scholars locate archival sources that inform our thinking on premodern gender? While Early Modern Trans Studies has officially passed the point of “emergent,” the relationship between trans studies methods and the archive has not always felt intuitive.
At our “Trans Archives” workshop at the Newberry in 2025, we opened a wide-ranging conversation about what early modern trans studies archives might look like and how to overcome real and perceived barriers to this kind of work. At Early Modern Trans Archives 2.0, speakers will offer examples of trans archival methods, suggest new ways for trans studies to infiltrate archives like the Newberry, and model strategies for archival scholars to work with trans studies perspectives and research questions. A hands-on component will encourage participants to engage with the Newberry’s collection as well as nontraditional archives of trans studies that exist alongside and within it. We will close with a mentorship session where attendees can consult with Newberry librarians, scholars with archival experience, and scholars working in trans studies.

title: CLEAT Series: Chris Knowlton's 'Echo Network' Night 1
description:
Join us for a special two-night CLEAT Series presentation of Chris Knowlton’s Echo Network! This work is a dance, sound and technology performance that explores networked synesthesia, sensory substitution and the idea of sound as touch at a distance. The work draws biomimetic inspiration from mammals like dolphins, bats, wolves, elephants and whales who use echolocation, calls and songs to navigate low-visibility environments and strengthen social bonds. Haptic data from muscle sensors and pressure-sensing insoles worn by dancers drive immersive projections and real-time spatialized soundscapes in Elastic Art’s CLEAT system, allowing the audience and dancers to hear the dance. With elements first hatched during the 2023 Chicago Cultural Center Dance Studio Residency and further expanded in a 2025 work-in-progress showing, ‘Echo Network’ experiments with new modes of non-verbal accessibility in dance. The project imagines a naturalized digital social network as a place for embodied connection as the ensemble navigates themes of discovery, play, exchange, migration and loss.
7pm doors both Friday and Saturday evening.
Artist Bios
Christopher Knowlton (lead artist / director - he/him) is a queer transdisciplinary movement artist and research scientist who uses emerging technologies to create augmented and interactive performance work. Inspired by science, nature, play, improvisation and human-centered approaches to design, he has produced many solo and collaborative dance works that have been featured locally and internationally, spanning dance, film, new media, puppetry and storytelling. Chris is also a biomechanical research scientist at the Motion Analysis Laboratory at Rush University Medical Center.
Rachel Damon (collaborative dancer - she/they) is a designer, choreographer, producer, educator, and performer whose career connects classrooms, backstage, and presentation. As a Co-Director of Synapse Arts, they have been honored by support from MetLife, Chicago Dancemakers Forum, 3Arts, Illinois Arts Council, City of Chicago, Awesome Foundation, CliffDwellers Foundation, and more. Damon’s projects have been presented at MCA Chicago, The Detroit Institute of Art, Ingenuity Cleveland, TEK BOX Minneapolis, The Field Museum, Roy Hart International Arts Centre (France), and Vo’Arte (Portugal), and in parks, stairwells, and alleys galore. Damon has developed her dance-theatre, site-specific, craft, film, and kinetic textile works through residencies with The Ragdale Foundation, Links Hall, Chicago Cultural Center, Chicago Artists Coalition, Roman Susan Gallery, and South House (England).
Dylan Roth (collaborative dancer - she/her) is a Chicago-based dance artist. She received a Bachelor of Arts degree in Dance Performance Columbia College Chicago in spring 2012. Professionally, Dylan has performed with Aerial Dance Chicago, Banks Performance Project, Bodies in Urban Spaces, Carson Reiners, Cerqua Rivera Dance Theatre, Deeply Rooted Dance Theater's Emerging Artists Ensemble, Esoteric Dance Project, Kelly Anderson Dance Theatre, Khecari, Meadows Dance Collective, Synapse Arts, Sildance/AcroDanza, We Stand Sideways Dance, and The Space Movement Project.
Chrissy Martin is a transdisciplinary performance artist and educator with roots in contemporary dance forms, contact improvisation, Afro-Caribbean dance, postmodern experimental music, vocal jazz, and physical theater. Chrissy blends these forms to rigorously examine her intersecting queer and neurodivergent identities. Martin is an avid member of the global contact improvisation community and has facilitated and taught workshops across the Midwest. Chrissy’s integrated movement style is deeply informed by a lifelong somatic practice. She has taught dance and somatics at Cleveland State University, Columbia College Chicago and DePaul University, and is currently an Assistant Professor at Northwestern University. chrissymartinmakes.com instagram: @chrissybounce
Enki Andrews (projection designer - he/him) is a Chicago-based Multimedia Interactive Artist experimenting with physical phenomena to discover how humanity views itself in light of our finite human perceptions and how expanding those perceptions and reflections enhances our self-awareness. The Natural Sciences and Art ground his work as an inter-disciplinarian having earned degrees in Physics and Philosophy and an advanced degree in Hydrogeology while pursuing his art. Much of his work is inspired by Complex Systems, whether they be Bio-tech interactions, Bio-bio interactions or interactive multimedia installations.
Scott Rubin (sound designer - he/him) is a Chicago-based interdisciplinary artist, composer, and improvising violist whose work interrogates relationships between sound and movement through analog and digital means. His recent projects have involved collaborations with musicians and dancers, often incorporating interactive acoustic/electronic improvisation, expanded performance practices, motion-sensors, and live video. In these projects, he engages themes of intimacy, control, and the sublime.

 It’s 2011 in Upstate New York, and nine freshmen women sit in a boat together every morning at 6am on their collegiate rowing team, competing with each other up for the fastest times, lowest body weights, and most influential seats, until race day when they are asked to put it all aside and row together as comrades in one boat. title: Deana Carter
description:
Doors open one hour prior to showtime
TICKETS ON SALE: Friday, July 10th at 10 AM
Tickets start at: $40.00
(Additional fees may apply)
Drenched in sun-kissed natural beauty both inside and out, Nashville native, Deana Carter, didn’t take a seemingly easy route to stardom, but instead chose to defy the conventional expectations of the typical Nashville artist blueprint and make her own mark. And she did, undeniably taking the industry and fans by storm with her wildly successful multiplatinum international debut “Did I Shave My Legs For This?” more two decades ago. Anchored by the dreamy super hit ” Strawberry Wine”, Carter showcased her own blend of country and retrorock sprinkled with the folksy singer/songwriter qualities that have garnered Deana Carter well deserved respect and wild acclaim.
With EIGHT albums under her belt, Carter explores many subjects commonly shared over a quaint dinner, afternoon coffee or a sunny day hike with a good friend. Her last release of Southern Way of Life was her first dive as Label CEO on her own Little Nugget Records, distributed by Sony/Red. These songs weave through the sometimes rocky terrain of adulthood, including loss of love, relationships on many different levels, trials, tribulations and simply put – life. As always, Instinctively autobiographical, the subject matter mimics the interesting ride of Carter’s own life – so far. The daughter of famed studio guitarist and producer Fred Carter, Jr., Deana grew up exposed to the wide variety of musicians her father worked with, including Willie Nelson, Bob Dylan, Waylon Jennings, Simon & Garfunkel, Muddy Waters, Dolly Parton, and many more. Their strong influence would eventually seep into Deana’s own country-pop style, which reflects qualities that can also be heard in similar artists now, such as Miranda Lambert and reflective of artists like Sheryl Crow. Developing her songwriting skills by trial and error at writer’s nights throughout Nashville, Carter eventually signed a writing deal with Polygram and soon after a record deal with Capitol Records. One of her demo tapes happened to fall into the hands of none other than Willie Nelson, who remembered Deana as a child. Impressed with how she’d grown as a songwriter, Nelson asked Deana to perform along with John Mellencamp, Kris Kristofferson and Neil Young as the only female solo artist to appear at Farm Aid VII in 1994. Her debut album, “Did I Shave My Legs For This?” boasts six songs co-written and with the album co-produced by Carter, was released to strong reviews in late summer 1996. By the end of the year, the record had climbed to the top of both the country and pop charts, quickly achieving multi-platinum status, with 3 number one singles in a row. A “first” for the genre, Deana’s celebrated debut album held this distinction and many ground breaking achievements for more than 5 years and has become one of Country Music’s most treasured classics of the 90’s. “Everything’s Gonna Be Alright” followed in late 1998 and in 2001
Carter realized her dream of performing with her dad on an intimate holiday album, aptly titled “Father Christmas.” Making a strong move towards adult pop Carter released “I’m Just a Girl” on Arista Records in 2003, the same year Capitol Records released a Greatest Hits compilation. Follow-ups “The Story of My Life” in 2005 and “The Chain” in 2007 were both released on Vanguard Records. In an effort to pay homage to her musical roots and preserve her legendary father’s label Nugget Records, that famously presented some of the best in country music some 40 years ago, Carter opened her own label, Little Nugget Records, on which her latest album “Southern Way of Life” was released.
Carter now divides her time between Los Angeles, Florida and Nashville, writing and producing for both the pop/rock and country markets when not on the road touring or making movies. Her superstar success continues to be evident as the chart topper “You & Tequila”, co-written with Matraca Berg and recorded by Kenny Chesney, was nominated as CMA’s “Song of the Year”, as well as two Grammy nods, notable the coveted “Song of the Year” , and, also, received a nomination as ACM’s “Song of the Year”. You and Tequila received a coveted ‘Songs I Wished I’d Written’ by the NSAI in Nashville, something Deana treasures, coming from her hometown music community. Carter also co-wrote and produced an album for recording artist Audra Mae & the Almighty Sound, while putting the finishing touches on her own “Southern Way of Life.” She has recently held a Governor’s seat on the Grammy Board for the Recording Academy and served on the Producer’s & Engineer’s Wing, The Membership Committee, & held an active voice for Artists & Creators with Advocacy in Washington, D. C. & throughout the last year for Pandemic Relief. Singer, songwriter, producer – Deana Carter continues to defy conventional expectations, making waves as she makes great music, tours, & makes movies.

title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.
Hayward is made possible by a special gift from Show Sponsor, The Michael and Mona Heath Fund.
The Gift Theatre Company’s 2026 Homecoming Season is made possible, in part, by generous contributions from The Arts Work Fund · The Copernicus Foundation · Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events · The Gaylord and Dorothy Donnelley Foundation · The Illinois Arts Council · Melissa Thornley Consulting · The Paul Angell Foundation · The Rabb Family Foundation · The Saints · The Service Club of Chicago · The Shubert Foundation, Inc.

title: The Snow Queen
address: 1333 N. Milwaukee Ave, 2nd Floor, Chicago, IL, 60622
description:
Once there was, and once there was not, a little girl and a little boy
Best friends Gerda and Kay spend the changing seasons weaving stories and tending their beloved garden. As the flowers bloom, so do they. But when a shard of enchanted glass pierces Kay’s heart, everything changes. His laughter freezes. His warmth disappears. Swept away by the enigmatic Snow Queen to her kingdom beyond the aurora, Kay is destined to remain in an endless winter unless someone dares follow.
Fueled by unwavering love and impossible hope, Gerda embarks on a journey into the unknown. Along the way she encounters unpredictable elements, a talking raven, a band of singing robbers, whispering flowers, deceptive sweetness, and strangers who become family. With every trial she must decide not only how to save Kay, but who she is becoming.
Can Gerda withstand the bitter cold and the Snow Queen’s relentless desire to control the narrative? Will Kay reclaim the story that was stolen from him, or surrender himself to the silence of the ice?
A beloved folktale re-imagined through a new landscape, The Snow Queen explores the people who carry our stories when we no longer can—and the courage it takes to let them go. Equal parts whimsical, haunting, joyful, and deeply human, this production warms even the coldest hearts into blooming again.
[Appropriate for ages 12 to 112]

title: Hayward- A World Premiere by Netta Walker
description:
As part of our 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father’s funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter’s love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O’Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.

title: Tyrone Wells
description:
First things first. Let’s get this out-of-the-way. Tyrone Wells (I) wrote this bio. I figured, “who better to talk about myself than myself?”. 
I’m a lot of things in no particular order a preacher’s son, a brother, a husband, a dad, a real estate lover, a major-label artist, an independent artist, an opener, a headliner, a very self-conscious dancer (think “Footloose”, only without the cathartic cutting loose), a gardener, a wanna be surfer, a person who has needed therapy, a pickleball player, a barstool theologian, and this next one kind of goes without saying because you’re here reading my bio.. I’m a singer-songwriter. 
I’ve written a lot of songs. Probably approaching around 1,000 songs now to me, when I wrote them, they were all good songs. The luxury of time has informed me, some of the songs were maybe just good to me. And some of the songs, inexplicably, have millions upon millions of listeners. Meanwhile, others have tens upon tens. I don’t know why, I just write them and set them free. 
Ultimately, I’m trying my best to be honest, and write a song that I, and you can both love. I’m gonna keep trying. I’m so grateful that you have listened. Be it once, or be it a hundred times. I’ve got big love for you. I’ll be over here chopping away and reminding myself to be vulnerable. Peace and Love, XOXO Tyrone

title: GCS featuring ERIC GALES, DENNIS CHAMBERS and BILLY SHEEHAN
description:
GCS brings together three of the most electrifying musicians in modern music: two time Grammy nominated guitarist and vocalist Eric Gales, Modern Drummer Hall of Fame drummer Dennis Chambers, and five time Best Rock Bass Player Billy Sheehan. Each of these musicians has spent decades performing at the highest levels of blues, rock, funk, jazz fusion, soul, and progressive music. Together, they form a rare lineup where every player can lead, listen, and push the music into new territory. The sound of GCS won’t be confined to one category. It will draw from the full range of their musical lives, moving from heavy blues and hard rock to deep funk, soul, and jazz fusion, with room for fearless improvisation and the kind of live interplay that only players of this caliber can deliver. Three legends, three unmistakable musical forces, one stage. When GCS comes to your city, be there to witness what happens when three titans finally join forces.
Buy Now
Eric Gales: Two time Grammy nominated guitarist, vocalist, and songwriter whose explosive playing has made him one of the most respected artists in modern blues and rock. The Memphis native signed with Elektra Records at 15 and released his debut album at 16, earning Best New Talent honors in Guitar World’s 1991 readers poll. His unmistakable approach, playing a right handed guitar flipped upside down, is matched by a sound that moves naturally through blues, rock, funk, soul, and psychedelia. Across more than three decades, Gales has performed or recorded with artists including Carlos Santana, Buddy Guy, Joe Bonamassa, Gary Clark Jr., Lauryn Hill, and Christone “Kingfish” Ingram. His albums The Bookends and Crown reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Blues Albums chart, while Crown and A Tribute to LJK each earned Grammy nominations for Best Contemporary Blues Album. A three time Blues Music Award winner, Gales also contributed electric guitar to Ludwig Göransson’s Grammy and Academy Award winning score for Sinners.
Dennis Chambers: One of the most influential drummers of the modern era, celebrated for his deep pocket, remarkable speed, and ability to make highly technical playing feel completely musical. A self-taught prodigy from Baltimore, Chambers began playing drums at four, was performing in clubs by six, and joined Parliament/Funkadelic at 18. That early foundation in funk became part of a musical language that would eventually reach across jazz, rock, fusion, soul, and Latin music. Dennis has recorded and performed with Carlos Santana, John Scofield, John McLaughlin, George Duke, the Brecker Brothers, Maceo Parker, Mike Stern, and many others. His career also includes playing in the jazz fusion trio Niacin with Billy Sheehan and keyboardist John Novello. Dennis was inducted into the Modern Drummer Hall of Fame in 2001. Over his career he has become one of those rare drummers who can hold down an undeniable groove, drive a band with tremendous power, and take the music completely outside without ever losing its center.
Billy Sheehan: one of rock’s most original and influential bassists, known for turning the instrument into both a powerful rhythmic foundation and a commanding lead voice. After building his reputation with the Buffalo power trio Talas, Sheehan joined David Lee Roth’s band alongside Steve Vai and Gregg Bissonette, recording the platinum selling albums Eat ’Em and Smile and Skyscraper. He later co founded Mr. Big, whose worldwide hit “To Be with You” reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped charts around the world. Sheehan’s career also includes extensive work with Steve Vai, The Winery Dogs, Sons of Apollo, and Niacin with Dennis Chambers and John Novello. His signature style blends deep groove with three finger picking, chords, harmonics, two handed tapping, and controlled feedback. Voted Best Rock Bass Player five times in Guitar Player’s readers poll, Sheehan earned a place in the magazine’s Gallery of Greats.

title: The Best of Steve Martin & Martin Short with The Steep Canyon Rangers and Jeff Babko
description: The Best of Steve Martin & Martin Short is a show that redefines the form in unexpected and profound ways, from two of the funniest, most influential and acclaimed talents of the past century. Their humor is often subversive, but it is always a joyous self-deprecating romp from two comedy masters driven to make each other laugh as much as the audience. The jokes come at you at a rapid-fire pace with little set-up and big punch lines as they mock Hollywood and the fickle nature of celebrity, but the comedy truly soars when they lovingly (and relentlessly) roast each other. Martin and Short’s chemistry and timing on stage reflects a friendship forged over three decades which developed when they met for the first time on the set of the 1986 film “Three Amigos.” These two titans of comedy have been touring together since 2015, when they launched their first live show entitled “A Very Stupid Conversation.”

title: Hovvdy
description: Hovvdy’s Will Taylor and Charlie Martin have occupied a distinct corner of the modern-day indie landscape for more than a decade. Having evolved from their understated slowcore beginnings in Austin, Texas, they’re now seasoned veterans of the scene. Across their first five studio albums, the duo established their trademark sound of twangy indie rock, 2000s-inspired pop-country, and emotional acoustic ballads with strong pop sensibilities. Their last two records saw them processing life’s most intense emotions more openly than ever before, from declarations of love in its many forms on 2021’s True Love, to grappling with loss and personal change on their latest self-titled album, Hovvdy. But the songs of Big World have them trading in overt emotional directness for subject matter that leans enigmatic, contemplating their place in the world through a mosaic of songs that sees the band at their most secure and self-aware.

title: Janet Bean + Ghost Voice - Album Release
description:
Ghost Voice
Ghost Voice is a Chicago-based trio of pedal steel (Tom McGettrick), Wurlitzer 200 electric piano (Alison Hinderliter), and upright bass (Jeff Parker) playing a range of excerpts of “small-c” classical works, from Villa-Lobos' Bachianas 5 Aria to the Agnus Dei Aria in Bach's Mass in B minor.
Ghost Voice brings together instruments from the indie/rock/country worlds and points them in an unexpected direction, using the pedal steel as a foundational voice rather than as color or ambience, for example. Although the orchestration is unique, Ghost Voice is not merely experimental; rather, the combination of instruments has been carefully chosen to create a haunting new sound.
Like the instruments, the artists in Ghost Voice bridge musical worlds. Tom McGettrick also founded surfy-crime jazz instrumental band Mar Caribe and has performed with Lawrence Tome, Janet Bean, Sally Timms, Jon Langford and many other country/indie/folk/rock acts, as well as recently playing the pedal steel in Chicago Shakespeare Theater’s production of Brokeback Mountain. Alison Hinderliter (Scotland Yard Gospel Choir, The Handcuffs) and Jeff Parker (Joel Paterson, Paul Asaro, Natalie Scharf, Erwin Helfler, Chicago Cellar Boys), are both classically trained and have extensive experience in rock, indie, and jazz bands, so they are able to give these works the precise playing they deserve, while retaining the popular touch that the audience deserves.
Janet Bean
Janet Beveridge Bean brings to the Hideout her solo project, The Concertina Wire, for a rare live performance. Bean, as described by the Mekon’s Sally Timms, conjures dark psychological dramas in her songs. She uses her striking voice and presence to create a world of beauty and unease the listener will not soon forget. Bean is co-founder, co-songwriter, drummer, and vocalist for the great, muscular Chicago guitar band eleventh dream day. She is also co-founder, co-writer, and guitarist for the off-kilter-beautiful Freakwater, her country-folk group with Catherine Irwin. She’s performed and released albums with Jim Elkington as the Horses Ha and Jaime Fennelly’s Mind Over Mirrors, as well as her prison-bound, infamous dadist revolutionary duo, Moxie Tung, with Sally Timms.

title: All Eight
description:
It’s 2011 in Upstate New York, and nine freshmen women sit in a boat together every morning at 6am on their collegiate rowing team, competing with each other up for the fastest times, lowest body weights, and most influential seats, until race day when they are asked to put it all aside and row together as comrades in one boat. Crew would be chaotic enough on its own, but off the water, their coach shows up at their parties and drinks with them, makes lewd comments about their bodies, and is allegedly sleeping with one of them. So when one rower secretly rats him out for allegedly sleeping with a student and is seemingly rewarded with the best seat in the boat when he’s fired, her motives come into question– as does her position of privilege on the team.
Over the course of their freshman year, All Eight examines how the world of collegiate sports drives these young women with varied power to fight to win– races, love, power– at the expense of even each other.

title: Black Harvest Film Festival: TRY A LITTLE TENDERNESS
description: TRY A LITTLE TENDERNESS considers love not as romance alone, but as a sustained practice of care. Across families, friendships, neighborhoods, and diasporic communities, these films illuminate the quiet acts of devotion that bind people to one another. Through caregiving, cultural preservation, sacrifice, humor, grief, and remembrance, they reveal tenderness as a quiet but enduring form of resilience. Spanning intimate narratives and richly observed portraits from across the Black diaspora, the program asks how love is carried, inherited, and continually renewed across generations. Together, these works affirm that care is not merely an emotion, but a practice of survival, stewardship, and collective flourishing.

title: WINGTIPS (10 Year Anniversary) / Blood Handsome / Slugscape / DJ Lidia Vomito
description: Doors: 8PM / Show: 9PM / 21+WINGTIPS are a Midwest-based darkwave/electropop duo consisting of VincentSegretario and Hannah Avalon. The bands sonics are best described as anandrogynous sound of transition. Interpolating darkly shimmering layers ofangular guitar and pulsating darkwave beats, WINGTIPS sharpen their anthemicrush with an increasing penchant for melody and an atmosphere equallyinformed by post-punk as sweeping electronica.Their debut full-length, EXPOSURE THERAPY released in 2019, is acontextualization of new romantic for post-millennial end times, and a refreshingmix of synthpop and darkwave with hooks so compelling they are cinematic inscope. In September 2021, WINGTIPS released their sophomore LP, CUTTINGROOM FLOOR. The record is a momentous shift from a previous stylisticallydarkwave approach into a realm of maximalist dark pop, and even techno bodymusic, while also maintaining many of the sonic textures from whence the bandcame.In 2024, WINGTIPS released their third full-length record, ON TRIAL. Featuringcollaborations with the likes of TIM CAPPELLO (The Lost Boys, Tina TurnerBand), and the cutting edge New York-based RONNIE STONE, the album is yetanother shift for the band into an even more evolved musical identity. Tonally,the dichotomy between tracks marks the furthered maturity of WINGTIPSapproach to their unique blend of dark dance music, and texturally lush dreampop. The album also marks the first release where the entirety of recording,mixing, and post-production was completed by the band themselves,maintaining a core ethos that DIY is key to precisely communicating artisticlanguage.In 2026, WINGTIPS welcomed drummer KASEY LEE ROGERS to their livelineup, marking the first time in over a decade the band has presented itself in athree-piece configuration.

Lil' Ed & The Blues Imperials: Chicago Blues Royalty
"Electrifying, raucous, pure Chicago blues...Lil' Ed is a guitarist extraordinaire...slashing slide and flamboyant stage persona." –Chicago Tribune
"Rough and ready blues played with unmitigated intensity...Swirling, snarling, riveting slide...The Blues Imperials pound out riffs and rhythms like they're overdosing on boogie juice. Scorching and soulful, joyous and stomping." –Living Blues
In a city overflowing with unrivaled blues talent, Lil' Ed & The Blues Imperials have been standing tall for over 30 years as the undisputed royalty of Chicago blues. Fueled by Lil' Ed's gloriously rollicking slide work, deep blues string bending, and rough-edged, soulful vocals, the band's big sound is as real and hard-hitting as Chicago blues gets.
As the Chicago Sun-Times aptly describes, "Lil' Ed & The Blues Imperials are the hottest purveyors of bottleneck boogie to come out of Chicago since Hound Dog Taylor." Their electrifying live performances, marked by Lil' Ed's flamboyant stage presence and the band's relentless energy, have earned them a devoted following both in their hometown and around the world.
Through their uncompromising commitment to the blues tradition and their ability to infuse it with a fresh, modern edge, Lil' Ed & The Blues Imperials have cemented their status as one of the most respected and influential blues acts to emerge from the Windy City. As they continue to captivate audiences with their raw, soulful sound, this legendary band remains a shining beacon of Chicago's enduring blues legacy.

Dead by dawn! In this not-exactly sequel/sort-of remake, Bruce Campbell's Ash arrives once again at the proverbial cabin in the woods for a vacation with his girlfriend. Lovecraft fame), unleashing a demonic force that possesses Ash’s girlfriend—and, well, let’s just say the romantic getaway goes seriously south. When the archaeologist’s daughter shows up with three companions, they find the semi-deranged Ash, now minus a (demon-possessed) hand, battling the forces of darkness tooth and nail (make that shotgun and chainsaw). Taking the premise of his original film and 10 times the budget (courtesy of Dino De Laurentiis of all people), Sam Raimi lets his imagination run completely wild, topping the earlier film with anarchic and at times deliriously surreal set pieces of outrageous excess, headlong camera work and berserk, punishing Three Stooges-esque violence. Amidst the mayhem, there stands the one and only Bruce Campbell, truly giving it his all: in the end, the entire film becomes a showcase for his unique talents. - Text courtesy of Film at Lincoln Center

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.
