title: Sunday Somatics – Healing with Yoga
description:
This beginner-friendly yoga series features a heart-centered, healing slow flow practice intimately linked to the Smart’s How Do We Heal? 2026-2027 exhibition. Held in the museum lobby, the series features gentle movements and contemplative prompts that begin by exploring the various sources of suffering from which we might seek to heal—the physical, emotional, structural, ancestral—then move to methods and practices for healing. This 75-minute class culminates with aromatherapy, breathwork, and contemplative viewing of intentionally selected pieces from the How Do We Heal? collection. Class is led by certified yoga instructor Rhya Moffitt who guides practice with the intention of cultivating inner stillness, awareness, and presence. In collaboration with Arts + Public Life and Spiritual Life.
 Free; RSVP encouraged. Limited number of mats available.
 The first four sessions move through various sources of suffering:
 1. physical (health & illness): October 18th
2. emotional (loss, grief, and renewal): October 25th
 3. structural / collective (displacement): November 1st
 4. ancestral (trauma): November 8th
 The last two sessions get into the how with a focus on:
 5. wholeness, integration, (mind, body, and spirit): November 15th
 6. supportive healing modalities (healing objects): November 22nd
 Rhya Moffitt holds a RYT-500 certification through the Yoga Alliance. She studied at the Samyak Institute of Yoga and Ayurveda in Mysore, India, where she earned certifications to teach yoga, meditation, and breathwork. Her personal practice focuses on the Ashtanga yoga tradition, bija mantra meditations, and mantra chanting. In Chicago, Rhya teaches and programs community yoga events in conversation with the arts and healing work at Haji Healing Salon, Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, and Arts + Public Life.
 Rhya is also a Neubauer Family Fellow, Lindsay Dissertation Completion Fellow, and PhD candidate in the Department of English Language and Literature at UChicago. Her research focuses on Black anxiety, madness, and consciousness. Rhya views her yoga practice and teaching as a necessary wellness intervention that complements her intellectual work.

title: Beer Ghosts: A FoBAB Hangover Brunch
description:
In the 19th century, thousands of young women traveled to Wisconsin’s hop fields to work the annual harvest, helping fuel the rise of America’s brewing industry. Yet their stories and contributions remain largely overlooked.
Join historian and author Jennifer Jordan for the launch of her newest book, Beer Ghosts: In Search of Lost Hops and the Women Who Grew Them, which brings these women and their remarkable histories to life, revealing their contributions to the rise of legendary breweries like Miller, Pabst, and Schlitz.
In conversation with Beer Culture Center founder and Executive Director Liz Garibay, Jennifer will explore the women's labor, lives, and camaraderie, and the lasting mark they left on American beer.
We’ll bring the spirit of those harvest days to Dovetail with hop picker plates inspired by the hearty communal dinners that fueled long days of picking, and live fiddling -- the soundtrack to evenings when the women kicked up their heels and danced after a day in the fields. Naturally, beer drinking will also be involved.
Each Ticket Includes:
.5L of a Dovetail Beer.
A sample of Beer Ghosts Cream Ale, brewed by Water Street Brewery and Old World Wisconsin.
A Hop Pickers Plate by Beard & Belly (note: this plate is created using research from the book and is meat and cheese heavy).
Live fiddling from Brandi Berry of the Old Town School of Folk Music.
A donation to the Beer Culture Center!
We're proud to partner with Dovetail Brewery, University of Chicago Press, The Book Cellar, Beard & Belly, Old World Wisconsin, and Water Street Brewery for this special celebration of women's history, beer, and community.
This event is presented as part of FoBABE, Dovetail's annual celebration of women in beer during Festival of Barrel Aged Beer (FoBAB) weekend.

title: Fatherland
description:
DIRECTED BY
Paweł Pawlikowski
WRITTEN BY
Paweł Pawlikowski,
Henk Handloegten
STARRING
Sandra Hüller,
Hanns Zischler,
August Diehl
FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: Contact Zones: NO
description: In 1988, Chilean dictator General Augusto Pinochet took the remarkable step of holding a national plebiscite to determine whether he would remain in power as an elected official. Shot in the U-matic video format of the era, NO dramatizes how advertising creatives (Ren Saavedra, a composite of several real people played by Gael Garca Bernal) helped design a national campaign to convince Chileans to vote Pinochet out, reframing the negative vote in the most optimistic possible terms. Director Pablo Larran takes seriously the possibility that even though the General was ousted, the neoliberal economy that he ushered in would remain.

description:
Over the last six years, the Chicago Park District has quietly fostered a critical arts incubator for new and emerging composer/performers in the Marquette Park Composer’s Workshop. 9 original suites of music and 7 full-length albums later, Marquette Park Composer's Workshop is ready to engage in deeper and more responsorial suites--here, in communication with the artwork housed in the Vanderpoel Gallery. Select member-composers have toured the gallery and chosen pieces of the fine art housed within which spoke directly to them. Then, pieces were written in response to the works in question--pieces which will be performed live at this gallery concert and which will make use of the Vanderpoel Gallery's fine Steinway pianos.
This concert will be integrated into the Vanderpoel Gallery's celebration of the 169th anniversary of John Vanderpoel's birthday. Do come for an evening of original musical compositions housed in the gallery holding the work which inspired them!

Romare Bearden,

A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

title: Exhibition Opening Program: Hollywood on Trial: The Blacklist and the Red Scare
description:
In October 1947, the House Un-American Activities Committee turned its attention to Hollywood, calling actors, writers, directors, and producers to testify about alleged Communist influence in the film industry. What followed transformed careers, divided Hollywood, and ushered in an era in which political suspicion could determine who was allowed to work.
Join us for the opening program of Blacklist: The Hollywood Red Scare and a conversation exploring how the blacklist took hold, why Hollywood became a political battleground, and what happened to the people and industry caught in its path.
Thomas Doherty, cultural historian, Brandeis University professor, and author of Show Trial: Hollywood, HUAC, and the Birth of the Blacklist, joins Ellie Gettinger, who brings the exhibition’s curatorial and historical perspective. Film critic and cultural commentator Richard Roeper moderates a conversation examining the 1947 HUAC hearings, the Hollywood Ten, the forces that sustained the blacklist, and how this period reshaped American film and culture.
Presented in conjunction with Blacklist: The Hollywood Red Scare, on view at Illinois Holocaust Museum & Education Center November 1, 2026 through April 11, 2027.
Reservations are required. Free to the public.

title: Nois Quartet with Diana Leviton Gondek
description:
Think you know what a saxophone quartet sounds like? ~Nois is here to change your mind.
Hailed by Musical America as “the American saxophone quartet du jour,” Chicago’s ~Nois Quartet celebrates its 10th season doing what it does best: pushing four saxophones into places you never expected them to go.
For their Rendezvous Arts debut, ~Nois brings a program as adventurous and versatile as the instrument itself. Arturo Márquez’s Danzón No. 5 and Paquito d’Rivera’s Wapango bring irresistible rhythmic energy, while a wonderfully unexpected Schumann arrangement reveals an entirely different side of the quartet.
From there, we move firmly into the music of today, with works by Sarah Kirkland Snider, Emma O’Halloran, Augusta Read Thomas, Shelley Washington, and Travis Laplante. These are composers writing with completely different voices, giving ~Nois the chance to move from intimate and atmospheric to playful, explosive, and exhilarating.
Over the past decade, the quartet has premiered more than 120 new works and built a national reputation as an ensemble redefining what the saxophone quartet can be.
Now we get to experience them up close.
Four saxophones. Ten years together. One seriously unexpected hour of music.
Our featured visual artist for this program is Diana Leviton Gondek, a Chicago artist whose work begins with stories.
Drawing from moments and experiences in her own life, Diana creates paintings that invite each viewer to discover their own meaning within them. Her background in watercolor remains an important influence, but her work has evolved to incorporate thin layers of oil and mixed media, creating richly layered pieces that feel personal, expressive, and entirely individual.
Diana studied Fine Arts before becoming an Art Director at Northwestern University and later returning to her own studio practice. Her work has been exhibited throughout Chicago, across the United States, and internationally, and can be found in the permanent collection of the Chicago History Museum.
She has also created public and commissioned work for organizations including Special Olympics, and her art has been featured in numerous exhibitions, publications, and television segments.
Like the music of ~Nois, Diana’s work reminds us how much can happen when familiar forms are seen, heard, and experienced in a completely new way.

For 31 years, the NYC-based and critically acclaimed Slackers have been touring the world with their blend of Ska, Reggae, and Soul.

title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.

title: All Eight
description:
It’s 2011 in Upstate New York, and nine freshmen women sit in a boat together every morning at 6am on their collegiate rowing team, competing with each other up for the fastest times, lowest body weights, and most influential seats, until race day when they are asked to put it all aside and row together as comrades in one boat. Crew would be chaotic enough on its own, but off the water, their coach shows up at their parties and drinks with them, makes lewd comments about their bodies, and is allegedly sleeping with one of them. So when one rower secretly rats him out for allegedly sleeping with a student and is seemingly rewarded with the best seat in the boat when he’s fired, her motives come into question– as does her position of privilege on the team.
Over the course of their freshman year, All Eight examines how the world of collegiate sports drives these young women with varied power to fight to win– races, love, power– at the expense of even each other.

title: Hayward- A World Premiere by Netta Walker
description:
As part of our 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father’s funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter’s love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O’Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Hayward will be presented at Steppenwolf’s 1700 Theater

description:
November 15 | Presented in partnership with Jupiter Magazine, this special presentation celebrates the pioneering cinematic work of Burkinabè filmmaker Fanta Régina Nacro. The program features an illustrated lecture by Afi Venessa Appiah, an NYU Cinema Studies scholar and creator of Emblematic Elusions, a publication series exploring eroticism, gender, and subversive visual culture in African cinemas. The lecture is followed by screenings of three landmark films by Nacro: PUK NINI (1996), LE TRUC DE KONATÉ (1998), and BINTOU (2001), offering an introduction to one of African cinema’s most significant filmmakers.

title: Sawyer Avenue, Sunday Afternoon
description:
DIRECTED BY
Bill Morrison
October 12, 2025: masked and unidentified agents from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) seize a man on a residential street in Chicago without a warrant. His neighbors – some still wearing their bathrobes – try to stop the vehicle taking him from leaving their neighborhood. In the vein of the Oscar-nominated Incident, which recounted the killing of a man by the police, and employing an approach akin to forensic journalism, Bill Morrison dissects and reconstructs this moment of struggle using a skillful montage of footage from police body cameras as well as the mobile phones wielded by those trying to intervene. From inside the car, Sawyer Avenue, Sunday Afternoon viscerally conveys the chilling experience of the man’s illegal arrest and the helplessness of all those witnessing the violence of a state consumed by uncontrollable, security-driven nationalism. - Émilie Bujès, Visions du Réel, artistic director
Post-screening panel with organizers Rey Wences, Senior Director of Deportation Defense at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights (ICIRR); Antonio Gutierrez, co-founder of Organized Communities Against Deportations (OCAD); and Gabriel Paez, a teacher and featured neighbor in Sawyer Avenue, Sunday Afternoon. The panel will be moderated by María Inés Zamudio, reporter and co-producer of the film.
Following the screening and panel, join us in the Music Box Lounge and Garden where Invisible Institute will provide an opportunity for the audience to share their thoughts about the film and their experience with rapid response to ICE efforts in Chicago, and share resources for how to get involved with Latino Union.

title: The Fabulous Thunderbirds
address: 105 East Main Street, Saint Charles, IL, 60174
description:
For over 30 years, The Fabulous Thunderbirds have been the quintessential American band. The group’s distinctive and powerful sound, influenced by a diversity of musical styles, manifested itself into a unique musical hybrid via such barnburners as “Tuff Enuff” and “Wrap It Up”. Co-founder Kim Wilson, the sole original member, still spearheads the group as it evolves into its newest incarnation. The thread throughout the T-Birds career has been the respect the group commanded for its peerless musicianship and devotion to the sounds of blues, R & B and rock ‘n roll. In fact, Muddy Waters called Wilson his favorite harmonica player and vocalist. “Muddy Waters was very good to me,” Wilson says. “He almost adopted me. I’ll never forget him.” The Fabulous Thunderbirds reached a commercial peak with the album, “Tuff Enuff”. The single of the same title as well as the singles “Wrap It Up” and “Look At That”, all went top 40. The song, “Tuff Enuff” was featured in the film “Gung Ho” starring Michael Keaton. The Band: Kim Wilson (lead vocals, harmonica), Johnny Moeller (guitar), Bob Welsh (piano/guitar), Rudy Albin (drums), Steve Kirsty (bass)

title: BLACK HARVEST CLOSING NIGHT: SOLOMON NORTHUP’S ODYSSEY
location: The School of the Art Institute of Chicago's Gene Siskel Film Center
description:
November 15 | Adapted from Solomon Northup’s landmark 1853 autobiography Twelve Years a Slave, Gordon Parks’ powerful historical drama follows Northup, a free Black musician from Saratoga, New York, who is deceived, kidnapped, and sold into chattel slavery in 1841. Stripped of his freedom, family, and identity, Northup endures twelve years of unimaginable brutality while refusing to surrender his dignity, artistry, or hope. One of Parks’ most ambitious cinematic achievements, SOLOMON NORTHUP’S ODYSSEY stands as a vital work of Black film history and a profound meditation on survival, resistance, and the enduring pursuit of freedom. Film preservation organization IndieCollect scanned the original camera negative and did extensive color correction in consultation with DP Hiro Narita. Black Harvest is honored to present the film as the festival’s Closing Night presentation.
New 4K Restoration by IndieCollect
Ticket includes one free beer, wine, or non-alcoholic beverage.

Celebrating its 32nd year in 2026, the Black Harvest Film Festival is Chicago’s annual showcase for Black film across the diaspora. Born from an urgent need to celebrate the Black experience, the Black Harvest Film Festival unites filmmakers and audiences to showcase the power of Black cinema. This annual festival highlights emerging and established talents and historical narratives, enriching the landscape of Black culture. The festival curates both short and feature length films, proudly presenting influential auteurs and emerging filmmakers of color side by side.
The film festival will be held at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center November 6–15, 2026.

title: Manchester Orchestra - I'm Like a Virgin Losing a Child 20th Anniversary Tour
description:
Following their acclaimed 2021 album The Million Masks of God, Manchester Orchestra is back with The Valley of Vision, a brand new project that takes on the weighty themes of adulthood, faith and redemption through a wealth of fresh new sounds and textures. But if The Million Masks of God served as a cry for help - exploring a man’s encounter with the angel of death, inspired by frontman and songwriter Andy Hull’s reflections on grief as well as the battle with cancer faced by guitarist Robert McDowell’s father - The Valley of Vision offers a collective, cathartic expression of gratitude. Throughout the 27-minute album, you can almost feel the band take a giant exhale and then put its arms around you.
Continuing to push themselves into fascinating and immersive creative realms with each release has always been the mantra for Manchester Orchestra, and The Valley of Vision finds the band reinvigorated once again. Across the six-song salvo and VR film out March 10th, the band conjures a story that is further illuminated through a cinematic experience by writer-director Isaac Deitz, created with 3D-computed radiography technology.
Hull started writing and recording The Valley of Vision in the summer of 2021, sparking a spontaneous and new approach to releasing his band's music. “Making this was an exciting idea of what the future could be for us in terms of how we create.”
Hull was inspired to begin writing the record while rummaging around in his suitcase looking for his lyric notebook and instead found The Valley of Vision, a 1975 book of old Puritan prayers his mom had given to him the previous Christmas. “I realized it should be our title too, because to me, it meant you can’t see the forest for the trees, but you’re recognizing you’re in the valley, and you can eventually get out,” he says.
Sonically, those energies evoke places Manchester Orchestra has visited on prior albums without ever really setting up a permanent home. In fact, there’s not much guitar at all on The Valley of Vision, and Andy Prince’s bass operates in sub-synth frequencies rarely utilized before. In other instances, drum parts by Tim Very were excised from one song and repurposed in other places they weren’t originally intended to go. The whole feeling is one of peacefulness, even zen — perhaps because recording sessions at a converted manor in Muscle Shoals, Ala., were “almost a complete abandonment of all the instruments we’re used to using,” Hull says.
“None of these songs were written with the band being in the same room in a live setting,” he continues. “They were really like science experiments that started from the bottom and were added to gradually over time, to catch the vibe of each one.”
Opener “Capital Karma” and “Quietly” are both songs Hull composed via his idiosyncratic self-taught methods on piano, which involve him physically writing notes on the keys to remind himself what he’s actually playing. “The Way” is a beautifully atmospheric, piano-and-beats-powered ballad, which Hull credits Million Masks producers Ethan Gruska and Catherine Marks with helping him shape after struggling for years with how to present it.
Elsewhere, the uplifting “Lose You Again” is the first Manchester Orchestra song in a long time that could be played with acoustic guitars around a campfire, while “Letting Go” threads wisps of emotive, effects-drenched vocals through gorgeous shimmers of sound.
“We decided, let’s live in that feeling,” Hull says. “When we tried to add anything that took us out of it, it started to feel contrived and forced. We try to listen to our instincts when it comes to that. As far as just going for some of the sounds, we’re intrigued by doing things the wrong way or attempting things we haven’t done before and getting inspired by them.”

THE SLACKERS
For 31 years, the NYC-based and critically acclaimed Slackers have been touring the world with their blend of Ska, Reggae, and Soul.
Since 1991, the Slackers have released fifteen albums and countless singles, while their 1000s of live performances feed their fans with energetic sets of ecstatic music.
The press state that the Slackers are “the best ska band in the world” (Rude International), “the pick of the US crop” (Metal Hammer), “the sound of New York’ (New York Times), “is about as close to perfect as it gets” (Ink 19), and “one of the best bands in the United States” (axs.com).
In April 2022, The Slackers released a new album, “Don’t Let The Sunlight Fool Ya” (Pirates Press) which quickly shot to the top of the US billboard charts. This is the first time that a Slackers’ album has charted! Ironically after 30 years as a band, this qualified them as a Billboard ‘new artist.’ The Washington Post noted that the Slackers “remain at the top of their game.”
The chart topping performance of “Don’t Let The Sunlight Fool Ya” capped a 2 year comeback of the Slackers. When Covid stopped live shows in 2020, the Slackers pivoted to livestreams and made 5 full band concerts that were broadcast internationally. After the shows, they stayed in the studio and recorded the tunes that became Sunlight.
Returning to live gigging in the 2nd half of 2021, the band celebrated their 30th anniversary with 30 shows across the United States and Canada.
In 2022, the Slackers have 90 shows booked in the United States, Canada, UK, and Europe. At 31 years old, the band has been renewed and is looking to grow their cult following into its 4th decade.

title: SOUTHALL w/ MARFA
description:
Read Southall calls his band’s new self-titled album “the gasoline for the love machine” — 11 raw, loud songs blending country, rock & roll, Red Dirt grit, and hints of metal and soul. It’s the first release under their new name, Southall, marking a shift from a frontman-led project to a true band effort, with every member contributing songs and ideas.
“It’s different people with different influences making music together,” says Southall. “I’ve always believed in these guys, and now fans can hear that too.”
Produced by Eddie Spear (Zach Bryan’s American Heartbreak) and recorded at Leon Russell’s Church Studio in Tulsa, the album roars with collaborative energy. Drummer Reid Barber adds metal urgency, bassist Jeremee Knipp grounds it, Braxton Curliss brings texture on keys, and guitarists John Tyler Perry and Ryan Wellman push sonic boundaries — all tied together by Southall’s gritty vocals.
The lead single “Scared Money,” written by Barber, channels Stonesy swagger and blue-collar drive. “I walked out of class, straight to the patch,” Southall sings — a nod to his Oklahoma roots. Tracks like “Out Alive” and “By Surprise” explore modern anxieties and life’s bigger questions with powerful riffs and thoughtful lyrics.
With over 130 million streams and a growing national presence, Southall isn’t just a band — it’s a movement built on hard work, honesty, and the drive to represent where they’re from.

Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: Rockin’ in the Park
description:
Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.
Concerts run from 7–10 PM. Admission is free. Outside food and coolers are prohibited. Parking is available at the Parkway Bank Park parking garage and is free with validation from any Parkway Bank Park venue.
2026 Lineup
Thursday, July 9: New World Men*
A powerful tribute to Rush, bringing the spirit, precision, and intensity of the legendary band’s live shows to the stage.
Thursday, July 16: Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press*
Beloved Chicago party band Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press delivers huge harmonies, sharp musicianship, and a wildly fun setlist built for singing, dancing, and staying out later than planned.
Thursday, July 23: Departure*
Departure recreates the look, sound, and feel of Journey, packing their set with high-energy performances of the band’s biggest hits.
Thursday, July 30: Live the Who*
Direct from Detroit, Live the Who pays tribute to The Who’s explosive 1968–1974 era with the sound, look, and raw energy of the iconic rock band.
Friday, July 31: 24K Magic / George Michael Reborn
24K Magic brings the Bruno Mars party with slick choreography, bold style, and hit after hit. George Michael Reborn keeps the night moving with the sound, moves, and charisma of George Michael and Wham!
Thursday, August 6: Brooklyn Charmers*
Brooklyn Charmers bring fresh energy and serious precision to the music of Steely Dan, honoring the band’s smooth hooks, sharp lyrics, and unmistakable sound.
Thursday, August 13: Echoes of Pompeii*
This 10-piece Pink Floyd tribute takes audiences through every era of the band’s catalog, from the early Syd Barrett days to later classics.
Thursday, August 20: Southern Accents*
Southern Accents recreates the music, style, and sound of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers with contagious energy and serious attention to detail.
Thursday, August 27: No Quarter*
No Quarter delivers the full sound, power, and spirit of Led Zeppelin with a tribute show built for fans who want more than just the hits.
Friday, August 28: Bee Gees Gold / The Wayouts
Bee Gees Gold recreates the harmonies, look, and sound of the Bee Gees, from early favorites to disco-era classics. The Wayouts open up the garage with a high-energy tribute to 1960s rock.
Thursday, September 3: Rhythm of the Rocketman*
Rhythm of the Rocketman celebrates Elton John with a high-energy tribute packed with beloved hits like “Rocket Man,” “Tiny Dancer,” “Your Song,” and “Bennie and the Jets.”

title: INTERMISSIONS: FRANÇOIS CHAIGNAUD & AYMERIC HAINAUX
location: The Renaissance Society, Cobb Lecture Hall, 4th Floor
description:
A tour de force of rhythm, sound, and movement, Mirlitons is a visceral performance by choreographer François Chaignaud and musician Aymeric Hainaux. As two voices and two bodies meet in this space, converging on a central stage, their collaboration melds beatboxing, song, and dance. Performed to date across Europe in wide-ranging venues, from Brussels to Paris to Vienna, Mirlitons now arrives in Chicago. At the Renaissance Society, where it appears as part of the Intermissions series, Chaignaud and Hainaux’s performance surges to life with a vivid intensity in this reverberant room under the high vaulted ceiling.
 In Chaignaud’s words: “The scene is an arena. Two masked bodies, martial, unrecognizable, humble, and rattling. Microphones, loudspeakers, risers, bells, shoes. A ritual of presentations, a confrontation, a knot, a denouement. A total saturation of frequencies and muscles: a therapy through excess. Bodies and sounds torn between the melancholy of vanished rituals and the aggressiveness of actuality. Lips and heels in search of a forgotten code. A gracious and enduring duel of beatbox and percussions: a wall, a halo, an ancient world lost in the face of toxic perspiration, buried in the two fighters.”
 Curated by Karsten Lund with Michael Harrison.
 Launched in 2017, Intermissions is an ongoing programming series devoted to performance and other inventive time based works, staged in the Renaissance Society’s empty gallery in between exhibitions. This recurring platform features two artists every year, supporting a wide variety of live projects.
 Mirlitons is supported by FUSED, a program of Villa Albertine and Albertine Foundation.

title: Michael Vallera, Stephen Holliger
description:
Michael Vallera (b. 1984) is a Chicago-based musician and visual artist who uses the guitar and electronics to explore stasis, texture, and an overall sense of intimate sonic space. His visual work employs photographic images and collage to communicate similar themes, highlighting aspects of internal symmetry and balance.
In 2010, he received his MFA from The School of the Art Institute of Chicago with a concentration in Sound, with a particular focus on studio techniques related to long-form composition and drone music. Structures of repetition and dissonance are staples of his sound-based practice, influenced equally by principles of minimalism and the unique history of experimental guitar musics, drawing critical comparison of his work to the likes of Keith Rowe and Christian Fennesz.
He has collaborated through performance and recording with artists such as Lee Ranaldo, Loren Connors, Alan Licht, Doug McCombs, Elliott Sharp, and Steve Hauschildt. He performs as Cleared with percussionist Steven Hess and as Maar with visual artist and musician Joseph Clayton Mills.
//
Stephen Holliger's work occupies the space between composition, sound art, and experimental ambient music. His practice draws from modular synthesis, guitar, pedal steel, tape manipulation, field recordings, and live looping. Long-form tones and slowly changing textures create environments in which small sounds can become significant: a voice, a room, the resonance of metal, the trace of an instrument, or the imperfect remains of an old recording. The work is interested in memory as material — not as a fixed archive, but as something continuously altered by time.

title: 2nd Set With Andy Brown Quartet
description:
Bandleader Andy Brown has been one of the busiest guitarists in Chicago over the last two decades, leading his own bands and backing visiting jazz stars all over the city, as well traveling nationally and internationally with a variety of groups. He specializes in what he calls “old-school jazz guitar.”
The Andy Brown Quartet brings together four of the finest jazz musicians on the Chicago scene. Featuring Andy on guitar, Jeremy Kahn on piano, Joe Policastro on bass and Phil Gratteau on drums, this quartet combines the member’s shared musical inspirations and presents a lyrical and hard-swinging working band that has delighted audiences and critics alike. As a group they have performed weekly at Andy’s Jazz Club since 2012. Their Delmark records release Direct Call received 4 stars in Downbeat Magazine and was selected as one of the magazine’s Albums of the Year. Their latest recording is the 2023 release Good Atmosphere.
In a performance review the Chicago Tribune’s jazz critic wrote: “Inspiring music-making isn’t necessarily loud, aggressive, self-aggrandizing or heavily promoted. Consider what happens every Sunday night at Andy’s Jazz Club, where the superb but serenely understated Chicago guitarist Andy Brown leads a quartet. Like him, his bandmates speak softly but poetically. Brown’s pastel tones, softly stated melody lines and delicately rolled chords conveyed remarkable intimacy.”

title: Heavens To Betsy / NO MEN
description: Doors: 8PM / Show: 9PM / 21+More than three decades after they founded heavens to betsy, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer still have something important to say.Just as riot grrrl punk rock and feminism pushed for inclusivity, bodily autonomy, and gender equality in the early-to-mid 90s, there is arguably an even greater need for the scene to rematerialize in an age where womens voting rights and healthcare access are under siege, as is the safety of any marginalized community. Now, the longtime friends and musicians have answered the call by reuniting as heavens to betsy, the DIY punk project they famously founded back in the riot grrrl halcyon days, among like-minded Olympia artists in Bikini Kill, Team Dresch, and Bratmobile.Corin and Tracy first met growing up in Eugene, Oregon, bonding over a shared love of music before forming heavens to betsy after Corins move to Olympia and immersion in the burgeoning riot grrrl scene. Their first performance came at the International Pop Underground conventions landmark Girl Night, where the fledgling duo played for an audience that included members of Fugazi, Bikini Kill, Bratmobile, and Calamity Jane. Buoyed by the support of their peers, heavens to betsy quickly became one of the defining voices of a movement that reshaped punk rock and feminist culture alike.Between 1992 and 1994, heavens to betsy released three 7 records and their now-classic full-length, Calculated, via Kill Rock Stars. Powered by Corin Tuckers unmistakable howl and Tracy Sawyers driving musicianship, their songs tackled subjects rarely addressed in punk at the time: rape culture, body image, queerness, friendship, and intersectional politics. Just as importantly, heavens to betsy became a space for Corin and Tracy to process their own experiences while giving other women a place to unpack theirs, transforming personal rage andvulnerability into songs that helped define a generation of punk.

detected her daughter’s singing abilities and enrolled the toddler in piano classes 
and encouraged her as a teenager to be an active member of the choir at the 
family’s place of worship. But it was not until the 1990s that Laretha began to 
cultivate a personal relationship with Blues music.
Emerging 
as one of the premiere female Blues vocalists in the City of Chicago in the 
late 1990s, Laretha has performed at such legendary Blues hotspots as The 
Kingston Mines, BLUES on Halsted and since 2010 is a spectacular presence here 
at BLUE CHICAGO.
Her 
debut album – Dance the Blues Away – is an eclectic mix of traditional Blues 
infused with remnants of contemporary R&B and Soul. The album reveals 
Laretha’s reverence for conventional Blues music while flaunting her fluent 
transition into contemporary R & B and Soul.
According 
to Ms. Weathersby, “the power of Blues music lies in its ability to relate to 
each and every member of the human race. People of all different backgrounds 
can connect with the universal concepts of love, triumph and tribulation, which 
are the very elements upon which Blues music is based. I consider it an honor 
and joy to incorporate that human element into my live performances and it is 
with passion and humility that I accept the honor and challenge of preserving 
Blues music for future generations.”
www.LarethaWeathersby.com

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Pierre Bismuth: Love Bless America
location: Neubauer Collegium for Culture and Society
description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. The film traces the magic and workaday practice of “inspiration,” taking the traditions of religious music as a point of departure for a multi-layered reflection on love, music, and the divine. In addition to this new film, Bismuth will present a series of digital images resembling American flags emblazoned with lyrics from the hymn.
 Curated by Dieter Roelstraete.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is free and open to the public. Gallery hours: M–F, 9–4.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is supported by the Neubauer Family Foundation and the Brenda Mulmed Shapiro Fund. Additional support for this exhibition was provided by Bernard Friedman, the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, and the France Chicago Center at the University of Chicago.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

This fun, hands-on program welcomes families to discover the life and work of Jones while exploring the question “Whose murals get saved?” Together, participants will enjoy a guided mini‑mural activity inspired by Jones’s vibrant style, featuring bold colors and African print designs. It’s an engaging, creative experience for all ages, perfect for families who love to learn, make art, and explore Chicago’s cultural stories.
Presented as part of the Renaissance Project, this event invites participants to actively engage with the rich and often untold stories of Black history and heritage at Chicago Public Library.
This program is made possible with support from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to the Chicago Public Library Foundation.

title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
description:
DIRECTED BY
David Greaves,
Liani Greaves,
William Greaves
WRITTEN BY
William Greaves
STARRING
Romare Bearden,
Arna Bontemps,
Ida Mae Cullen
A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: CEST Workshop: Xenia Cherkaev
description:
Current Ethnography and Social Theory Workshop on Monday, November 16, 4:30-6:00pm (Please note the date change)
 “Householding the City: Indeterminate Property as a Theory of Governance”
 Presenter: Xenia Cherkaev, Senior Research Fellow, Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology and Economic Experimentation
 Discussant: Hazal Corak, PhD Candidate, Anthropology
 Location: Haskell Hall 315 (please note the room change)
 Abstract: What does it mean for bureaucrats to run their municipalities as households? People in provincial Russian towns complain about local officials not doing enough to be good khoziaistvenniks. Etymologically, the term derives from khoziaistvo, “household.” Practically, it means being concerned with substantivist local affairs (roads, kindergartens, animal control) and deftly maneuvering around laws and rules to keep things running. We social scientists have two common idioms of the “household” as public governance: as paternalist corporate structures and as self-interested clientelism. The khoziaistvennik instead asks us to think in the non-transactional logics of householding. Historically, the term originates as a role in the Soviet economy: a corporate structure built on explicitly indeterminate property relations and conceptualized as a giant “socialist household” (sotstialisticheskoe khoziastvo), de facto reliant on people skirting its rules to redistribute materials through their personal ties. This was the khoziaistvennik’s task. The publicly celebrated ethic of mutual aid enlivened and justified it. Outlining this history, I put Soviet theories of property into conversation with anthropological theories of clientelism, exchange, and householding to ask what is expected of khoziaistvenniks today, now that the socialist household is gone. Specifically, I ask about the khoziaistvennik’s curiously apolitical nature.
 For a copy of the pre-circulated paper, please contact the workshop coordinators, Helena Ratté (ratte@uchicago.edu) and/or Hanqi Yang (hanqiy@uchicago.edu).
 Food and refreshments will be available during the workshop. If you have any accommodation needs (e.g., dietary restrictions, accessibility considerations), or any questions, please do not hesitate to reach out to the workshop coordinators.

title: Samantha Iyer—Agrarian Superpower: Food, Development, and the Global Ascendancy of the United States
location: Social Science Research Building, John Hope Franklin Room (Room 224)
description:
A paper will be circulated to all registered participants approximately one week before the event.
 The United States’ superpower status is often associated with its industrial, financial, and military might. Yet its global power after the Second World War hinged in part on something often seen as backward: agriculture. In contrast to Britain, the predominant global power of the nineteenth century, which depended on its current and former colonies for food and raw materials, the United States produced vast agricultural surpluses. During the 1950s, an era of decolonization and rising Cold War competition, the United States became the dominant exporter of food staples to industrializing nations in the Third World through its massive food aid program.
 Through the lens of food and agriculture, this book offers new ways to understand the roots of the post–Second World War global order and the US position in it. Samantha Iyer traces how two former British territories and agricultural competitors of the United States, India and Egypt, became two of the largest importers of US food aid. She investigates the origins and consequences of the US-centric postwar food regime by examining changes in the production, distribution, and consumption of agricultural surpluses from the late nineteenth century to the early 1970s. Bringing together life in villages, towns, and cities with national, imperial, and international affairs, Iyer demonstrates that food aid was the expression of a changed political, economic, and ecological world that the United States did not create alone. Drawing on sources in Arabic, French, Urdu, and English, Agrarian Superpower is a groundbreaking comparative history of food, agriculture, and development.

title: Rockin’ in the Park
description:
Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.
Concerts run from 7–10 PM. Admission is free. Outside food and coolers are prohibited. Parking is available at the Parkway Bank Park parking garage and is free with validation from any Parkway Bank Park venue.
2026 Lineup
Thursday, July 9: New World Men*
A powerful tribute to Rush, bringing the spirit, precision, and intensity of the legendary band’s live shows to the stage.
Thursday, July 16: Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press*
Beloved Chicago party band Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press delivers huge harmonies, sharp musicianship, and a wildly fun setlist built for singing, dancing, and staying out later than planned.
Thursday, July 23: Departure*
Departure recreates the look, sound, and feel of Journey, packing their set with high-energy performances of the band’s biggest hits.
Thursday, July 30: Live the Who*
Direct from Detroit, Live the Who pays tribute to The Who’s explosive 1968–1974 era with the sound, look, and raw energy of the iconic rock band.
Friday, July 31: 24K Magic / George Michael Reborn
24K Magic brings the Bruno Mars party with slick choreography, bold style, and hit after hit. George Michael Reborn keeps the night moving with the sound, moves, and charisma of George Michael and Wham!
Thursday, August 6: Brooklyn Charmers*
Brooklyn Charmers bring fresh energy and serious precision to the music of Steely Dan, honoring the band’s smooth hooks, sharp lyrics, and unmistakable sound.
Thursday, August 13: Echoes of Pompeii*
This 10-piece Pink Floyd tribute takes audiences through every era of the band’s catalog, from the early Syd Barrett days to later classics.
Thursday, August 20: Southern Accents*
Southern Accents recreates the music, style, and sound of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers with contagious energy and serious attention to detail.
Thursday, August 27: No Quarter*
No Quarter delivers the full sound, power, and spirit of Led Zeppelin with a tribute show built for fans who want more than just the hits.
Friday, August 28: Bee Gees Gold / The Wayouts
Bee Gees Gold recreates the harmonies, look, and sound of the Bee Gees, from early favorites to disco-era classics. The Wayouts open up the garage with a high-energy tribute to 1960s rock.
Thursday, September 3: Rhythm of the Rocketman*
Rhythm of the Rocketman celebrates Elton John with a high-energy tribute packed with beloved hits like “Rocket Man,” “Tiny Dancer,” “Your Song,” and “Bennie and the Jets.”

And all of this is concentrated into two days of show floor time to maximize exhibitor and visitor time.

title: Hank Garrett
description:
Hank Garrett at Subterranean on November 16
Since 1994, Subterranean has been a cornerstone of the Wicker Park live music & nightlife scene. Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: Laura Anglade
description:
Brooklyn based Jazz chanteuse Laura Anglade is originally from the village of Brousse-le-Château in the south of France, though she grew up in the US and spent several years living in Canada. Laura’s performances are a reflection of her roots: rich in simplicity, an appreciation for the past and finding wonder in ordinary moments. Laura brings clarity and depth to interpretations shaped by the legendary voices of Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald, Shirley Horn, Carmen McRae, Michel Legrand and Barbra Streisand, among others. Her 2022 release “Venez Donc Chez Moi” earned a Juno nomination and in 2023 she was awarded the Prix Opus for Jazz Concert of the Year.
An international touring artist, Laura has headlined jazz festivals across the US, Canada, Mexico, UK and Europe, captivating audiences through her innate storytelling. Her conversational style bridges the gap between singer and listener, making each performance intimate and personal. Her artistry has brought her to renowned stages including Paris L’ Olympia, London’s Royal Festival Hall, New York's Town Hall, and a regular at the Festival International de Jazz de Montréal. She has also toured in support of acclaimed artists like Melody Gardot and Gregory Porter.
Laura’s third album, “Get Out of Town” (Nettwerk Music Group), was released on May 23, 2025 to tremendous praise and she has seen her audience grow exponentially. Laura was featured on Stephen Colbert's “Late Show Me Music” series, where she performed her version of the beloved Rodgers & Hart standard, “Manhattan ”. She continues to tour and will be performing in January 2026 at Winter Jazz Fest in New York City.

location: Harris Theater for Music and Dance
description:
How to Subscribe to the Beyond the Aria?
Were you a 25/26 BTA Subscriber? Click here to login + renew your seats.
Want to subscribe to BTA? Click here to choose a general admission, Choral Riser package.
There is currently a waiting list for Table Seating Subscriptions. Please contact Madison Jones, Manager of Donor Events and Communications, to be placed on the waiting list.
Presented in partnership with Lyric Opera of Chicago, the Harris Theater's Beyond the Aria series pairs some of the most celebrated voices in opera today with developing artists from the Patrick G. and Shirley W. Ryan Opera Center. Each concert is enjoyed cabaret-style with special one-night-only programs performed on the iconic Pritzker Pavilion stage.
Soprano Ying Fang, celebrated with “a voice that can stop time” (Financial Times), and baritone Ian Rucker return to the BTA stage for the second installment of the series this season. They are joined by Series Artistic Director Craig Terry and mezzo-soprano Camille Robles, who makes her BTA debut.
Artist Lineup
Ying Fang, soprano
Ian Rucker, baritone
Camille Robles, mezzo-soprano
Craig Terry, piano
About Lyric Opera of Chicago
Lyric Opera of Chicago is committed to redefining what it means to experience great opera. The company is driven to deliver consistently excellent artistry through innovative, relevant, celebratory programming that engages and energizes new and traditional audiences.
Under the leadership of General Director, President & CEO Anthony Freud, Music Director Enrique Mazzola, and Special Projects Advisor Renée Fleming, Lyric is dedicated to reflecting, and drawing strength from, the diversity of Chicago. Lyric offers, through innovation, collaboration, and evolving learning opportunities, ever-more exciting, accessible, and thought-provoking audience and community experiences. We also stand committed to training the artists of the future, through The Patrick G. and Shirley W. Ryan Opera Center; and to becoming increasingly diverse across our audiences, staff, programming, and artists—magnifying the welcoming pull of our art form, our company, and our city.
Through the timeless power of voice, the splendor of a great orchestra and chorus, theater, dance, design, and truly magnificent stagecraft, Lyric is devoted to immersing audiences in worlds both familiar and unexpected, creating shared experiences that resonate long after the curtain comes down.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.
 Related Programming
 Opening Celebration, Cochrane-Woods Art Center, Wednesday, October 21, 6:00 PM

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Pierre Bismuth: Love Bless America
location: Neubauer Collegium for Culture and Society
description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. The film traces the magic and workaday practice of “inspiration,” taking the traditions of religious music as a point of departure for a multi-layered reflection on love, music, and the divine. In addition to this new film, Bismuth will present a series of digital images resembling American flags emblazoned with lyrics from the hymn.
 Curated by Dieter Roelstraete.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is free and open to the public. Gallery hours: M–F, 9–4.
 The Neubauer Collegium Gallery is supported by the Neubauer Family Foundation and the Brenda Mulmed Shapiro Fund. Additional support for this exhibition was provided by Bernard Friedman, the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, and the France Chicago Center at the University of Chicago.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.
