title: Guided Tour of the Newberry
description:
In 1893, the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Chicago, Grover Cleveland started his second non-consecutive term as president, and the Newberry building opened to the public. On this guided tour, you’ll learn about the history behind the founding of the Newberry. You’ll also discover all the ways you can engage with the library today.
Founded in 1887, the Newberry had three temporary locations before moving into its permanent home across from Washington Square Park in 1893.
The library was designed by architect Henry Ives Cobb, with input from Newberry head librarian William Frederick Poole. Cobb envisioned a grand edifice on par with the civic landmarks of Europe; Poole favored a more modest design that would facilitate user access to books and other resources. In the end, they compromised. The Newberry is a blend of their competing visions.
Aerial photograph of the Newberry, 2022
Architectural detail on the Newberry's facade
A quiet study space on the Newberry's third floor
Over the years, the Newberry has grown and evolved, notably with the addition of a climate-controlled stacks building in the early 1980s and a renovation that updated spaces and restored original architectural details on the library’s first floor in 2018.
You’ll get a healthy dose of history on this tour. But you’ll also get to see the Newberry in action in the present. Tens of thousands of people visit the Newberry every year, and there are many ways that we make the library’s collections, programs, and resources accessible and relevant to them.
This tour is free, and no advance registration is required. We'll meet in the lobby of the Newberry and begin the tour from there.

title: Brown Bag Lecture with Dr. Aurore Motte, Université de Liège
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC), La Salle Banks Room
description:
The Making of Texts in Ancient Egypt
 What can a manuscript teach us even before we read its contents? Far more than simply a medium for text, a manuscript preserves traces of its creation, its use and those who produced it. Through the study of the Books of the Dead, scientific texts, literary works and accounting records, this lecture invites you to discover the techniques, skills, and choices that lie behind the production of these texts. Writing medium, inks, layout, corrections, marginalia and other paratextual marks reveal a history that is often hidden: that of the scribes and the creation of written texts in the time of the pharaohs.
 Aurore Motte is currently a postdoctoral researcher of the National Fund for Scientific Research (Belgium), working in the Ancient Worlds research unit, Department of Antiquity Sciences, Faculty of Philosophy and Letters at the University of Liège. Her research interests focus on ancient Egyptian (icono)texts, which includes textual criticism, textual transmission, (socio)pragmatics, scribal practices, paratextual studies, and the materiality of writing.

title: IBD Seminar| Lessons from single molecule (and single photons)
location: Gordon Center for Integrative Science, Room W301
description:
Speaker: Steve Presse, Ph.D.
 Department of Physics, Arizona State University
 In this talk, I take a broad perspective on the lessons we have learned over the past three decades
 by interrogating the dynamics of single molecules. I reflect on the fundamentally stochastic picture of life that has emerged as statistical physics has come alive through optical tweezers, single-molecule fluorescence, patch-clamp recordings, and related experimental techniques. I will discuss the Presse lab’s role in contributing a mathematical language based on stochastic differential equations, Bayesian inference, and Bayesian nonparametrics, well suited to interpreting stochastic dynamical observations from experimental output. As time allows, I will discuss single molecule-single photon tracking of the assembly of aerolysin and the degree to which stress response is impact by cellular inheritance versus cellular production. Although our contributions here are in their infancy, I will discuss aspirational goals pertaining to a statistical physics of disease modeling and diagnostics. Throughout the talk, I will argue how AI is rapidly accelerating, but can never replace, Physics as our foundation of scientific understanding.
 Faculty Host: Benoit Roux, BMB

title: Mexico’s Disappearance Crisis: Crimes Against Humanity and the Politics of Denial
description:
This lecture revisits Mexico’s disappearance crisis in light of the 2026 decision of the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances, which found well-founded indications that enforced disappearances have been and continue to be committed as crimes against humanity, in the context of multiple widespread or systematic attacks against civilian populations involving public authorities as well as criminal organizations acting with state complicity or acquiescence. It examines how patterns of disappearance have evolved from the “Dirty War” to the militarized “war on drugs,” through changing configurations of state violence, organized crime, collusion, territorial control, and impunity, and considers the significance of the Committee’s decision to refer Mexico’s situation urgently to the UN General Assembly. Finally, the lecture explores the politics of denial surrounding the crisis, including the Sheinbaum government’s efforts to minimize state responsibility, challenge international findings, and reject the characterization of enforced disappearances as crimes against humanity.
 José Antonio Guevara Bermúdez is a Mexican lawyer, human rights expert, and academic with more than 25 years of experience in international human rights law, international criminal law, transitional justice, and international humanitarian law. He is currently Academic Director of the Memory and Tolerance Museum in Mexico City and Associate Professor at the Autonomous University of Tlaxcala.
 From 2014 to 2020, he served as a member and Chair-Rapporteur of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, and as a member of the Coordination Committee of the UN Human Rights Council’s Special Procedures. He previously served as Executive Director of the Mexican Commission for the Defense and Promotion of Human Rights and held senior human rights positions in the Mexican government and diplomatic service, including at Mexico’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations in Geneva.
 He has taught at universities in Mexico and abroad and was Tinker Visiting Professor at the University of Chicago in 2025. He has authored and co-authored numerous publications on human rights and international justice. He holds a Law Degree from Universidad Iberoamericana and a Ph.D. in Fundamental Rights from Universidad Carlos III de Madrid.
 This event is organized by the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies (CLACS) with support from the Katz Center for Mexican Studies.
 Lunch will be provided.

title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
description:
DIRECTED BY
David Greaves,
Liani Greaves,
William Greaves
WRITTEN BY
William Greaves
STARRING
Romare Bearden,
Arna Bontemps,
Ida Mae Cullen
A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: The Algorithmic Past: AI and the New Conditions of Historicity
description:
AI technologies, both discriminative and generative, are profoundly transforming the very conditions of historicity: the technical, epistemological, and political conditions under which the past becomes visible, imaginable, intelligible, and narrative. Automated operations of detection, classification, description, search and retrieval, correlation, restoration, completion, simulation, and generation are reshaping our relation with the past. Further developing his work on latent spaces and the transformations of the archive (published in the article “Latent Spaces: AI, Art, and the Archive”, October 196, Spring 2026, pp.18-60), and drawing from his experience as curator of an exhibition with a significant media-archaeological dimension (The World Through AI, first presented at the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 2025, and then at the Schirn Kunsthalle in Frankfurt and the SESC 24 de Maio in São Paulo in 2026) Antonio Somaini will present a series of reflection on what it means for the past to become “algorithmic”.
 About the lecturer: Antonio Somaini is Professor of Film, Media, and Visual Culture Theory at the Université Sorbonne Nouvelle in Paris, and a Senior Member of the Institut Universitaire de France (IUF). In recent years he has been visiting professor at Yale and at Harvard. In 2025 he has been the chief curator of the exhibition The World Through AI at the Jeu de Paume museum in Paris, which is currently presented at the Schirn Kunsthalle in Frankfurt and at the SESC 24 de Maio in São Paulo. Among his recent publications, the essays “Latent Spaces: AI, Art, and the Meta-Archive” (October 196, Spring 2026, pp.18-60), “A Theory of Latent Spaces” (in the catalogue of the exhibition The World Through AI, Paris: Jeu de Paume / JBE Books, 2025, pp. 21-51), “Algorithmic Images. Artificial Intelligence and Visual Culture” (Grey Room 93, Fall 2023, pp. 74-115), and the book Culture visuelle. Images, regards, médias, dispositifs (with Andrea Pinotti, 2022). He is currently working on a new exhibition entitled Energies of AI and scheduled
 to be presented at the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture, and Technology) in Lisbon in September 2027.
 Reception will follow.

title: Future Café: The Future of Liberty
description:
Future Café is a student-organized series that provides the opportunity and space for undergraduates to collectively imagine utopian possibilities and long-term futures. Join us for our next meeting to discuss what liberty will look like 100, 500, or 5,000 years from now.
 “The raison d’être of politics is freedom, and its field of experience is action,” Hannah Arendt once wrote. Yet is liberty merely the absence of interference, or does it also require the possibility of participating in shaping the world we inhabit? If political freedom requires more than the possession of individual rights, what might liberty itself come to mean in the future?
 At a time when liberty is invoked across competing political movements and ideological divides, its meaning appears increasingly contested. Appeals to liberty have justified both resistance to state authority and the exercise of that authority, the protection of individual autonomy and the pursuit of collective self-determination. But whose liberty is being defended, and under what conditions? Can liberty be meaningfully universal when the circumstances in which it is exercised remain profoundly unequal? Can liberty be exercised without reproducing the very relations of power from which it promises emancipation?
 Looking ahead, how might emerging technologies, shifting political institutions, and new forms of social organization transform the possibilities and limits of liberty? Can liberty be reconciled with security, equality, and collective responsibility, or do these ideals necessarily come into conflict? Might future societies come to understand autonomy less as independence from others than as something made possible through interdependence? Could the future of liberty require us to reconsider not only the liberties we seek to preserve, but the very conditions under which freedom becomes possible?
 This event is free and open to all University of Chicago undergraduate students; registration is recommended.

KOVAL Distillery crafts a line of whiskey, gin, and specialty spirits using unique organic grains and signature “heart cut” techniques with only the absolute best quality distillate. Whether you’re chasing your next big laugh or looking for a fresh perspective, come experience the talent, energy, and creative edge that keep Chicago’s independent scene alive.
That’s not nostalgia. That’s real history—and it’s still being made.

title: Ashes and Diamonds
description:
DIRECTED BY

Andrzej Wajda

In the spring of 1945, weary and disillusioned by the war against the Nazis that has just ended, uncertain about a future under Communist rule, two resistance fighters are under orders to assassinate the incoming district leader. One of the fighters, the brooding Maciek, played by Zbigniew Cybulski (often called “the Polish James Dean”), falls in love with a local barmaid and is suddenly torn about how to move forward. As Wajda said about ASHES AND DIAMONDS, almost universally regarded as his masterpiece, “I have tried to reveal to movie audiences the complicated and difficult world of a generation to which I myself belong.” This anguished, romantic, and deeply personal film is an all-time favorite of both Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese, who placed it as #3 on his top 10 list for Sight and Sound.

About the Book:
All Arnie Tenderton wants this Christmas—all he’s ever wanted—is to be a published author. For decades he has toiled over one novel after another. Each was missing something. Until now.
He’s finally written his perfect book.
What he needs next is a literary agent, someone who can get his book into publishers’ hands. Not just any agent will do, of course. Arnie wants the best. Arnie wants Claudia Conley.

 The East German underground artist and dissident Lutz Dammbeck met Thomas Plenert in 1978. title: Other Lives, Kelcey Ayer
description: Kelcey Ayer is a Colombian-American artist based in Los Angeles. In 2024, after spending 20 years as a co-founder/singer/songwriter of indie-rock veterans Local Natives, in addition to his brooding side-project Jaws of Love., he decided to walk away from both projects to embrace something new. For years Ayer felt split down the middle between these two projects, but once his son was born in early 2023, everything changed. The experience of becoming a father seems to have stitched these two sides of Ayer into one whole, new person. The result is Ayer’s first two EP’s under his given name entitled No Sleep and Hand Me Downs, both self-engineered and self-produced in his home studio in east LA, and released in 2025. From the passing down of stories to his newborn son about dead neighborhood dogs, to the sleepless mania every new parent shockingly discovers, both EPs cover the horrifying realities, minuscule details, and daily bursts of endless love that come with fatherhood. Ayer is currently finishing his first solo debut record under his own name.

title: A Good Year w/ Lipsticism
description:
$18 Adv + Fees | 21+
Copenhagen’s A Good Year announce Play, out May 22nd via Escho, and release the new single “Back of a Car” featuring Koilwood.
“Back of a Car” (feat. Koilwood) Has an energetic and softly played breakbeat with Koilwood’s voice something between a whisper and a song float atop the big soundscape. Koilwood, the moniker of Alexxis Glory Princess Steadham, is a Las Vegas native now rooted on the west coast of Norway. “Back of a Car” is her first collaborative release.
“Back of a Car” is a good example of A Good Year’s aesthetic, fusing the electronic and programmed with the real and played, creating a sort of magical realism of their own — Whether it’s a really good drumbeat, resonating wooden guitars or dwelling electric sounds from a sci-fi movie murmuring in the background, these contrasting sounds are shaped by the unique, intuitive process the group has built over several years.
Play is an album that came about without a plan or intent to make a record. It emerged from experiments—and collaborations: moments caught, the energy of playing together, half-finished ideas, and new friends, all sent across the internet and back.
The album features voices and contributions from Horse Vision, Tiffi M, Helena Gao, MØ, and first-time recordings by Koilwood and Suisse Air.
For Tobias Laust Hansen (producer, former Liss drummer) and Albert Hildbrand (video artist), Play started with the intent to jam in a new way, adding a visual element. “It often starts with drums and an idea for an image or video. The visuals can direct the music, and the music can inspire the visuals.” Some close friends, some brand new acquaintances, the features and guests on the album were essential to tying the collage together. “The music became a vessel for connection, a way to reach out to people we admire, but also a way to create a social element within these sometimes introverted jams.”
The duo considers Play their debut record, but it is technically their second release. In 2024, they created the film “Sofina” a “psychedelic travel movie” made as a kind of exorcism after losing their mutual best friend, Søren Holm, the singer of Liss. The project was never intended to be more than catharsis, a space to clear their minds. They released the film’s soundtrack as pure documentation, and thus, A Good Year was born. “Early on we figured out the process isn’t about ownership or expertise — it’s about the pleasure of a space with no rules, where learning from each other is the only goal”

title: Porcelain / Zastava / Attic Reels
description: Doors: 8PM / Show: 9PM / 21+ , "rdquo" -> Everything has changed," sings frontman Steve Pike on , "rdquo" -> Apocalypse", a track from Austin post-hardcore band Porcelain's sophomore LP, Today's Minor Victories; , "rdquo" -> Not for better but for worse." It's a sentiment that reflects a familiar millennial experience: comparing the world you dreamed of growing into with the constant indignities of late capitalism, the interminable imperialist violence around the globe, and the rapidly escalating climate crisis as we barrel past the point of no return. And on a micro scale, it reflects a stage of life marked by great tectonic shifts, by youthful innocence fully giving way to grief and disillusionment. On Today's Minor Victories, apocalypse is both personally and literally the backdrop, and Porcelain's churning, roiling, snarling post-hardcore is the tool of choice with which to hack through the weeds. The members of Porcelain --- Pike, guitarist/vocalist Ryan Fitzgibbon, bassist Jordan Emmert and drummer Eli Deitz --- are all Austin scene veterans, having played in locally beloved bands such as Exhalants, Super Thief, Votive and US Weekly. When they came together as Porcelain in 2022, it was with the benefit of more than a decade of orbiting each other and building mutual admiration. With Pike in particular growing tired of the more straightforward, aggressive noise rock that he had been playing for years, the idea was to gather four gifted musicians and play whatever felt right. , "rdquo" -> [We threw] everything on the table, and I feel like all four of our influences really came in," Pike says. , "rdquo" -> Especially on this record, I feel like you can hear so many elements of everything that we all really enjoy." Around the release of their self-titled debut album in 2024, Porcelain hit the road prolifically, honing their fierce live chemistry across the country and sharing bills at home with such legends as Unwound, The Blood Brothers and Touché Amoré. Songs that would end up on Today's Minor Victories became staples of the live set, going through various lives as the band worked out their kinks together. , "rdquo" -> We really wanted to make sure this batch of songs were pretty road-tested," says Emmert.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: PHS Seminar: “Demographic Anxieties: Bodies, Borders, and Reproductive Injustice in Palestine/Israel” by Gala Rexer, PhD, MPH
description:
Abstract: Demographic Anxieties examines how the Israeli settler-colonial state and its borders shape Palestinian women’s reproductive freedom. Grounded in a Black feminist reproductive justice framework, this work foregrounds the sexual politics of settler colonialism by demonstrating how Israeli policies profoundly impact Palestinian women’s reproductive rights, health, and decision-making. Based on in-depth interviews and more than two years of ethnographic research with Israeli medical staff and Palestinian women undergoing fertility treatment, the book takes Israeli hospitals, fertility departments, maternity wards, and infrastructures of care as sites of inquiry into the governance of Palestinians’ lives.
 Demographic Anxieties examines everyday encounters between Palestinian patients and Jewish Israeli doctors and argues that, alongside spectacular and disastrous forms of Israeli state violence, we must also consider more quotidian forms of surveillance and control. Written from an anticolonial feminist perspective, it asks what Palestine, as a site of knowledge production, enables, complicates, or demands from a transnational feminist approach to reproductive justice.
 Speaker Bio: Gala Rexer is a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow in the University of Warwick’s Sociology Department and an Honorary Research Fellow at University College London’s Sarah Parker Remond Centre for the Study of Racism and Racialisation (SPRC). She was previously a Visiting Research Fellow at NYU and Yale University, as well as the SPRC’s inaugural postdoctoral fellow. Her first book, Demographic Anxieties: Bodies, Borders, and Reproductive Injustice in Palestine/Israel, was recently published by the University of California Press. Broadly, her ethnographic research examines how political, environmental, and spatial conditions shape reproduction.

description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

description:

Once upon a time in a land called Sicilia, King Leontes is infected by an uncontrollable jealousy over his pregnant wife, Hermione. title: Guided Tour of the Newberry
description:
In 1893, the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Chicago, Grover Cleveland started his second non-consecutive term as president, and the Newberry building opened to the public. On this guided tour, you’ll learn about the history behind the founding of the Newberry. You’ll also discover all the ways you can engage with the library today.
Founded in 1887, the Newberry had three temporary locations before moving into its permanent home across from Washington Square Park in 1893.
The library was designed by architect Henry Ives Cobb, with input from Newberry head librarian William Frederick Poole. Cobb envisioned a grand edifice on par with the civic landmarks of Europe; Poole favored a more modest design that would facilitate user access to books and other resources. In the end, they compromised. The Newberry is a blend of their competing visions.
Aerial photograph of the Newberry, 2022
Architectural detail on the Newberry's facade
A quiet study space on the Newberry's third floor
Over the years, the Newberry has grown and evolved, notably with the addition of a climate-controlled stacks building in the early 1980s and a renovation that updated spaces and restored original architectural details on the library’s first floor in 2018.
You’ll get a healthy dose of history on this tour. But you’ll also get to see the Newberry in action in the present. Tens of thousands of people visit the Newberry every year, and there are many ways that we make the library’s collections, programs, and resources accessible and relevant to them.
This tour is free, and no advance registration is required. We'll meet in the lobby of the Newberry and begin the tour from there.

title: Transported: The Everyday Magic of Musical Daydreams
description:
Elizabeth Margulis will discuss Transported: The Everyday Magic of Musical Daydreams. She will be joined in conversation by Lawrence Zbikowski. A Q&A and signing will follow the discussion.
 About the book: Reliving past heartbreak. Picturing a serene future. Imagining a fantastical scene. Across genres, music has an uncanny ability to carry us into distinct inner worlds.
In Transported, acclaimed music cognition researcher Elizabeth Margulis explores the phenomenon of musical daydreams–the vivid, spontaneous, emotionally charged images, stories, and memories we lapse into while listening to music–and argues that these everyday reveries offer a powerful and underappreciated window into how we think, feel, and connect.
Combining cutting-edge neuroscience, psychology, ethnography, and revelations from her own teaching and pathbreaking research, Margulis shows not only that musical imaginings are widespread and meaningful–but also that daydreams which seem deeply personal are often widely shared. Music can alleviate anxiety, ignite creativity, and foster connection in our increasingly fragmented era.
At a time when attention is perpetually under siege, Transported makes a powerful case for music as one of the last spaces where the mind is still free to wander–and reminds us that these wanderings are more meaningful and more important to our individual and collective well-being than we’ve ever realized.
 About the author: Elizabeth Margulis is Professor and Director of the Music Cognition Lab at Princeton University. She was trained as a pianist before turning to musicology and cognitive science. Her previous scholarly books have won prizes from the Society for Music Theory, the American Musicological Society, and the American Society for Composers, Authors and Publishers, and been translated into seven languages. Her research has been featured in outlets ranging from NPR’s All Things Considered to the BBC, and funded by multiple grants from the National Science Foundation. Transported is her first book for general audiences.
 About the interlocutor: Lawrence Zbikowski is Addie Clark Harding Professor in the Department of Music and the College at University of Chicago. His most recent book Foundations of Musical Grammar (Oxford University Press) builds on research on fundamental aspects of human communication to explore the basis for the construction of meaningful musical utterances.

title: ISAC Visiting Scholar Lecture with Prof. Dr. Verena Lepper
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC)
description:
Elephantine. Island of the Millennia
 Elephantine is an island on the Nile River in southern Egypt. This trade and border center was home to a uniquely diverse population. Here, a whole range of languages, cultures and religions existed side by side. It is the only place where 4,000 years of unbroken cultural history can be traced through written sources. Thousands of texts can be found on papyrus or clay shards written in ten different languages and scripts, including Hieroglyphics, Hieratic, Demotic, Aramaic, Coptic and Arabic. Today, they are held in 60 collections in 24 different countries worldwide and have been deciphered before being translated and catalogued.
 After a seven-year research project funded by a European Research Council Grant titled Localizing 4000 Years of Cultural History: Texts and Scripts from Elephantine Island in Egypt, for the first time, more than 10,000 papyri and ostraca from the island have been digitally unlocked by an international research team.
 Through international cooperation, the “papyrus puzzle” can thus be solved – also with the help of cutting-edge new methods from the digital humanities. Mathematicians and physicists made it possible thanks to computer tomography to “virtually” unfold the rolled papyri and papyrus packages, making them legible for the first time in history.
 Verena is the Anissa and Paul John Balson II Senior Curator of Antiquities & Head of Antiquities, J. Paul Getty Museum
 Verena joined the Getty Museum’s Department of Antiquities in 2025. A distinguished Egyptologist and curator, she served for 17 years as curator of Egyptian and Oriental Papyri at the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection, Berlin (Staatliche Museen zu Berlin). She has led major international exhibitions and research projects in Germany and abroad, including in Doha, Abu Dhabi, and at Harvard University. Verena also directed the Institute of Ancient Near Eastern and Hellenistic Religion at Humboldt University in Berlin where she is Honorary Professor. To strengthen cultural diplomacy between Germany and the Arab world, she founded the Arab-German Young Academy of Sciences and Humanities (AGYA) in 2013, which she continues to lead. A graduate of the University of Bonn, she holds a PhD in Egyptology, Semitic Studies, and Oriental Studies after having studied at Bonn, Oxford, and HarvardUniversity . She is the author of 20 books and numerous articles.

A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

title: Emanuel Fiano - Nāmusā: On Divine Law in Late Antiquity
description:
Registration required by November 16 - Prof. Fiano’s paper will be pre-circulated.
 This presentation examines the formation of a notion of divine law in the late-antique Syriac Christian world. Drawing on a corpus spanning the second to the eighth centuries and encompassing multiple genres—from early apologetics to doctrinal treatises and legal codes—the paper 1) proposes that some Syriac sources construed divine revelation as a nāmūsā, a binding normative order structurally continuous with the Mosaic Torah, though with reconfigured contents; 2) interrogates the Syriac reception and transmission of Roman civil law and its role in shaping that conceptualization; and 3) analyzes the musings found in the introductions to Syriac legal codes, particularly regarding the distinction between divine and human law and whether Christians were understood to have been entrusted with any genuinely secular precepts. Special attention is given to the Jewish genealogies of Christian nomism and their afterlives in Syriac legal culture, as well as to exegetical connections with rabbinic texts.
 Emanuel Fiano is Associate Professor in the Department of Theology at Fordham University. He received an undergraduate degree in Religious Studies from Sapienza University of Rome and went on to earn an MA and a PhD in Early Christianity from Duke University’s Graduate Program in Religion (with Certificates in Interdisciplinary European Studies and in College Teaching). During his graduate training, he was a Summer Fellow at Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection and studied as a Visiting Researcher at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, at the CNRS in Paris, and, as a Charlotte W. Newcombe Doctoral Dissertation Fellowship holder, at UC Berkeley. Most recently, Fiano has been a Research Fellow at Dumbarton Oaks. He has taught Italian, Biblical Hebrew, and the history of Christianity at Duke and at Elon University. The courses he has been teaching at Fordham include Sacred Texts of the Middle East; Ancient History; Syriac language and literature; Coptic language and literature; Jews and Christians in Antiquity; Ancient Theological Controversies; and Law and Religion in Antiquity—in addition to graduate tutorials on subjects germane to his research interests.
 Presented by the Joyce Z. and Jacob Greenberg Center for Jewish Studies, the Early Christian Studies Workshop, and the Ancient Societies Workshop.

title: August H. Nimtz — Revisiting Black Marxism Four Decades Later in the Era of Trump
description:
Over the last decade, Cedric Robinson’s Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition has had a tremendous influence on scholars and activists alike, deeply shaping debates on the place of race within capitalist societies. Is race subsumed by class, with the latter the sine qua non of capitalism? Do race and class act independently within modern societies? Or does capitalism inevitably express a deeper racial impetus in the West? 
 In his recent book, Black Marxism: A Marxist Critique (Monthly Review Press, 2026), Nimtz lays out the limits of Robinson’s much-celebrated text, showing it represents a sophisticated, but ultimately flawed, version of Black nationalism. Nimtz defends Marxism from Robinson’s accusations of myopia on matters of race, suggesting that, in charging Marx and Engels with Eurocentrism, he either failed to understand, or misrepresented, their work—and that, in effect, many thinkers inspired by Black Marxism blatantly misrepresented Marxist texts. 
 An authentic Marxism, argues Nimtz, remains the most reliable real-world method for human liberation, not least among peoples of African descent. Speaking for himself as a contemporary of Robinson’s, he grounds Black Marxism: A Marxist Critique in an account of his own upbringing in New Orleans, and his development throughout the struggles of the 1960s, explaining how and why he came to radically different conclusions.
 —
 This lecture is presented in conjunction with 3CT’s Marx + Theory reading group, led by Anton Ford and Gabriel Winant.

title: Capitalism’s Legal Regime
location: Sky Suite at the Harris School of Public Policy
description:
How do legal systems shape capitalism and the creation of wealth? Join us for a thought-provoking conversation with Katharina Pistor, a leading scholar of law, property rights, and corporate governance, to explore this question.
 Often described as an economic system, capitalism, Pistor argues, is fundamentally . Her latest book, The Law of Capitalism and How to Transform It, reveals how laws governing property, contracts, corporations, and finance convert assets, promises, and ideas into capital. She posits that this system generates unprecedented wealth, contributing to increasing inequality while simultaneously straining social and political cohesion and challenging democratic governance.
 Pistor will be joined by Steven Durlauf, founding director of the Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility, and Damon Jones, the Center’s Associate Director.
 Durlauf, whose work focuses on inequality and intergenerational mobility, will share insights into how economic structures shape opportunity and wealth. Jones, whose research spans tax policy, household finance, and labor economics, will illuminate how legal and administrative complexity contributes to unequal outcomes.
 The conversation will be moderated by Jacob Goldin, Richard M. Lipton Professor, a leading scholar of tax law and administrative systems whose research examines how taxation structures shape outcomes for low-income households across groups.
 This event offers a valuable opportunity to engage with pressing questions about capitalism, inequality, and the legal and policy changes needed to build a more just and sustainable economic future.

 Wednesday, November 18, 2026 6 pm to 8:30 pm

title: Havok, Hellripper, Slackjaw, Xoth
description:
HAVOK
Inspired by the burgeoning American thrash metal revival of the mid-2000s, Denver, Colorado’s Havok emerged in 2004 with an aggressive, neck-snapping style that evoked Bay Area thrash legends like Exodus, Metallica, and Testament. They broke into the Billboard 200 in 2013 with their acclaimed third full-length effort, Unnatural Selection, and continued to refine their uncompromising sound on future endeavors like Conformicide (2017) and V (2020).
Havok assembled in 2004 and proceeded to ply their retro-fitted classic thrash trade via a series of self-financed releases: a 2005 demo, a 2006 single, and a 2007 EP, curiously named Pwn ’em All. These efforts duly got them signed to Candlelight Records, which released Havok’s debut album, Burn, in 2009 and then sent them off to tour with bands like Exodus, Anthrax, Destruction, Primal Fear, and Hammerfall. All of this roadwork only tightened up the group’s impressive chops, and prepared members David Sanchez (lead vocals, rhythm guitar), Reece Scruggs (lead guitar), Jessie de los Santos (bass, backing vocals), and Pete Webber (drums) for the recording of their sophomore album, Time Is Up (produced by thrash stalwart James Murphy: Death, Obituary, Disincarnate, Testament, etc.), which was released in early 2011.
Michael Leon replaced de los Santos on bass for 2013’s Unnatural Selection, which earned positive reviews and saw Havok make their Billboard debut. The band toured steadily during the rest of the year, and they switched labels from Candlelight to Century Media. Leon left the group after three years to join Soulfly and was replaced by Nick Schendzielos of Cephalic Carnage, who made his studio debut on Havok’s fourth album, Conformicide, which was released in March 2017. Three years later, the band returned with new bassist Brandon Bruce in tow and issued their aptly named fifth long-player,
HELLRIPPER
Hellripper is a black/speed metal band based in the Scottish Highlands.
All orders placed via Bandcamp are handled and shipped personally by the band.
ALL HAIL THE GOAT!
SLACKJAW
Slackjaw is an American heavy metal trio based in South Carolina. The band was formed when Dallas Young (vocals, rhythm guitar, bassist), also widely known online as Soup, met Brady Riggenbach (lead guitarist) in 2017. Jacob Rigdon (drummer) was added to complete the trio in July 2021. Despite various lineup changes, Dallas and Brady held the band’s vision together by taking on multiple roles in the studio, with Brady being the studio drummer on almost every track to date. Through a mutual interest in Black Label Society and Pantera, Dallas and Brady quickly started writing material. The band’s first single, “Caught in the Crossfire,” and their first studio album, “Ritual of Dissonance,” were met with astounding appraisal from old and new fans alike. When the band formed, they gathered an impressive online following with no management, label, or supporting tour. With influences such as Pantera, Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth, Meshuggah, Black Label Society, Tool, and many others, there’s no question this metal band has one goal: to follow in their predecessors’ footsteps and make albums that will stand the test of time.
XOTH
Since bursting forth from the cosmic ether in 2014, Seattle’s Xoth (pronounced ZOTH) has evoked fan and critical acclaim for their innovative approach to extreme metal. 2019’s Interdimensional Invocations has become a cult classic, blending technical death metal, black metal, and thrash in a novel synthesis that eludes categorization.
In partnership with Dawnbreed Records, their third triumph Exogalactic is an ambitious leap forward. It’s as if they’ve excavated musical relics from Earth’s core and melded them with sounds from the far reaches of the universe. Each song is an event horizon, stirring subgenres into a timewarp of past and future sonic chaos.
Amidst the vortex of sound, the mixing sorcery of Joe Cincotta at Full Force Studio (Obituary, Suffocation) manifests an auditory odyssey and the artwork of Shindy Reehal at Shindy Design sets the tone for the voyage. Xoth is not just music; it’s a journey across the celestial landscape led by interstellar luminaries.
“Through four years of trials and tribulations, we are thrilled to finally unleash an album that has demanded immense dedication, fortitude, and sacrifice. The results of our experiment have surpassed our wildest imagination!”
Xoth is: Tyler Sturgill – Guitar & Vocals Woody Adler – Guitar Ben Bennett – Bass Jeremy Salvo – Drums

title: Meet Calvin B. Jones: Make a Mini-Mural
description:
From 1976 to 1987 artist Calvin B. Jones along with fellow artist Mitchell Canton painted six murals on the South and West sides of Chicago. Jones was active in the Black Arts Movement of the 1960s and 1970s and aesthetically influenced by Chicago's AfriCOBRA collective (African Commune of Bad Relevant Artists), known for painting with bold dues they called Cool-Ade colors.
Learn more in our archives!
This fun, hands-on program welcomes families to discover the life and work of Jones while exploring the question “Whose murals get saved?” Together, participants will enjoy a guided mini‑mural activity inspired by Jones’s vibrant style, featuring bold colors and African print designs. It’s an engaging, creative experience for all ages, perfect for families who love to learn, make art, and explore Chicago’s cultural stories.
Presented as part of the Renaissance Project, this event invites participants to actively engage with the rich and often untold stories of Black history and heritage at Chicago Public Library.
This program is made possible with support from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to the Chicago Public Library Foundation.

title: Mountainfilm On Tour
description: Why we're bringing it to Chicago Mountainfilm hasn't screened in Chicago in seven years. We're bringing it back to Pilsen because this city's film community is ready for bigger nights, and the audience for adventure and conservation stories here runs far wider than filmmakers. Filmmaker Friday Chicago has spent the last two years building a room where Chicago filmmakers meet, trade notes, and make things together. Mountainfilm on Tour is the next step: a 600-seat night at Thalia Hall, open to anyone who loves the outdoors, cares about the places we protect, or just wants to see great documentary work on a big screen with the people who made it. "As Filmmaker Friday keeps growing, we're always looking for organizations to build with, people who want to keep elevating the Chicago film scene and reach audiences well beyond filmmakers. The culture and community in Chicago are unique to this city, so when the opportunity came up to bring Mountainfilm here, I couldn't pass it up. It's been seven years since Mountainfilm was last in Chicago, and we're excited to bring it to Pilsen. Looking ahead, we want to host bigger, more consistent events like this one as our community and partnerships keep growing." Armin Korsos, founder of Filmmaker Friday Chicago and Caymanite "Mountainfilm on Tour is the natural next step for Filmmaker Friday. The series has grown faster than we ever planned, with around 3,000 people coming through in 2025, and this is the first night we've built to match that scale." Armin Korsos About Filmmaker Friday Chicago Filmmaker Friday Chicago is a monthly networking and panel series for the city's film community, founded by director Armin Korsos in June 2024. In 2025 alone, it drew approximately 3,000 unique attendees. Each month brings together directors, cinematographers, editors, producers, and the people who hire them, for panels, workshops, and an open room to meet. Mountainfilm on Tour is the series' largest event to date and the first of the bigger community screenings it plans to host going forward. Filmmaker Friday is presented alongside Caymanite, the Chicago branded documentary and commercial company Armin founded in 2021. title: Kanal
description:
DIRECTED BY
Andrzej Wajda
WRITTEN BY
Jerzy Stefan Stawinski
STARRING
Teresa Izewska,
Tadeusz Janczar,
Wienczyslaw Glinski
During the celebrated four-minute long shot that introduces us to the beleaguered underground of fighters in Warsaw resisting the Nazi occupation in 1944, the narrator tells us, “These are the heroes of the tragedy. Watch them closely for these are the last hours of our lives.” The centerpiece of Wajda’s “War Trilogy,” and the first Polish film to depict the Warsaw Uprising, Kanał follows the fighters through a hopeless but heroic journey that will take them into the city’s sewer system, the only place they can survive. Winner of a Special Jury Prize at Cannes (along with Bergman’s THE SEVENTH SEAL) and became the first of Wajda’s films to open in the U.S. when it premiered at Dan Talbot’s New Yorker Theater in 1961.

 Outside the Lines is a student-run fine arts organization at the University of Chicago. The group hosts on-campus figure drawing sessions on Wednesdays evenings, weeks 2-9 of each quarter in Midway Studios. All are welcome regardless of previous experience and skill.
 Zespo is a Chicago-based artist who works primarily in painting. He received an MFA from the University of Chicago (2018) and a BFA from the American Academy of Art College in Chicago (2014). He has exhibited his work in solo and two-person exhibitions at Pueblo Unido Gallery at Centro Romero (Chicago, IL, 2025), the independent artist-run space Cuarto de Servicio (CDMX, México, 2024), and the Denison Art Space in Newark (Newark, OH, 2018). His work has been recognized by grants, fellowships, and juried exhibitions including the 2018 Ground Floor exhibition at the Hyde Park Art Center, the 3Arts Make A Wave grant, and a residency at the Oxbow School of Art. In addition, Zespo serves as Artistic Director for the Lit & Luz Festival, facilitating cultural exchanges and collaborations between Chicago and Mexico, and as Program Administrator for the Open Practice Committee, the visiting artist program of the Department of Visual Arts at the University of Chicago.

title: Rockin’ in the Park
description:
Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.
Concerts run from 7–10 PM. Admission is free. Outside food and coolers are prohibited. Parking is available at the Parkway Bank Park parking garage and is free with validation from any Parkway Bank Park venue.
2026 Lineup
Thursday, July 9: New World Men*
A powerful tribute to Rush, bringing the spirit, precision, and intensity of the legendary band’s live shows to the stage.
Thursday, July 16: Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press*
Beloved Chicago party band Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press delivers huge harmonies, sharp musicianship, and a wildly fun setlist built for singing, dancing, and staying out later than planned.

Departure recreates the look, sound, and feel of Journey, packing their set with high-energy performances of the band’s biggest hits.

Direct from Detroit, Live the Who pays tribute to The Who’s explosive 1968–1974 era with the sound, look, and raw energy of the iconic rock band.

title: Cairo Station

Youssef Chahine · 77m · DCP
 Despite its calamitous failure at the Egyptian box office, Cairo Station epitomizes beloved auteur Youssef Chahine’s hybridization of Western genres (here, Italian neorealism and sociological noir) against the backdrop of domestic political turmoil. The collapse of monarchy and building of a republic, the emergence of Egypt as a leader of African decolonization, Nasser’s 1956 triumph in the Suez Crisis, and accelerated industrialization and cultural revival ushered in a new era of nationalist optimism. Chahine, however, tells the tragic story of those left behind by revolution.

Bruno Ganz is Damiel, an angel perched atop buildings high over Berlin who can hear the thoughtsfears, hopes, dreamsof all the people living below. Made not long before the fall of the Berlin wall, this stunning tapestry of sounds and images, shot in black and white and color by the legendary Henri Alekan, is movie poetry. And it forever made the name Wim Wenders synonymous with film art.

Logan Center Performance Penthouse

“Panmnemism references the ability of inanimate objects to store experiential information as memories.” Adam Menlin
At this moment in history, we are encountering the stories of America at 250. If we engage the “Sankofa” of looking backward and forward, we may uncover a series of complex truths that offer a lens for how to navigate the moment.
Join us for an interdisciplinary storytelling workshop with storyteller Emily Hooper Lansana and multidisciplinary artist William Estrada. The workshop will take place at the Logan Center for the Arts. The Logan Center makes space to contemplate, create and experience art while engaging diverse communities. We will explore identity by examining the connection between objects and memory. Participants will be invited to investigate a series of objects and to respond by sharing memories that arise. The sharing will take place in the form of oral storytelling and visual response. This three-hour intensive workshop will include opportunities to traverse personal and cultural history, to engage in collective conversation, and to creatively develop oral and visual pieces that capture the experience.
This session is part of a larger collective project curated by Emily Hooper Lansana that explores interdisciplinary storytelling, culture, and memory and is included in the curated UChicago Arts Series America@250 - Now is the Time: Artists go to Work
This workshop is supported by the Logan Center’s Chill Endowment and friends of the Logan Center.

WRITTEN BY

FATHERLAND centers on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick, taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after 16 years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.
With FATHERLAND, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning IDA and COLD WAR, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love, and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

title: Chicago Flamenco Nights
location: Gary and Laura Maurer Concert Hall Presents
description:
A weekly showcase of world music and dance featuring the best local and touring talent! Most shows are Wednesday nights at 7:30 PM.
Most World Music Wednesday concerts are free with a $10 suggested donation. To guarantee your entry make your reservations in advance - either online or by calling the box office at 773-728-6000. Reservations unclaimed 10 minutes before showtime will be released to waiting patrons.
Under the direction of international flamenco artist Curro de Candela, Flamenco Nights is a dynamic production that unites some of Spain's most celebrated flamenco artists with Chicago's finest performers, creating a vibrant and unforgettable cultural experience. While directing and working with Chicago natives Carmen de Chicago and Andrea Salcedo, both featured artists in this upcoming show, Curro experienced the city's extraordinary artistic community firsthand and developed a deep appreciation for Chicago's incredible music and arts scene. Flamenco Nights invites audiences on a captivating journey through the passion and tradition of flamenco music, song, and dance while seamlessly weaving in and featuring the rich heritage of jazz. Through Curro's artistic vision, these two distinct traditions come together to create a powerful celebration of cultural exchange. Flamenco Nights offers audiences an exciting and immersive experience, revealing the unexpected connections between flamenco, jazz, and the artistic spaces where they meet.
Featuring: Curro de Candela, Andrea Salcedo, Carmen de Chicago, Diego Amador Jr., Eric Schneider. Finalized artist list to come!
Curro de Candela is the youngest and last representative of the artistic dynasty founded by José Greco, the first great international star of Spanish dance. This dynasty also includes the renowned and brilliant dancer Lola Greco, who received the National Dance Award. Curro's father, Domenico, also a dancer, is José Greco's nephew and Lola Greco's cousin.
Today, Curro is a celebrated artist - one of the most highly regarded flamenco dancers, directors, producers, and composers in Madrid. He founded his own company at the age of 22, and works with a team of exceptional musicians, blending his love of flamenco with Cuban, classical, and American music to each of his productions.
Curro continues to create, produce, and direct new works, and is currently developing his most ambitious production to date, serving as musical producer; artistic director choreographer, and principal dancer alongside some of today's finest artists.
Carmen Alvarez was born in Chicago, the city where her artistic journey began. She started her dance training at the age of five and graduated magna cum Laude with a degree in Dance from Western Michigan University. Carmen is classically trained in ballet, modern, jazz, contemporary, flamenco and Spanish dance, as well as in voice and acting. She has performed at international dance Festivals in South Korea, Chicago, and Detroit. Her curiosity for flamenco was sparked from a young age, watching her father dance flamenco and play Latin percussion throughout the Chicagoland area.
In 2026, Carmen is making her debut as a flamenco artist in Chicago, performing throughout the city where it all began. Carmen is honored and excited to embark on this next chapter of her artistic journey, sharing her love of flamenco with audiences both in Chicago and abroad. She could not do any of this without the love and support of her family and Curro.
Originally from Jalisco, Mexico, Andrea Salcedo is the first Mexican woman flamenco guitarist and has been recognized as an international reference by the Spanish newspaper El País. She grew up in Chicago, where she arrived at the age of ten, and graduated with honors from Northern Illinois University, earning a Bachelor's degree in Classical Guitar under the guidance of guitarist Fareed Haque. She began her flamenco studies in 2012 with Spanish guitarist Jesus de Aracely in Chicago. Since 2019, she has been based in Spain, where she continues her training with Aquilino Jiménez "El Entri” and José Manuel Montoya at the Fundación Conservatorio Flamenco casa Patas in Madrid.

title: Humbird w. Bad Posture Club
description:
Stars wheel overhead, bursting and dying and forming. Celestial bodies, anchored by ancient orbits, careen through space. Here on Earth, bodies need tending, hearts need mending. Sometimes it seems that the long night will never end. But stars and planets remind us: change is the only constant.
Humbird’s fourth full-length album, Morning When It Comes, is a promise made in the midst of a long night. With glittering hooks, big-hearted grooves, and clear-voiced melodies that cut straight to the truth, Humbird offers twelve new secular hymns that draw inspiration from the cosmos above to comfort us in our humanity down below.
For lead songwriter Siri Undlin (she/her), this album first took shape as a set of poetic compasses for navigating mental and physical illness. “I found certain melodies and rhymes to be like North Stars,” she notes, the songwriting process functioning as a balm and a map for reckoning with internal worlds of pain and discomfort. This process isn’t new for Undlin: whether singing as a kid in school stairwells, around the kitchen table with family, conducting extensive folklore and musical research worldwide as a Watson Fellow, or touring through the US and EU/UK on the heels of her 2024 album Right On, music has always been her tool for navigating the world. “I wrote these songs when I was really sick, and it could've very easily been a really depressing album,” she says. “But in the studio, it was important to all of us to find the ways these songs could harness mischief and exuberance – not to downplay the density of the emotions, but to represent the complexity and contradictions that occur on any given day of our lives.” Recording Morning When It Comes with trusted collaborators in Eau Claire, Wisconsin transformed these twelve self-soothing songs into a bigger, more universal conversation about stability, surrender, and the power of being in community.

title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.
Hayward is made possible by a special gift from Show Sponsor, The Michael and Mona Heath Fund.
The Gift Theatre Company’s 2026 Homecoming Season is made possible, in part, by generous contributions from The Arts Work Fund · The Copernicus Foundation · Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events · The Gaylord and Dorothy Donnelley Foundation · The Illinois Arts Council · Melissa Thornley Consulting · The Paul Angell Foundation · The Rabb Family Foundation · The Saints · The Service Club of Chicago · The Shubert Foundation, Inc.

title: Fran Lebowitz
location: North Shore Center for the Performing Arts
description:
In a cultural landscape filled with endless pundits and talking heads, Fran Lebowitz stands out as one of our most insightful social commentators. 
Her essays and interviews offer her acerbic views on current events and the media – as well as pet peeves including tourists, baggage-claim areas, after-shave lotion, adults who roller skate, children who speak French, or anyone who is unduly tan. The New York Times Book Review calls Lebowitz an "important humorist in the classic tradition." Purveyor of urban cool, Lebowitz is a cultural satirist whom many call the heir to Dorothy Parker. 
Lebowitz on special interest groups: “Special-interest publications should realize that if they are attracting enough advertising and readers to make a profit, the interest is not so special.” 
Lebowitz on frankness: “Spilling your guts is exactly as charming as it sounds.” 
Lebowitz on herself: “Success didn't spoil me, I've always been insufferable.” 
This is Lebowitz off the cuff. Her writing - pointed, taut and economical - is equally forthright, irascible, and unapologetically opinionated. 
Lebowitz worked odd jobs, such as taxi driving, belt peddling, and apartment cleaning (“with a small specialty in Venetian blinds”), before being hired by Andy Warhol as a columnist for Interview. That was followed by a stint at Mademoiselle. Her first book, a collection of essays titled Metropolitan Life, was a bestseller, as was a second collection, Social Studies. By turns ironic, facetious, deadpan, sarcastic, wry, wisecracking, and waggish, Lebowitz’s prose is wickedly entertaining. Her two books are collected in The Fran Lebowitz Reader, with a new preface by the author. The Fran Lebowitz Reader has been published in nine languages including French, Korean, Russian, Spanish, and Turkish. In 2021 it was published for the first time in the United Kingdom and became a bestseller. Lebowitz is also the author of the children’s book, Mr. Chas and Lisa Sue Meet the Pandas.

title: Shallow Alcove Album Release
description:
**Come celebrate the release of Shallow Alcove’s debut album ‘Pain Is A Heavy Door."**
**Shallow Alcove** is a band built from a long-standing friendship between Grace Krichbaum, Dan Harris, Peter Groppe, Jack Harrington, and Noah Dardaris. Their sound carries the folk sensibilities of Upstate New York alongside the indie influence of New York City, woven together with layered harmonies and deeply personal songwriting. There’s an intimacy to their sound that makes each song feel less like a performance and more like a conversation with someone you’ve known forever.
Their debut album, Pain Is A Heavy Door, is a record about becoming someone new without quite knowing how to leave the person you were behind. Across the album, friendship, love, grief, uncertainty, and the passage of time blur together, turning everyday moments into something tender and expansive. At its core, the album is about learning to accept the uncomfortable parts of growing up and finding people who make you feel a little less alone in them.
What began with friends writing songs in bedrooms and basements in Upstate New York has grown into a band split between New York and New Jersey, but Shallow Alcove’s roots have remained the same: storytelling with the people they love. Pain Is A Heavy Door is a document of that friendship from the laughter, grief, shared meals, borrowed beds, bad karaoke, and growing pains that shaped the people making it. It is an album about accepting the weight of change while holding onto each other through it.

It Left the Group Chat (ILTGC) is a monthly sketch-variety show by and for POC, queer, and women/trans/non-binary comedians, a kiki born from the stories that never make it out of the group chat but probably should. Each month we pick a theme, write a brand-new batch of sketches, bring in guest comics, do some improv, and add the audience to the chat for the night.

title: Pénjamo: Staged Reading Presentation
description:
Drawing on playwright Nancy García Loza’s own family history, Pénjamo: A Pocha Road Trip Story explores bicultural identity, self-discovery, and the myths and realities of ancestral homelands. Join us for a staged reading of Pénjamo and be among the first to experience this play that challenges the monolithic narrative of Mexican migration to the United States.
The play is set shortly after the passage of the 1986 Immigration Reform & Control Act, whose amnesty provisions allowed immigrant families to visit their countries of origin for the first time, just as they were starting to build a sense of belonging in the United States.
Guests are invited to continue the dialogue during a Q&A between the audience and the playwright, reflecting collectively on identity and belonging.

title: Silence Speaks: Writing Visuals
description:
Come join the Chicago Audiomakers Collective and The Understudy for a special listening party.
Together we’ll listen to Silence Speaks: Writing Visuals, a story about a famous mime in 1960’s Russia. At a time when words were dangerous, he found a way to speak up by using silence. Snap Judgment’s John Fecile wanted to tell his story but he faced a challenge: how to translate a visual medium into audio. John will be on hand to discuss the making of Silence Speaks and to answer your questions about the art of audio storytelling.
John Fecile is an audio producer, filmmaker, and storyteller. His work has appeared on NPR and been featured in The Guardian, The New York Times, Snap Judgment, and Al Jazeera. He has won awards in the US and UK, including Bronze at the 2017 Third Coast International Audio Festival for his documentary Blink Once for Yes.
Chicago Audiomakers Collective is a group that exists to foster and grow the audio community in Chicago. We believe that Chicago is full of incredible talent and it’s a city where things are undeniably happening. But, we as a community of artists, producers, and talent, aren’t as connected as we want to be.
They host regular events and provide resources like a audiomakers directory and vendor map for both professionals and hobbyists alike.
Check them out at http://chiaudiocollective.com/ or follow them on Instagram @chiaudiocollective.
