title: Benmont Tench
location: Gary and Laura Maurer Concert Hall Presents
description:
The title song on Benmont Tench's new album, The Melancholy Season - his second solo record after four decades at the keyboards in Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers - began as a poem, inspired by the autumn chill of a Southern California evening under the constellation Orion.
"We put a lot of thought into this record," Tench says, but he gratefully credits the help that came along the way. Jackson Browne "was really gracious with his studio," Groove Masters, where the album was mixed. It was Glyn Johns' idea to start “I Will Not Follow You Down” with nothing but a beat on a drum after Tench performed the song for him a few years ago. "When I finished, he said, 'If I was producing it, I would start with a drum doing what you were doing with your foot.'"
And Tench "couldn't be happier" about finding a home for The Melancholy Season at Dark Horse Records, "an emotionally resonant label for me" through Petty's close friendship with George Harrison. "I met George maybe three times. But I have that connection through Dhani to his dad, through Tom to George. And they have George's music, Cat Stevens, Joe Strummer–these are writers. To be in that company, it's perfect."
The Melancholy Season is upon us. But on this record, in these songs, there is plenty of room for joy–and a lot to celebrate.
https://www.benmonttench.com/

title: Dogs on Shady Lane
description:
Dogs on Shady Lane at Subterranean on November 18
Since 1994, Subterranean has been a cornerstone of the Wicker Park live music & nightlife scene. Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: Nicole Atkins
description:
“This whole album is almost like my fight against loneliness,” says Nicole Atkins of her latest release, Drama. “A lot of the songs came out of the fact that my husband and I basically have a long distance relationship. We're both on the road. He's a tour manager. I'm an artist. We can be apart for months at a time.” Those feelings of isolation and separation, complicated by sleep problems and some career uncertainty, left Atkins feeling overwhelmed at times. “I had to write myself through a lot.”
As the material started to take shape, she felt like she was “building a life raft,” and not only for herself. “With everything going on in the world, it's easy to forget that we're all the same,” she says. “We're being disconnected and pulled apart. We're longing for connection. That's what I want to write and sing about, and hopefully by doing that, make people feel a little less lonely.”
The life rafts on Drama are sturdy, with smart design and a buoyancy that's a tonic for our times. The Spectorized girl group rush of “Trippin' On Teardrops,” the pulsing Memphis soul-styled “For No One,” the James Bond-meets-Stevie Nicks noir of “Danny,” and the ABBA-worthy, anthemic “Singing In The Mirror.” As always when dissecting Atkins' neo-classic sound, it's fun to play with mash-up descriptions – even she offers her own colorful takes - “What if Brian Eno, Scott Walker and Lee Hazlewood were all partying?” and “It's like a Broadway show playing on a dive bar stage.” But beyond the adjectives and metaphorical accolades, you arrive at one simple fact. Atkins has the alchemical ability to transform her influences into singular sonic statements. As a songwriter, she leans into the personal. And as a singer, her unabashedly dramatic voice flies far above easy comparison. Think of her as a retro futurist, a transcendental medium, and very much an artist following her own muses.
Her journey began in Neptune City, New Jersey, where she developed her taste and sensibility early. “There's a poetic isolation at the Jersey shore,” she says. “All the tourists leave, and you're stuck with this really gloomy, but beautiful place, and nothing to do. Also, there were all these summertime musicians who'd play every night on the beach. I grew up thinking that was a normal job.” Raiding the record collections of her parents and grandparents drew her to dramatic singers from Candi Staton to Roy Orbison. When she found an old acoustic guitar in the attic of her uncle's house, her course was set. “Actually, I either wanted to be a rock star or a professional wrestler,” Atkins says, with a laugh.
In a weird way, she became both. After the splash of her major label debut Neptune City in 2007, she toured with The Black Keys and Nick Cave, did TV appearances and got tons of press. But when that didn't translate into big sales, she tumbled into years of music business limbo. While she kept making solid albums, Atkins admits she lost focus and her sense of joy. A move to Nashville with her husband provided a tonic that helped her climb back in the ring. “There's a great community of songwriters here, so I feel supported,” she says. “Songwriting has become a normal part of my life. Eat lunch, listen to a record, write a song. It's nice to be in a place where you have poetic-minded friends all around who just keep you in the flow of it.”
Among those friends is Chris Isaak, who she has regularly toured with for years (he duets with her on the wonderfully moody “Cue The Symphony”). “Chris has been so supportive,” she says of the “Wicked Game” singer, who in 2021 partnered with Sun Records as an artist and curator of new music. “When he heard the songs I was writing, he said, 'I should sign you to Sun.' And suddenly, it was like, 'Wow, I'm gonna make a record again!'”
It had been six years since her last, Italian Ice, and Atkins admits she had some self-doubt. Enter another Nashville pal, Patrick Sansone. The producer and Wilco multi-instrumentalist proved to be the perfect foil for Drama. “Pat knows so much about that chamber pop style of music, and that's my North Star and home base,” Atkins says. “I write like I write - sometimes it sounds '80s, sometimes it sounds '60s, sometimes it sounds '50s. And Pat always gets it. He was able to help me sprinkle that baroque sound throughout the whole record, so it all made sense together.”
Accompanied by her touring band (John Paul Keith on guitar, Danny Banks on drums, plus guests Eric Slick of Dr. Dog, Dan Creamer of The Texas Gentlemen and Scottish troubadour Davey Horne), rhythm tracks were cut over four days, capturing a live sound (“For me, it's always about how the song will translate on stage,” Atkins says). Then she and Sansone hunkered down in his home studio for overdubs. “I've never worked with somebody who I trust that much to add arrangement touches and parts to my songs,” Atkins says. “And even occasionally if I didn't love some part he did, he wouldn't be hurt. Pat's such a pro, and a positive force.”
With a summertime release, and touring planned for early 2027, Atkins feels optimistic about the album, noting a change in the music world at large. “When I first came out, I was kind of on an island,” she says. “Nobody other than Richard Hawley was doing new takes on past love for melodies. There's more of a scene now. Lemon Twigs, Steven Sanchez, The Last Dinner Party, Haute & Freddy. I felt like they gave me permission to just be myself.”
And as on previous albums, she ups the ante by aiming to “write modern songs that could be part of the Great American Songbook.” But in her own way. “I'm not trying to rehash or celebrate some bygone era,” she says. “I'm just taking what I like melodically from the past, and channeling it into my songs. I like to make them deeply personal. The question I come back to is - how do I make this sound exactly like me?”
Drama sounds exactly like Nicole Atkins.

title: 2nd Set With Charles Heath
description:
Originating from Chicago, IL, Charles “Rick” Heath IV is a versatile and renowned musician from local to international levels. Playing anything from Jazz and Blues to Gospel and Latin music, his signature sound is prominent in the recording studios, concert settings, live Broadway theater platforms, and as the drummer for late pianist and jazz legend Ramsey Lewis. Some of his proudest accolades include works with Donald Byrd, McCoy Tyner, and Slide Hampton. He also served as the resident drummer with the national tour of Oprah Winfrey and Quincy Jones’ theater production of “The Color Purple.” He is often rotating hats of composer, band leader, recording artist, musical director, producer and teacher and simply inspires and outreaches to his surrounding communities at all times.
Heath’s prominent sound can be heard on recordings with Ramsey Lewis, Robert “Babe” Irving III, Bobby Broom, Zvonimir Tot, Larry Gray, Sergio Perez, Ken Chaney and the Roger Harris Trio. He proudly launched his first independent recording project entitled “Conversations” encompassing the sound of his very own Charles Heath Quartet.

title: Makaya McCraven
description: Doors: 8PM / Show: 9PM / 21+ Makaya McCraven is a prolific drummer, composer and producer. His newest album, In These Times, is the triumphant finale of a project 7+ years in the making. It's a preeminent addition to his already-acclaimed and extensive discography, and it's the album he's been trying to make since he started making records. McCraven believes that the word , "rdquo" -> jazz" is , "rdquo" -> insufficient, at best, to describe the phenomenon we're dealing with." The artist, who has been aptly called a , "rdquo" -> cultural synthesizer", has a unique gift for collapsing space, destroying borders and blending past, present, and future into poly-textural arrangements of post-genre, jazz-rooted 21st century folk music. Profiled in Vice, Rolling Stone, the Guardian, and NPR, among other publications, he and the music he makes today are at the very vanguard of that phenomenon. According to the New York Times, , "rdquo" -> McCraven has quietly become one of the best arguments for jazz's vitality". The artist explained to NPR in 2019, "I don't think what I'm doing is necessarily that far off of the legacy of jazz that I grew up in ... I think one of the things that gives it strength is that people want to argue over it. That's a good sign. That means there's life here." Born in Paris in the Autumn of 1983 to Hungarian singer and flutist Ágnes Zsigmondi and African-American expat jazz drummer Stephen McCraven, Makaya was raised in a vibrant, creative community in the Northampton, Massachusetts area, where his father often played with artists like saxophonist and ethnomusicologist Marion Brown, multi-instrumentalist Yusef Lateef, and saxophonist Archie Shepp, as well as a cadre of African Gnawa musicians. That scene, with its enticing blend of cultures, helped establish his philosophy around jazz as folk music. Meanwhile, his mother's music blended Eastern European folk traditions, concurrently shaping his conceptions about the role of music in building and reflecting communities.

title: Mike Wheeler Blues Band w/ Demetria Taylor
description:
Demetria Taylor 
has been performing at BLUE CHICAGO 
since 2010. She is the seventh 
child of eight from the family of the late blues legend Eddie Taylor Sr. and is 
helping keep the legacy of her father alive.
Eddie is best known as the rhythm 
guitarist in the band of Jimmy Reed but he also had his own solo career and 
recorded some wonderful sides for the VJ label including the classic "Bad 
Boy". Her mother Vera Taylor was also a blues singer. Demetria has fond 
memories of blues greats and friends of the family coming by the house-- 
including Floyd Jones, Carey Bell, Sunnyland Slim, Johnny Littlejohn, Sam Lay, 
Willie Kent, Tail Dragger, Eddie Shaw, Johnny B. Moore and Magic Slim.
Born in Chicago, 
Demetria grew up surrounded by Blues music listening on records to her biggest 
influences including Etta James, Bessie Smith, Big Mama Thornton and most 
importantly, "The Queen of The Blues" Koko Taylor (no relation to the 
Eddie Taylor family).
Demetria started 
playing drums at age 14, coached by her older brothers Larry and Tim, both 
professional blues drummers. She played in family shows across Chicago which 
also featured brother Eddie Taylor Jr. on guitar. She also sang in the gospel 
choir at Trinity All Nations Church on Chicago's south side.
"I put God 
first and everything else will work out", says Demetria. "I feel that singing is something I was born to do. 
Sometimes on the stage my eyes tear up as I feel the music I'm singing. I love 
to listen to all types of music, but the blues caught my ear. I'll never give 
up my dream."
Demetria has 
toured nationally and internationally and performs in many clubs and festivals 
including the Chicago Blues Festival. Her first album, Bad Girl, is on Delmark 
Records. Demetria was nominated in 
2012 Blues Music Awards for 
"Best New Debut Artist".

title: Thelma & Louise
description:
DIRECTED BY
Ridley Scott
WRITTEN BY
Callie Khouri
STARRING
Susan Sarandon,
Geena Davis,
Harvey Keitel
Having begun his career by making a woman the central figure of a science-fiction action movie (Alien), Ridley Scott cemented his feminist credentials with this bracingly smart, funny and touching portrait of female friendship and solidarity. When put-upon housewife Thelma (Geena Davis) and her waitress gal-pal Louise (Susan Sarandon) set off on a weekend getaway in the latter’s 1966 Ford T-bird, a drunken altercation in the parking lot of a seedy cowboy bar turns these vacationers into fugitives from justice. Soon, they’re blazing a trail across Monument Valley with befuddled boyfriends, FBI agents, a surprisingly sympathetic detective (Harvey Keitel) and Brad Pitt’s six-pack in pursuit, moving ever further away from their humdrum lives and towards an existential void as wide as well, the Grand Canyon. A mid-career triumph for Scott, Thelma & Louise won a Best Original Screenplay for Callie Khouri’s script and five additional nominations including Best Director, Actress (for Davis and Sarandon) and cinematography (by the late, great Adrian Biddle). - Text courtesy of Film at Lincoln Center

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago

Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.

title: ISAC Exhibit: Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia
location: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC) Museum
description:
Seven years ago, Hartapu was little more than a name. Then, in 2019, an inscribed stone pulled from an irrigation canal in central Türkiye introduced the world to a king who claimed to have conquered Phrygia—one of the most powerful kingdoms of the ancient world. Suddenly, a ruler and a kingdom largely unknown to history demanded a place on the map of Iron Age Anatolia. The stone was found at Türkmen-Karahöyük, a massive tell rising 35 meters above the Konya Plain, that must have been Hartapu’s capital. Though the site had gone largely unnoticed by archaeologists, it is one of the largest Iron Age sites in Anatolia—and excavations launched in 2024 by ISAC and Bilkent University (Ankara, Türkiye) are only beginning to reveal the city’s historical development.
 Hartapu ruled in the eighth century BCE, during a period of intense rivalry between great powers—Phrygia to the west, the Neo-Assyrian Empire to the east—and his kingdom sat squarely between them. The exhibition tells his story through ancient inscriptions, archaeological finds, and new technologies, including 3D printing and advanced imaging, that are transforming how scholars study the past. Contemporary works by artist SaraNoa Mark offer a counterpoint, reflecting on landscape, memory, and the labor and care of preserving the past.
 The ISAC Museum special exhibition Hartapu: The Forgotten King of Anatolia is on view from September 17, 2026 through March 14, 2027. It is accessible with museum admission during museum hours.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Foundations of Economic Integration since the Nineteenth Century
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
The straightjackets undergirding common narratives – “free market” against “state intervention”, “free trade” against “mercantilism,” or “financial liberalization” against “regulation” – betray the need to explore the diversity of forms global economic integration or disintegration may assume. We believe that detailed archival research and a distinct historical framework can elucidate the heterogeneity of linkages in the global economy over time.
 We seek contributions that more precisely map the forces compelling economic integration, examine why such connections have repeatedly frayed or been disrupted, and move beyond common binary or linear narratives on the topic.
 The conference will take place over two days, with one day hosted at Sciences Po Paris and the other at the University of Chicago Center in Paris. It will open and close with two keynote lectures.

description:
This exhibition features new works by the French artist and filmmaker Pierre Bismuth. The centerpiece is a long-form meditative film documenting a creative collaboration between Joshua Abrams and Sharon Udoh, two leading figures from Chicago’s jazz and improvised music scene. Bismuth tasked them with composing a 21st-century spiritual based on a lyrical hymn he wrote for the project. title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding.

title: Computational Social Science Workshop: Pathways in Professional Data Science with Rajat Paul and Sruti Kathan (IBM)
description:
Rajat Paul will share insights from his nearly 3 decade long career at IBM. He will be joined by Sruti Kanthan, Data Scientist at MACSS 2021 graduate. Rajat and Sruti will discuss their own pathways into Data Science and Consulting, industry trends, and how job seekers can best prepare for the job market.
 Rajat Paul is a technology leader with more than 25 years of experience in digital strategy, business process automation, and artificial intelligence. A Carnegie Mellon University alumnus, he is an Associate Partner and Chief Automation Architect at IBM Consulting, where he leads intelligent automation and business process management initiatives for the U.S. Federal sector. He has spent nearly three decades at IBM, working across healthcare, financial, human resources, and case management systems, including Medicare, Medicaid, and law enforcement coordination programs. As Chief Automation Architect from 2018, he designed and implemented the IBM Intelligent Automation Platform, an AI-driven, FedRAMP-compliant managed service combining RPA, BPM, content management, OCR, and natural language processing. Rajat is recognized as a thought leader in BPM and RPA, with deep experience across platforms such as IBM BAW, Pega, Appian, Blue Prism, and UiPath. His current focus includes generative AI, AI agents, and fraud, waste, and abuse prevention.
 Sruti Kanthan is an NLP data scientist at IBM, where she consults for the Department of Veterans Affairs. She is building an evaluation framework for a RAG-based Q&A tool that helps veterans with claims, which lets the testing team assess model performance with less manual review by subject matter experts. She also leads Watsonx.gov integration, designing a reusable governance framework for other teams and projects. Earlier at IBM, she led a cancer care tracking initiative on the VA’s Health Analytics Platform, identifying veterans at risk of delayed care because of clerical errors. Sruti holds a master’s in Computational Social Science from the University of Chicago (2021). Her thesis used machine learning to trace a shared cultural lineage between two mythological epics. Sruti then completed an Applied Data Fellowship at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, working with the American Association for the Advancement of Science on membership analysis and DEI initiative evaluation. She is passionate about using data science to improve diagnosis and care delivery, especially for historically underserved populations.

 Sruti Kanthan is an NLP data scientist at IBM, where she consults for the Department of Veterans Affairs. title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Article 19: The Global Right to Free Expression
description:
The right to freedom of opinion and expression is a cornerstone of international human rights law. Codified in Article 19 of both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), it protects the freedom to hold opinions and to seek, receive, and impart ideas, regardless of frontiers. This event examines how that right operates in the international human rights context and why defending it matters today.
 We are joined by Leopoldo Maldonado Gutiérrez, appointed UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression in July 2026. A Mexican lawyer with nearly 20 years of experience defending journalists and civic space, he spent thirteen years with ARTICLE 19, rising to Regional Director for Mexico and Central America. His work includes investigating spyware and surveillance targeting civil society and shaping policy on platform governance and artificial intelligence.
 The conversation will be moderated by the Chicago Forum Faculty Director Tom Ginsburg.
 This event is part of the Global Free Expression Project, which carries the mission of the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression into the international arena. In partnership with the University of Chicago Law School’s Global Human Rights Clinic and the Pozen Family Center for Human Rights, the Chicago Forum seeks to support a leading global mandate on freedom of expression and opinion with sustained research, convening, and analytical assistance.
 Attendees can join in person or virtually. Lunch to be provided for in person guests.
 Lead support for the Chicago Forum’s Zell Speaker and Event Series comes from the Zell Family Foundation.

description:
This talk explores how criminal assistance shapes public perceptions of organized criminal groups, and how its effectiveness depends on the political lens through which citizens interpret criminal assistance. In Mexico, criminal assistance has become more visible since the COVID‑19 pandemic, and targeted assistance by criminal actors mirrors the state’s own targeted distribution of goods. By leveraging these parallels, we assess how criminal governance influences public evaluations of OCGs, illuminating how non-state actors compete for legitimacy in contested governance environments.
 ​Camila Angulo is an Assistant Professor of Political Science at Indiana University Northwest. Professor Angulo’s research focuses on the political economy of development in Latin America, criminal governance, violence, and public opinion. Her work has been published in academic journals such as World Development, the Journal of Politics in Latin America, Governance, the Wisconsin Law Review, and Colombia Internacional.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

title: Autumn Reading Group – Meeting 3
description:
(A commitment to all three sessions is required for registration.)
 The date of this session is reflective of the finalized schedule.
 Join us for our third Autumn Quarter reading group meeting to discuss James Lang’s 2020 book Distracted: Why Students Can’t Focus and What You Can Do About It.
 Why is it so hard for students – and for us – to pay attention? We know that distraction isn’t good for learning, but it can be hard to resist other demands on our attention. With regard to learning, distraction is widely seen to be an impediment, something to avoid at all costs. But recent research reveals that our brains aren’t designed for intense focus all the time, and distraction can sometimes even help us. Although we often want our classrooms to be distraction-free zones, Lang points out that in requiring focus all the time, we’re working against our brains’ natural function. Lang offers ways for us to think about the classroom not as a ‘distraction-free zone’ but rather as a place that nurtures students’ attention.
 Reading Group meetings are informal and provide an opportunity to share reactions, questions, and thoughts about implementation and practice, however, for planning purposes, we ask that those interested in participating only register if they plan to attend all three sessions.

title: RDI Workshop Series - Sony Coranez Bolton
description:
RDI Workshop Series: Professor Sony Coráñez Bolton
 November 19, 2026 | 4:00-5:30 pm | Kelly 108
 This workshop is based on the second chapter of Coráñez Bolton’s second book, Dos X: Disability and Racial Dysphoria in Latinx and Filipinx Culture (University of Texas Press 2025). The chapter engages in a disability reading of Frederick Jackson Turner’s watershed essay “The Significance of the Frontier in American History” (1893). It argues that Turner conceived of ability as a form of property central to and accumulated through the settler projection of U.S. American power. “Ability as Property” serves to understand a historical flashpoint that anchors the beginnings of US transpacific expansion in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
 Sony Coráñez Bolton is Anthony S. Chan ’72 Professor in Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies and Professor of English & Spanish at Amherst College. He is the author of Crip Colony: Mestizaje, US Imperialism, and the Queer Politics of Disability in the Philippines (Duke 2023), winner of the 2024 Lora Romero First Book Prize presented by the American Studies Association. It demonstrates the ways that colonialism and disability are part of a unified ideological structure in Philippine mestizo politics. His second book, Dos X: Disability and Racial Dysphoria in Latinx and Filipinx Culture (University of Texas Press 2025) uncovers the logics and aesthetics of racial misrecognition in Latinx and Filipinx culture and politics. His work has appeared in Critical Ethnic Studies, Disability Studies Quarterly, Journal of Asian American Studies, Periphêrica, and Verge: Studies in Global Asias.

title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
description:

A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group – many of whom had not seen each other in fifty years – reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Shot on 16mm film, newly restored and now directed by Greaves’ son David, this landmark film is at once a self-exploration and an inquiry into the heart of the critical mass of energy called the Harlem Renaissance. William Greaves’ intent was not only to document these artists and intellectuals as they spoke about their lives and work but also to plumb the meaning of the extraordinary creative period in which they lived to help us better understand how culture has been passed on from one generation to another and the role that the artist plays in keeping it alive.

title: Anjan Chatterjee & Judith Schaechter on Neuroaesthetics
description:
Neurologist, Professor, and Director of the Penn Center for Neuroaesthetics Anjan Chatterjee and glass artist Judith Schaechter discuss how the brain perceives, creates, and responds to art. The program will draw on Schaechter’s experience as artist-in-residence at the Center and Chatterjee’s ongoing research into the brain and aesthetic experiences. What might artists and scientists learn from one another? How can expanding our understanding of perception deepen our capacity to appreciate beauty?
 Free; registration encouraged.
 Judith Schaechter lives and works in Philadelphia. Her work is collected internationally and is represented in the collections of the Smithsonian, the Metropolitan Museum in New York, the Victoria and Albert in London and the Hermitage, among others. She is the recipient of numerous awards including the Guggenheim Fellowship in 2005 and her work was in the 2002 Whitney Biennial. 1n 2013, Judith was inducted to the College of Fellows of the American Craft Council. She received a lifetime achievement award from the Glass Art Society in 2022 and in 2023, she was named a Smithsonian Visionary Artist.
 In 2020-21, Judith’s work was the subject of a retrospective exhibition organized by the Memorial Art Gallery of Rochester, NY, which traveled to the Toledo Museum and the Des Moines Art Center.
 Anjan Chatterjee is Professor of Neurology, Psychology, and Architecture at the University of Pennsylvania and the founding director of the Penn Center for Neuroaesthetics. He received a BA in Philosophy from Haverford College and MD from the University of Pennsylvania. A past Neurology Chair at Pennsylvania Hospital, his research addresses neuroaesthetics, spatial cognition, language, and neuroethics. He wrote The Aesthetic Brain and co-edited Brain, Beauty, and Art, as well as Neuroethics in Practice, and The Roots of Cognitive Neuroscience. His editorial services have included neuroscience, psychology, aesthetics and bioethics journals. He received the Norman Geschwind Prize in Behavioral and Cognitive Neurology from the American Academy of Neurology, the Rudolph Arnheim Prize for contributions to Psychology and the Arts from the American Psychological Association, the Gustav Fechner Award for life-time contributions from the International Association of Empirical Aesthetics, the Leadership in Innovation Award from the Global Wellness Institute, the Lawrence Forman Award for contributions to the betterment of society from Haverford College, and The Big Sea Award for the Promotion of Aesthetic Beauty from the Mediterranean Tourism Forum. He is a founding member of the Board of the International Neuroethics Society, past President of the International Association of Empirical Aesthetics, and of the Behavioral Neurology Society. He serves on the board of the College of Physicians of Philadelphia, and Philadelphia Fringe Arts. He previously served on the boards of Haverford College, the Global Wellness Institute, the Norris Square Neighborhood Project, and the Associated Services for the Blind and Visually Impaired.

title: Radical Resistance, Religion, and the Meaning of Social Change
description:
This event will be held in-person at the Newberry and online via Zoom. The online version of this event will be live captioned. Please register below.
How do the ideals of one generation become the inheritance of the next?
Join playwright and memoirist Zayd Ayers Dohrn and religious scholar Sarah Hammerschlag as they explore enduring intersections of faith, identity, political activism, and family memory, asking how the moral and spiritual questions of that era continue to shape our world today.
Dangerous, Dirty, Violent, and Young: A Fugitive Family in the Revolutionary Underground will be available to purchase in the Newberry Bookshop, and the author will sign copies after the talk.
This program is part of Beyond Belief: Religion and Social Change in 1960s Chicago, a wide-ranging Newberry initiative running through 2029. It is generously supported by Lilly Endowment Inc., through its Religion and Cultural Institutions Initiative.
Zayd Ayers Dohrn is an award-winning playwright, documentary podcaster, and director of the MFA in Writing for Screen + Stage in the Department of Radio/Television/Film at Northwestern University. His recent memoir, Dangerous, Dirty, Violent, and Young: A Fugitive Family in the Revolutionary Underground, recounts his early life as the son of Weather Underground radicals.
Sarah Hammerschlag, John Nuveen Professor of Religion and Literature, Philosophy of Religions, and History of Judaism at the University of Chicago Divinity School, takes a multidisciplinary approach to studying the intersection of religion, identity, and politics. Her most recent book, co-authored with Constance Furey and Amy Hollywood, is Devotion: Three Inquiries in Religion, Literature, and Political Imagination.
This program is free and open to all. Advance registration required.
Registration opens October 1.

title: Nathan Gelgud, "No Concessions" Gremlins 2 Film Screening @ Music Box
description:
About the Book:
Your favorite gang of militant movie lovers are back for an all-new season of hijinks and takeovers from their small town single-screen cinema. The Reel Politik guerillas discuss how to be an effective revolutionary while fighting the all-consuming evils of corporate Hollywood. Meditate! Fight your inner urge to binge watch! Engage in a cinema fast to truly appreciate the oeuvre of an auteur! Realism is bourgeois! In an attempt to thwart a Hollywood studio from co-opting the story of the Weather Underground, the gang then pursues its own cinematic celebration of their hero Bernardine Dohrn. With his trademark slapstick zingers, Gelgud lovingly skewers leftist radical politics while simultaneously illustrating how late stage capitalism has made ethical decision making fraught with compromise. At once a celebration of what makes Hollywood and independent local cinema great and a call to arms to protect it.
About the Author:
Nathan Gelgud has been drawing the Reel Politik comic strip since 2024; No Concessions! is the second collection of the strips published by Drawn & Quarterly. Gelgud has been a projectionist, a video store clerk, and a movie critic. He occasionally makes non-fiction comics about the arts for the New York Times and Hyperallergic, designs director-themed tote bags and t-shirts, and is a frequent guest on The Best Show with Tom Scharpling. title: STEM to the Future: A Comedic Review of American Innovation Since the 80's
description:
C2ST's annual Fall Social is back! Come revel in awe of the scientific breakthroughs that came from this prolific era of innovation.
This year's Fall Social was created to be a celebration of human ingenuity & scientific work & discovery. Our annual fundraiser & networking event brings together STEM professionals, educators, entrepreneurs, community leaders, supporters & friends for an evening of connection, laughter & philanthropy.
Through a playful retrospective on technological & scientific innovation since the 80's, C2ST and Co. will explore how big ideas, like the first artificial heart, or even the piano tie, shaped a new reality.
The Featured Experience: An Intentional Improv KeynoteThe centerpiece of the evening will be an interactive improv keynote that turns the traditional keynote on its head. Guests will help shape the presentation in real time with audience prompts, unexpected scenarios, innovation “what-ifs,” and the spontaneous challenges that become part of a comedic journey through decades of scientific innovation.
As all powerful STEM lessons demonstrate, innovation rarely follows a straight line. Experimentation, collaboration, failure, adaptation, and the willingness to try something unexpected are often what move an idea forward!
Guests can expect:
A fast-paced comedic look at memorable moments in the history of scientific and technological innovation.
Audience participation that directly influences the keynote.
Improvised scenarios inspired by real STEM breakthroughs and cultural moments.
Opportunities for guests to collaborate, laugh, and connect across disciplines.
A live band to accompany the evening of fun!
An 80's costume contest with a prize for the winner and runner-up!
A few surprises that cannot be rehearsed—because that’s the point!
More Than a Night OutThe evening will also be an opportunity to support C2ST's mission and work to expand and maintain access to STEM education, mentorship, and opportunities.
Whether you’re a lifelong STEM enthusiast, a casual technology observer, an educator, an entrepreneur, or simply someone who enjoys a good story about how we got from the ’80s to the age of AI, this is an evening designed to bring people together!
Expect technology. Expect nostalgia. Expect philanthropy. Expect the unexpected.
And most importantly, expect to be part of the show!

title: November Yearning & Learning Book Club
description:
Join us at our next meeting of the Yearning & Learning Book Club in November to discuss Refusing Compulsory Sexuality: A Black Asexual Lens on Our Sex-Obsessed Culture by Sherronda J. Brown!
Please note that this club is mask-required for in person attendees and adults only (18+)
If you like to read (in a gay way), join the club on Thursday, November 19th from 6-8 PM over Zoom or in-person in Gerber/Hart’s Raffety/Tran Community Room — 6500 N Clark St, 2nd Floor. Elevator located at end of hallway (past Howard Brown front desk)
To attend virtually, please register on Zoom in advance here.
We’ll engage in an open discussion, reading some excerpts that stuck with us & sharing our thoughts! If you’re able to finish the book by the book club date, great! If you aren’t, that’s all good, too, but please expect spoilers.
Refusing Compulsory Sexuality: A Black Asexual Lens on Our Sex-Obsessed Culture by Sherronda J. Brown: A Black queer feminist exploration of asexuality–and an incisive interrogation of the sex-obsessed culture that invisibilizes and ignores asexual and A-spec identity. The notion that everyone wants sex–and that we all have to have it–is false. It’s intertwined with our ideas about capitalism, race, gender, and queerness. And it impacts the most marginalized among us. (description from Penguin Random House)
Yearning & Learning is Gerber/Hart’s FREE queer quarterly book club, facilitated by Liz Johnson. (@reallylizjohnson) Half non-fiction, half fiction. Half contemporary, half classic. All to do with queerness, love, and the many forms of both.

title: 1st Set With Mario Abney
description:
As a Chicago native, Mario Abney’s trumpet playing fuses traditional and extended techniques in an inventive way. His uniquely personal vision for music endows it with an infinite array of tonal colors. He is recognized for his ability to create pure musical dialogues and hear music in a universally spiritual way. These qualities make him one of New Orleans’ most pioneering young jazz musicians.
Trumpeter, composer and bandleader Mario Abney’s musical career began at age 7 when he was introduced to the piano by his uncle Arthur. Influenced by both his uncle’s playing and the musical background of his church, Abney developed a love and fascination for music that grew throughout his years in high school. It was during this time that his interest turned from piano and drums to wind instruments; however, he continued to hone his percussion skills by playing drums for church services.
Mario’s first encounter with jazz was when he heard the sounds of trumpeter Wynton Marsalis. This sparked a fascination and soon Mario began to explore music by Louis Armstrong, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis and other great trumpet players who established this genre.
Fast forwarding to 2024, Mario Abney is once again gracing the stages of his beloved hometown Chicago. From iconic venues to up-and-coming spots, he’s become a regular feature with fans eagerly anticipating each and every performance.

title: Insight Meditation Sangha
description:
Insight Meditation is based on the early Buddhist teachings found in the Pali Canon and forms the basis for contemporary secular mindfulness practices. The group meets for 90 minutes, which includes instructions and chanting, sitting and walking meditation, and talks and discussions that illuminate the key teachings on meditation and insight. The meditations focus on developing tranquility (Samadhi), insight (Vipassana), and Lovingkindness (Metta). No prior experience necessary. 
 The weekly meditation is usually led by Jon Aaron, who has been teaching in the Insight tradition for over 20 years at New York Insight and other communities. He is also a certified teacher and teacher trainer in Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction.

title: Maria Pappas, "Maria the Pappas"
description:
ABOUT THE BOOK:
Maria the Pappas is an autobiographical portrait of Maria Pappas that explains not simply what she has done, but why she became the person she is. The memoir presents Pappas as a collection of apparent contradictions: a hard-driving politician and deeply emotional helper; a government reformer and flamboyant public personality; a Cretan Greek from West Virginia who became a fixture of Chicago politics; and a woman comfortable confronting powerful politicians while also spending enormous amounts of time with ordinary taxpayers, immigrants, clergy, community activists and people experiencing hardship. Pappas describes herself as bold, direct and authentic, but says the fundamental values underneath that personality are faith, honesty, loyalty and service.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR:
Maria Pappas is Treasurer of Cook County, Illinois, a post she has held since 1998. She was elected to a seventh four-year term in November of 2022.Pappas has remade the Office of Treasurer for Cook County, the world’s 16th largest government, into a vibrant, service-oriented office that develops and uses the latest technological tools for greater efficiency and economy.A lawyer with a degree in counseling psychology, her organizational and management skills have drawn the attention of foreign governments that have asked for her help with projects.

Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.

title: Gremlins 2: The New Batch
description:
DIRECTED BY
Joe Dante,
Chuck Jones (animation sequences)
WRITTEN BY
Charles S. Haas,
Chris Columbus (based on characters created by)
STARRING
Zach Galligan,
Phoebe Cates,
Howie Mandel (voice)
Possibly the most anarchic film ever unleashed out of Hollywood, Gremlins 2: The New Batch is a chaotic, live-action Looney Tunes cartoon that could only come from the mind of auteur Joe Dante. Taking the piss out of his own original Gremlins and sequels in general, Gremlins 2’s wild tone showcases what art can happen when a studio — in this case, Warner Bros. — gives over complete control to a director with a vision. That’s not to discredit the script from Charlie Haas (Over the Edge, Matinee), which folds right into Dante’s influences of cartoons, monster movies, and an irreverent sense of humor. Chock full of easter eggs and cameos, from Christopher Lee carrying an Invasion of the Body Snatchers pod to Leonard Maltin and the return of Dick Miller, Gremlins 2: The New Batch answers the question: What if someone made a live-action Mad Magazine parody of Gremlins?
About the Author:
Nathan Gelgud has been drawing the Reel Politik comic strip since 2024; No Concessions! is the second collection of the strips published by Drawn & Quarterly. Gelgud has been a projectionist, a video store clerk, and a movie critic. He occasionally makes non-fiction comics about the arts for the New York Times and Hyperallergic, designs director-themed tote bags and t-shirts, and is a frequent guest on The Best Show with Tom Scharpling. He lives in Los Angeles, where conducts comics-making workshops at Scribble.
About the Book:
Your favorite gang of militant movie lovers are back for an all-new season of hijinks and takeovers from their small town single-screen cinema. The Reel Politik guerillas discuss how to be an effective revolutionary while fighting the all-consuming evils of corporate Hollywood. Meditate! Fight your inner urge to binge watch! Engage in a cinema fast to truly appreciate the oeuvre of an auteur! Realism is bourgeois! In an attempt to thwart a Hollywood studio from co-opting the story of the Weather Underground, the gang then pursues its own cinematic celebration of their hero Bernardine Dohrn. With his trademark slapstick zingers, Gelgud lovingly skewers leftist radical politics while simultaneously illustrating how late stage capitalism has made ethical decision making fraught with compromise. At once a celebration of what makes Hollywood and independent local cinema great and a call to arms to protect it.

title: The Filthy Heathens, Shannon Baker And The Burners, Matt Keen & His Band
description:
THE FILTHY HEATHENS
The Filthy Heathens came together during the chaos of the pandemic, driven by a shared instinct to play loud, honest music with no safety net. What began with the chemistry between Bronson Hetzer, Ryan Palcic, and “Captain” Craig Bishop took shape fast when guitarists Cody Doench and Dawson Stepp joined the fold. Five members. No brakes. Blending Southern grit with alt-edge, classic country with hard rock, their sound defies easy classification. It’s rich, raw, and rooted in something deeper than genre. You can’t quite label it — and that’s the point. Inspired by legends like Skynyrd and Waylon, with a nod to modern acts like Blackberry Smoke and The Steel Woods, their songs are road-tested, unapologetic, and built to be felt. Known for high-octane live shows and a fast-growing fanbase, The Filthy Heathens have been hitting stages across the country with relentless momentum. One gig at a time, they’re building something real — and it’s catching on. Live, the band goes full throttle, pulling crowds straight into the moment. Their debut EP Etheridge dropped in May 2025, led by the singles “Tupelo Sun” and “Devils Like Me.” In February 2026, the band will release The Muscle Shoals Session, a raw, live-recorded EP captured at the legendary Muscle Shoals Sound Studio. No frills. No filters. Just who they are on stage. The fuse is lit. The momentum keeps building. The Filthy Heathens return to the studio in April 2026 — louder, tighter, and more dialed-in than ever.
SHANNON BAKER AND THE BURNERS
Shannon Baker and her catalogue of melodic original songs have been a mainstay in musical venues all over Chicago. The Burners (Dan Kane, Michael Fitz, Bobby Puetz, and Pat Corbett) added sonic layers to a rich collection of songs that leave an echo of nostalgia for the classics of while remaining consistently fresh throughout.

title: Open Mic
description:
More Info
OPEN MICat Gallery Cabaret
Got Talent—or Think You Do?
Every great music story starts somewhere. Yours could start here.
Welcome to Gallery Cabaret, home of the North Side’s longest-running open mic, where emerging talent takes the stage, seasoned musicians guide you into the spotlight, and anything can happen. Sing a song, try out new material, show off your skills, or grab a drink and discover your next favorite artist. Our hosts are professional musicians, the atmosphere is unmistakably Gallery, and the stage is open to anyone ready to take a shot.
Need a little inspiration? The Smashing Pumpkins, Urge Overkill, and Liz Phair all played open mic at Gallery Cabaret before becoming household names. And the Rolling Stones? They played through some of the very speakers still on our stage today.
From sharp stand-up and unfiltered storytelling to spoken word that makes you think, Gallery Cabaret is a stage for voices that deserve to be heard. We’re creating space for comedians, poets, storytellers, and fearless performers to experiment, connect, and bring something unexpected to the room. Whether you’re chasing your next big laugh or looking for a fresh perspective, come experience the talent, energy, and creative edge that keep Chicago’s independent scene alive.
That’s not nostalgia. That’s real history—and it’s still being made.
No cover. No pressure. Just great music, killer drinks, and a stage waiting for you.
Come for the music. Stay for the stories. Who knows? The next one might be yours.

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream
description:
“Give me your hands, if we be friends”
Sparkling with the festive spirit of the holiday season, Shakespeare’s magical romantic comedy is a delectable treat for the entire family. An enchanting story of love, marriage, and magic, this holiday “Dream” will fill you with happiness and hope.

Under the creative leadership of CST Artistic Director Edward Hall and taking its inspiration from Shakespeare’s own company and CST’s roots as the Shakespeare Repertory, a company of 14 actors perform both The Winter’s Tale and A Midsummer Night’s Dream, two of Shakespeare’s most beguiling fairy tales. This double header of productions makes for a thrilling theatrical experience, with two beautiful plays exploring the formidable power of love, laughter and forgiveness.

title: Yung Pueblo, "Journey"
description:
About the Book:
A year-long guide to letting go of stress and finding your purpose from #1 New York Times bestselling author, Time 100 Creator, meditator, and modern poet Yung Pueblo, one of today’s brightest lights in personal growth and compassion.
“Journey is a playbook for calming your nervous system, finding your center, and living with the kind of peace and gratitude that can enrich your life.”—Tom Brady
“Yung Pueblo has a remarkable way of writing exactly what you need to hear. Yet this book does something more: it invites you into the conversation.”—Mel Robbins, New York Times bestselling author of The Let Them Theory
Yung Pueblo’s Journey: The Year That Changes Everything is a uniquely accessible and actionable guide filled with words that heal and wisdom that lasts.
Growth is not a destination but a daily, inward journey to uncover two of the greatest prizes a human being can have: self-awareness and inner peace. Journey is filled with thoughtful, short writings that help you look at your life honestly and find practices that lead you to a new sense of inner balance and calm.
Journey will help you build life-changing qualities that are expressed in the visible world by the four major elements: fire, air, earth, and water.
You have immense power inside of you. Use it to build a life of intention and find the transformation you seek. Look to Journey: The Year That Changes Everything as a source of inspiration and a guide as you start a new era of flourishing in your life.
About the Author:
Diego Perez is a #1 New York Times bestselling author who is widely known by his pen name, Yung Pueblo. He has sold nearly two million books worldwide that have been translated into over twenty five languages. Named a Time100 Creator, he has an audience of over four million people online. He cofounded Wisdom Ventures, an investment fund focused on scaling compassion. He lives in western Massachusetts with his wife, Sara.
About the Conversation Partner:
Dr. Alexandra Solomon is internationally recognized as one of today’s most trusted relationship experts. As a licensed clinical psychologist, she translates research and clinical wisdom to help people expand their Relational Self-Awareness. She is an adjunct professor at Northwestern University, the face of MasterClass In Practice, the host of Reimagining Love, and the award-winning author of three bestselling books including Love Every Day. Her work is frequently featured in outlets like NPR, TODAY and New York Times.

title: Henry Cole Jazz Trio
description:
Cole became the first Puerto Rican resident on the island—and only the second nationwide—to receive the New Jazz Works Grant from Chamber Music America for his compositional work with Villa Locura, underscoring his standing as a composer of national significance.
He is widely recognized for his role as drummer for the Grammy Award–winning ensemble led by Miguel Zenón. As a core member of the Quartet for over two decades, Cole has shaped the ensemble’s rhythmic architecture across internationally acclaimed recordings and global tours and contributed to projects that have defined the contemporary Latin and jazz canon.
Cole’s work extends across genres, including collaborations with Tito Allen, Tego Calderón, Andy Montañez, CHano Domigüez, Ben Wendel, Gary Burton, Quincy Jones, Draco Rosa, Daddy Yankee , Natti Natasha and Calle 13 earning a Grammy Award for the latter, among others.
In his latest album, De Mayagüez (2025), Cole returned explicitly to his hometown as a conceptual foundation. The album examines place, memory, and forward motion, internalizing folkloric logic within modern compositional frameworks. It does not reference tradition as ornament; it advances it as structure and propulsion.

title: Project Cinema: Films for South London
location: National Public Housing Museum, 919 S. Ada Street, Chicago, IL 60607
description:
Public housing sites are frequently seen as frightening locations in the popular imagination. Filmmakers have used them as settings of terror and their residents as fearsome antagonists. But what happens when this convention is turned on its head? Join us for a wild and unpredictable adventure through south London’s council estates (public housing) in Joe Cornish’s film horror/comedy, Attack the Block (Rated R).
This screening provides context into the history of public housing in England, which shares many similarities with our own in the USA. This feature and the accompanying short films provide us with a view into the way another country has handled its own housing crises and gives us a mirror for how we can also understand our own.
FREE! Space is limited, please register in advance. Seating will be offered on a first come, first served basis.
The event space is wheelchair accessible and films are closed-captioned.
Food for purchase will be available – vendor to be announced.
Free popcorn will also be served!
Attack the Block (dir. Joe Cornish, 2011, 88 mins)
Rating: R (Drug Content|Creature Violence|Pervasive Language)
When aliens invade a poor neighborhood in London in this thrilling sci-fi romp, a group of rowdy teens decide to fight back and defend their home turf, while a woman whom they mugged inadvertently gets caught up in their struggle.
A Portrait of Central Hill (8 min)
A short documentary by Hark1karan and Alex Donaldson that explores the tight-knit community on south London’s Central Hill Estate and their ongoing resistance against demolition and gentrification.
The Winstanley Plays Itself (6 min)
A short film by a local historian blending archive material, maps, and text from the Survey of London to document the 1960s Winstanley Estate in Battersea.
Matryoshka Living (3 min)
Everyone wants a London postcode, but what lengths will renters go to in order to afford to live in the capital?

title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.
Hayward is made possible by a special gift from Show Sponsor, The Michael and Mona Heath Fund.
The Gift Theatre Company’s 2026 Homecoming Season is made possible, in part, by generous contributions from The Arts Work Fund · The Copernicus Foundation · Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events · The Gaylord and Dorothy Donnelley Foundation · The Illinois Arts Council · Melissa Thornley Consulting · The Paul Angell Foundation · The Rabb Family Foundation · The Saints · The Service Club of Chicago · The Shubert Foundation, Inc.

title: Jazz Stories: Elaine Dame
description:
Contemporary jazz vocalist **Elaine Dame** is a vocal powerhouse celebrated across the nation and when she sings, people stop and listen. Celebrated as “a jazz dynamo” by Time Out Chicago and renowned as “a gem in the city’s vocal jazz scene,” Elaine's commanding presence and extraordinary talent have made her a sought-after fixture at premier venues coast to coast.
From electrifying performances at the legendary Rainbow Room and 54 Below in New York City to headlining appearances at the Chicago Jazz Festival in 2015 and 2025, as well as a standout engagement at Herb Alpert’s Vibrato Jazz Grill in Los Angeles, Elaine consistently elevates every stage she touches. Her virtuosic interpretations blend modern standards with vintage vocal classics, resonating with both jazz aficionados and new audiences alike.
More than just a singer, Elaine exudes genuine joy and magnetic stage presence—qualities that elevate her performances to artful experiences. An alumna of The Theater Repertory Program at California State Northridge, she initially made her mark in Chicago’s vibrant theater scene before dedicating her exceptional talents solely to jazz. Her deep understanding of stagecraft and emotion is evident with every note, and the Chicago Reader lauded her as “a singer with a winning stage presence and chameleon-like vocal flexibility.”
Elaine Dame continues to redefine vocal jazz with her artistry, versatility, and innate magnetism.

Over the last thirty-five years, Canadian Music Hall of Fame inductee Steven Page has established himself as one of the most recognizable and enduring voices in music. title: Insight Meditation Sangha
description:
Insight Meditation is based on the early Buddhist teachings found in the Pali Canon and forms the basis for contemporary secular mindfulness practices. The group meets for 90 minutes, which includes instructions and chanting, sitting and walking meditation, and talks and discussions that illuminate the key teachings on meditation and insight. The meditations focus on developing tranquility (Samadhi), insight (Vipassana), and Lovingkindness (Metta). No prior experience necessary.
The weekly meditation is usually led by Jon Aaron, who has been teaching in the Insight tradition for over 20 years at New York Insight and other communities. He is also a certified teacher and teacher trainer in Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction.

title: Small Brown Bike
description:

Since 1994, Subterranean has been a cornerstone of the Wicker Park live music & nightlife scene. Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: Craig Finn & The Band of Forgiveness
description:
Craig Finn is a Minnesota-bred singer/songwriter based in New York City, best known as the singer of The Hold Steady. Finn spent the ’90's leading Minneapolis indie band Lifter Puller, which released 3 albums and an EP. After relocating to New York, he joined with Lifter Puller member Tad Kubler to form The Hold Steady in 2003. The Hold Steady quickly achieved critical acclaim and a worldwide fanbase with their unique pairing of dense lyrical narratives with big rock guitars. The Hold Steady’s ninth album, The Price Of Progress, was released in March 2023, commemorating the band’s 20th Anniversary.
Craig Finn released his 6th solo album Always Been on April 4. Produced by Adam Granduciel (The War On Drugs), the album features musical performances by Granduciel and members of The War on Drugs, Kathleen Edwards, Sam Fender, and more.
Always Been tells the story of a man who becomes a clergyman despite a lack of faith. The songs detail his rise, fall, and eventual redemption, while also shining a light to sharply reveal the other characters that populate the world he moves through. A limited edition, 92-page companion book Lousy With Ghosts accompanies the album and features 11 works of fiction by Craig Finn. These stories take place in the same universe as the record, giving deeper looks at the characters within.
Finn released his first solo album in 2012 with three additional solo LPs put forth from 2015 - 2019: Faith in the Future, We All Want The Same Things, and 2019's I Need a New War - which coalesced into a sign-of-the-times musical trilogy. Finn’s fifth album, A Legacy of Rentals was released in 2022 and received universal critical acclaim.
That’s How I Remember It is Craig Finn’s podcast series, launched in 2022. Co-produced and distributed by Talkhouse, the podcast series examines the connection between memory and creativity. Each episode features a discussion between Finn and one creator – including musicians, authors, filmmakers, and more – about the role memory plays in their art. These exclusive conversations reveal the different ways each creator synthesizes their remembered life experience to tell stories about themselves and the world we live in. Podcast guests have included George Saunders, Fred Armisen, Bill Hader, Lucinda Williams, Johnny Marr, Jason Isbell, Duff McKagan, Adam Duritz, Ben Gibbard, and many more.

title: 2nd Set With Mario Abney
description:
As a Chicago native, Mario Abney’s trumpet playing fuses traditional and extended techniques in an inventive way. His uniquely personal vision for music endows it with an infinite array of tonal colors. He is recognized for his ability to create pure musical dialogues and hear music in a universally spiritual way. These qualities make him one of New Orleans’ most pioneering young jazz musicians.
Trumpeter, composer and bandleader Mario Abney’s musical career began at age 7 when he was introduced to the piano by his uncle Arthur. Influenced by both his uncle’s playing and the musical background of his church, Abney developed a love and fascination for music that grew throughout his years in high school. It was during this time that his interest turned from piano and drums to wind instruments; however, he continued to hone his percussion skills by playing drums for church services.
Mario’s first encounter with jazz was when he heard the sounds of trumpeter Wynton Marsalis. This sparked a fascination and soon Mario began to explore music by Louis Armstrong, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis and other great trumpet players who established this genre.
Fast forwarding to 2024, Mario Abney is once again gracing the stages of his beloved hometown Chicago. From iconic venues to up-and-coming spots, he’s become a regular feature with fans eagerly anticipating each and every performance.
