title: Magi Merlin w/ MVTE
description:
$18 Adv + Fees | 21+
Magi Merlin’s music drifts between weight and levity with exceptional ease, turning from the nuances of intimacy to the realities of capitalism and womanhood. There’s no sheen of perfection here, no forced pop polish. Through her propulsive, avant-garde form of R&B she explores love, desire and growth and life’s deep existential truths, moving between splintered kick drums, futuristic synth lines and jungle breakbeats.
Her 2022 EP Gone Girl is music that feels genuinely alive, animated by a voice that blends unruly maximalism and earned wisdom, gliding across the chaos with a precision that only comes from deep intuition. A surprise EP, A Weird Little Dog, followed, arriving as she opened for Nubya Garcia across the US, with festival appearances at Osheaga, Festival d’été de Québec where she opened for Ty Dolla $ign, and most recently a European support run with Yaya Bey. Outside of the music, this spring she is making her acting debut in Chandler Levack’s Mile End Kicks, alongside Barbie Ferreira, Devon Bostick and Juliette Gariépy which screened at TIFF and SXSW.
There’s a special kind of kindred spirit that Magi writes for; her fellow obsessives. Screw the soft launch. Magi sings directly to the listener pressed up against the other side of the screen’s glass. POWER HOUSE, her debut album which releases on July 10, is exactly that. A recognition that each person, like the songs themselves, is a powerhouse, an invitation to embrace every aspect of what makes us human, whether that be ego or compassion, because every bit contributes to who we truly are and what we can offer the world. The album explores multiplicity, the idea that we are all so many different things and that they can all live in harmony at the same time.
The album moves through the female experience with both fury and precision. Magi writes from trust, leaning into instinct rather than mapping out the outcome, because to fix the gaze too firmly on one destination is to miss the kind of potential that usually only lives in the periphery. This produced Broken R&B, a genre she named and owns entirely, less a marketing category than an honest account of how she works, accountable to no existing template, her art direction and visual world as idiosyncratic and charged as the music itself. Over the last decade, she has co-written and co-produced largely alongside Funkywhat, a collaborator with whom she has built a shared musical language.

title: Luke Pytel Blues Band w/ Shirley Johnson
description:
Nicknamed the “Sweetheart 
of the Blues” by the staff at BLUE 
CHICAGO, Shirley has been gracing the stage here since the 1990s with her 
spectacular performances.
Like so many 
African-American vocalists, Shirley Johnson started out singing in church and 
then went on to embrace secular music. The Chicago resident, whose influences 
range from Mahalia Jackson to Koko Taylor, Etta James, and Ruth Brown, is a 
gritty, big-voiced blues singer who can also handle soul and gospel. Although 
Johnson has spent much of her adult life in Chicago, the Windy City is not her 
hometown; she was born in 
Franklin, VA and raised in Norfolk, VA. Shirley came from a very religious 
family and was only six when she 
started singing gospel in a church choir.
When Shirley 
reached adulthood in the late '70s, she pursued a career in secular music and 
made her presence felt in Norfolk's blues and R&B circles. She went on to 
become an opening act for Aretha Franklin, Jerry Butler, Z.Z. Hill, and other 
well-known artists who were passing through town. In the early '80s, she 
recorded some singles for two regional labels in Virginia and those recordings 
caught the attention of a man who was planning to start a label in Chicago. The 
aspiring record man expressed interest in recording Ms. Johnson and sent her a 
plane ticket to Chicago, but when she arrived in the Windy City she learned he 
didn't have enough money to pay for a session.
Nonetheless, she 
decided to remain in Chicago and became active on the city's blues circuit, 
where she has performed both Blues and Soul. The musicians she worked with in 
Chicago included Little Johnny Christian, Artie "Blues Boy" White, 
and keyboardist “Professor” Eddie Lusk (who was a staple at BLUE CHICAGO and 
took Johnson on the road with him on international tours.)
Since the '90s, Johnson has made many 
recordings and in 2000 is one of the vocalists recorded on BLUE CHICAGO’s CD 
entitled “Mojo Mamas.”

title: Blueprint
description:
Blueprint is the kind of improv that keeps audiences AND players on their toes. Each week, a different cast member designs a bold new improv format that their fellow performers will learn about at the same time as the crowd. Expect the unexpected as we build something completely original, live, right before your eyes.

Understudies - In a longform narrative, each player on stage knows that they will eventually understudy another player in the show. The lights change and they have to embody a different player, and each time the lights change, they can select another player to embody.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Poetry and the Practice of Healing: A Workshop on Orality and Literacy
location: Franke Institute for the Humanities Regenstein Library, Room S-102
description:
On Friday, November 20, the Franke Institute for the Humanities will host Orality & Literacy, the inaugural gathering of a new multidisciplinary conference series, Poetry & the Practice of Healing.
 Hosted by Professor Lucy Alford, Dr. Timothy McGinnis, and Professor Sarah Nooter, with support from the Franke Institute for the Humanities, the series will explore over the next three years how poetry and poetic traditions mediate injury and recovery in their many forms.
 Orality & Literacy will serve as the first entry point into an exploration of how the spoken and written word have long been intertwined in healing encounters. The gathering will include poets, clinicians, and scholars in wide-ranging discussions, thought experiments, and poetry readings.
 “Health literacy” can make the difference between navigating a labyrinthine insurance system and falling through its gaps, just as poor “cultural competency” can prevent a clinician from recognizing the suffering before them. A contemporary patient cannot move through the medical world without leaving a trace documented by scribes, AI listening assistants, and clinicians themselves, who mediate the moment of assessment through annotations on the screen.
 Similarly, throughout the long history of poetry, the roles of spoken performance and memory, as opposed to written authority and documentation, have been fiercely debated, as the significance of the medium in shaping the message has become clear.
 The gathering will take place at the Franke Institute. Participants will begin with roundtables in which they offer brief 5–7-minute reflections on the questions and ideas that emerge from these themes.
 Please join us on Friday, November 20, at the Franke Institute!

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

title: Student Research Spotlight: Hawaiian Protest in Print
location: Newberry Library, 60 W Walton St, Chicago, IL 60610
description:
Join the Kim-Park Program at Newberry Library for a Student Research Spotlight from Sam Maza, a PhD Candidate in English Language and Literature at the University of Chicago.
 Hawaiian Protest in Print examines the myriad printing methods employed by Hawaiian citizens to assert their sovereignty. Public reactions to the 1843 Paulet Affair and the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom can be witnessed in newspaper articles, as well as pamphlets, songs, and petitions.
 Project Abstract:
 When the first printing press arrived on the shores of Hawaiʻi in 1822, it broadcasted the Hawaiian language in galvanizing new mediums, such as the book and newspaper. Once the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi established mandatory education, literacy rates skyrocketed. What was once an informal system of sending mail along through passing ships became insufficient to meet the high demand for missives and thus the Hawaiian Kingdom’s postal system was established in 1850. Letters, both in manuscript and print, widely circulated amongst the Hawaiian population. Yet by the end of the century, the nation that had laid the foundation for this lively printscape had been overthrown. Hawaiian printers were jailed for expressing discontent with the new governing body that, soon after, declared English as the exclusive language of instruction. Yet the literary traditions of the Hawaiian people that long preceded the adversarial government persisted. One such literary tradition is the moʻokūʻauhau, which have served as a record of relationships since time immemorial. They depict the temporal associations between beings- whether that be people, celestial bodies, or concepts. These chronological connections are often used to depict ancestry (moʻokūʻauhau pili koko) but can also trace genealogies of knowledge (moʻokūʻauhau ʻike). This project is a moʻokūʻauhau of the Hawaiian Kingdom’s postal service, a vector for Hawaiian knowledge and protest. 
 This event is open to all with registration and will be held at Newberry Library.

title: Queer Prom: Portable Gray Launch Party
location: The Land School, 7200 South Dorchester Avenue
description:
The University of Chicago’s Richard and Mary L. Gray Center for Arts and Inquiry invites you to Queer Prom, a launch party for issue 16 of Portable Gray at The Land School, 7200 South Dorchester Avenue. 
 We invite you to join us on Friday, November 20, from 6 PM to 10 PM, for Gray Center’s Queer Prom at The Land School
 Serving as the official launch party for Gray Center’s Portable Gray, Issue 16: “Costume and Collapse,” the evening celebrates queerness, artistic experimentation, and the myriad ways we embody and express ourselves. The night will feature a reception, a catwalk of costumes designed during an earlier workshop facilitated by artist Uta Bekaia, and a dance party spun by DJ Duane Powell, alongside interstitial interview moments with journal contributors. Beverages and bites will be available throughout the night.
 Tickets are free, with a suggested donation of $15. Donors who give at any amount will receive a copy of Portable Gray.
 More on Portable Gray 16: Costumes And Collapse:
 Guest-edited by Leah Feldman, our spring 2026 edition explores the continued life of the wearable art, as at once a record of the past—imprinted by the presence of the body—as it fashions forms of survival in its stitches, patterns, and silhouettes, generating armor to shelter fabulous possibilities for future-becoming. Featuring contributions by: Alia Ali, Uta Bekaia, Rikki Byrd, Nick Cave, Stephnie Cristello, Rachel Dedman, Thomas F. DeFrantz, Hoda El Shakry, Leah Feldman, Jonathan Flatley, Theaster Gates, Omar Kholeif, Dato Koridze, Catriona MacLeod, Matt Morris, Tim Nicholson, Duane Powell, Dieter Roelstraete, Slavs and Tatars, and Kris Trujillo. The issue also features our latest reviews in PGR by: Isaac Bjorke, Annette LePique, Nicky Ni, Pia Singh, Regina Victor, Erik Wenzel, and Ellen Wiese.
 ***Costumes and prom attire is encouraged.*** 
 Register here:  https://www.eventbrite.com/e/queer-prom-at-the-land-school-tickets-2003992649962?aff=oddtdtcreator
 About The Land School
 The Land School, a new pedagogical platform at the site of the former St. Laurence Elementary School, proposes a radical model of artistic experimentation and archival stewardship, providing space, time, access, collaborative inquiry, process-driven programming, and performance, all led by an intergenerational cohort of artists, archivists, scholars, craftspeople, cultural workers, and creative organizations invested in culture as a service.

Northwestern University Brain Awareness Outreach (NUBAO) is a public outreach initiative founded in 2010 by Northwestern University's Interdepartmental Neuroscience (NUIN) PhD students dedicated to educating, exciting, and inspiring the Chicago community about the brain. Through collaborations with public schools and science education programs in the Chicago area, NUBAO organizes a number of hands-on lectures, workshops, and open house-style events in an effort to teach a variety of neuroscience topics to students of all ages and their families. The NUBAO volunteer base consists of a diverse group of mostly graduate students, in addition to undergraduate students, post-doctoral fellows, faculty, and research staff from numerous departments and scientific disciplines at Northwestern University.

title: 1st Set With Pharez Whitted
description:
There are many moments that can define a man’s life and for Pharez Whitted, this is one of them. He’s taken on the new role as Chicago’s Youth Symphony Orchestra (CYSO) Jazz Director and Howard Reich at the Chicago Tribune described Pharez perfectly – “Few Chicago musician-educators are more qualified than Whitted to build the new band, for he commands a richly deserved reputation as a trumpet virtuoso, seasoned educator and irrepressible champion of the music.”
Whitted is humble with his legacy and his deep roots in music go as far back as the 1930’s in Indianapolis where the Hampton Family Band first began performing. His mother Virtue, his uncle Slide Hampton and the other 10 siblings (12 in total) laid the foundation with their self-educated and courageous father, Clarke “Deacon” Hampton at the helm. With that level of determination and talent, Whitted was destined to inherit the gift of music.
If you asked Pharez what inspires his music, he’ll say that the world needs hope and beauty and his compositions were created for that purpose. His music is for the people, to lift them up and inspire beautiful thoughts and a harmonious vibe throughout the Universe. One love, one Universal voice.

title: Suicide Note with Fred Camper (Chicago Restoration Premiere)
description:
In 1975, artist and critic Fred Camper’s stepfather leapt from the fifteenth-floor window of the family’s apartment without so much as a note. Haunted by the annihilating void of a wordless suicide, Camper began cataloging the world left behind on rolls of silent Super 8 film. Over the next eight years, he would record and organize diaristic dispatches from New York City: street scenes in Herald Square, a fireworks show over New York Harbor, a record of the first art installation at PS1, lateral views from the World Trade Center. Stitching together overlapping strands of personal, architectural, and ecological concern, Suicide Note would function for Camper as “a portrait of Manhattan’s constricted spaces, and more generally of the way humans occupy space.” The result is a vivid tapestry of a society on the brink. (Fred Camper, USA, 1976-1984, approx. 105 minutes, 16mm)
 Restored by Chicago Film Society with the support of the National Film Preservation Foundation and Big Creek Cooperative. Introduction and post-screening discussion with filmmaker, artist, and critic Fred Camper.
 Film Studies Center events are free and open to the public. Doors open thirty minutes prior to showtime.

title: CRAIG FINN & The Band of Forgiveness
description:
FITZGERALDS NIGHTCLUB PRESENTS:
CRAIG FINN & The Band of Forgiveness
$42 general admission seated // $50/seat reserved tables
(Fully Seated Show)
Craig Finn is a Minnesota-bred singer/songwriter based in New York City, best known as the singer of The Hold Steady. Finn spent the ’90's leading Minneapolis indie band Lifter Puller, which released 3 albums and an EP. After relocating to New York, he joined with Lifter Puller member Tad Kubler to form The Hold Steady in 2003. The Hold Steady quickly achieved critical acclaim and a worldwide fanbase with their unique pairing of dense lyrical narratives with big rock guitars. The Hold Steady’s ninth album, The Price Of Progress, was released in March 2023, commemorating the band’s 20th Anniversary.
Craig Finn released his 6th solo album Always Been in 2025. Produced by Adam Granduciel (The War On Drugs), the album features musical performances by Granduciel and members of The War on Drugs, Kathleen Edwards, Sam Fender, and more.
Always Been tells the story of a man who becomes a clergyman despite a lack of faith. The songs detail his rise, fall, and eventual redemption, while also shining a light to sharply reveal the other characters that populate the world he moves through. A limited edition, 92-page companion book Lousy With Ghosts accompanies the album and features 11 works of fiction by Craig Finn. These stories take place in the same universe as the record, giving deeper looks at the characters within.
Finn released his first solo album in 2012 with three additional solo LPs put forth from 2015 – 2019: Faith in the Future, We All Want The Same Things, and 2019's I Need a New War – which coalesced into a sign-of-the-times musical trilogy. Finn’s fifth album, A Legacy of Rentals was released in 2022 and received universal critical acclaim.
In 2025, Finn debuted The Band of Forgiveness – an accomplished group of Minneapolis based musicians who bring a unique musical perspective to Finn’s solo compositions. In early 2026, The Band of Forgiveness toured the UK, culminating in a sold out performance at London’s esteemed Union Chapel.
That’s How I Remember It is Craig Finn’s podcast series, launched in 2022. Co-produced and distributed by Talkhouse, the podcast series examines the connection between memory and creativity. Each episode features a discussion between Finn and one creator – including musicians, authors, filmmakers, and more – about the role memory plays in their art. These exclusive conversations reveal the different ways each creator synthesizes their remembered life experience to tell stories about themselves and the world we live in. Podcast guests have included George Saunders, Fred Armisen, Bill Hader, Lucinda Williams, Johnny Marr, Jason Isbell, Duff McKagan, Adam Duritz, Ben Gibbard, and many more.
Grab dinner before the show at BABYGOLD BARBECUE
Or enjoy full service dining inside the club when doors open.

description: ABOUT JACKSON DEAN: With his strong gravel-toned vocals, wayward spirit, intentional songwriting and overall mystique, PLATINUM-selling singer/songwriter Jackson Dean has earned a reputation for his impressive live show and thought-provoking music. Since astonishing Nashville in 2022 with Greenbroke, the acoustic-forward debut that rocked as hard as it embraced freedom, the dusky-voiced songwriter from Maryland has always gone his own way rather than chasing trends. “Don’t Come Lookin’,” his propulsive No. 1 debut single, struck PLATINUM, giving Greenbroke a launching pad for a writer willing to pay the price and go the distance. His third studio album, Magnolia Sage, was released earlier this year to critical acclaim. A stellar collection of songs that move from sweeping to soothing, rocking to ruminative, the 11-track project creates a sound that is singularly Jackson Dean: alive, vital, frisky, sexy and rugged. title: Hayward
description:
As part of its 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by The Gift ensemble member Netta Walker.
Hayward reimagines Hamlet and Electra through the eyes of Luna, who reveals to her family — on the day of their father's funeral — that his ghost has come to see her. Beneath the haunting, this is a love story: a daughter's love for her father, and the complicated, unresolved feelings he left behind. The story follows a family shaped by the trauma passed down by a father who served in the Navy during the Gulf War. Across grief, they reach for each other, trying, imperfectly, to come back together.
Developed through the Pearl Cleage Writers Workshop with Goodman Theatre and Remy Bumppo Theatre Company, and named a semifinalist for the 2025 Eugene O'Neill National Playwrights Conference, Hayward is exactly the kind of bold new work The Gift Theatre was built to tell.
Learn more about The Gift Theatre online at thegifttheatre.org or follow on social @thegifttheatre #thegifttheatre
The Gift Theatre is a storefront nonprofit theatre company founded in Chicago’s Jefferson Park neighborhood, committed to creating accessible, inclusive and impactful theatrical experiences.
Our identity is defined by intimacy, collaboration and a belief that live storytelling can inspire and transform both artist and audience.
What began as a spatial limitation became a revelation. For nearly 20 years, we performed in a renovated shoe store—Chicago’s smallest Equity theater—where audience members sat just inches from the actors. That intimacy didn’t just shape our work, it shaped who we are as artists. We’ve learned to lean into the vulnerability and electricity that arise when actor and audience share the same breath, both fully present in mutual emotional exchange.
At The Gift, we are only interested in work that is challenging and transformative —stories that ask big questions and risk discomfort in pursuit of deeper understanding. We delight in the dark humor and unexpected joy that surface in life’s messiest moments, reminding us that even pain can carry connection and light. We believe that every story, at its heart, is a love story—rooted in longing and a search for communion.
Our programming isn’t bound by genre but guided by character-driven, emotionally rich storytelling rooted in truth. Whether surreal or starkly naturalistic, each play we share reflects our commitment to creating spaces of deep connection—among artists, between artist and audience, and within our community.
Presenting this show during our anniversary season in Steppenwolf's 1700 Theater feels like coming home — many in the ensemble first met at The School at Steppenwolf, and those experiences shaped how they think about telling stories.
Hayward is made possible by a special gift from Show Sponsor, The Michael and Mona Heath Fund.
The Gift Theatre Company’s 2026 Homecoming Season is made possible, in part, by generous contributions from The Arts Work Fund · The Copernicus Foundation · Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events · The Gaylord and Dorothy Donnelley Foundation · The Illinois Arts Council · Melissa Thornley Consulting · The Paul Angell Foundation · The Rabb Family Foundation · The Saints · The Service Club of Chicago · The Shubert Foundation, Inc.

As part of our 25th Anniversary Season, The Gift Theatre is proud to present Hayward by ensemble member Netta Walker.

description:

ADULT. & A Place To Bury Strangers * DANA
$25 Adv. / $30 Day of / 18+ / Doors: 8pm / Show: 9pm
ADULT. is not cooperating. For over 25 years, the dystopian Detroit synth-punk institution founded by Nicola Kuperus and Adam Lee Miller has embodied steadfast frustration, distrust, and apprehension. One might expect the edges to soften with time, but ADULT. is not interested in the comforts of legacy. The duos music has never sounded as visceral, urgent, and downright angry as it does on the culminating, uncompromising Kissing Luck Goodbye, their scorched-earth 10th LP and fourth with Dias Records. Built with upgraded gear and a whole new library of sounds, the material is crushingly dynamic, louder yet clearer, with Kuperus commanding delivery given greater prominence in the mix, outlining an arsenal of vivid, caustic calls, chants, and musings.
Fans around the world know Oliver Ackermann always brings surprises. For nearly two decades, the singer and guitarist of New York Citys A Place To Bury Strangers has fused post-punk, noise-rock, shoegaze, psychedelia, and avant-garde experimentation into music that feels volatile and alive. As the founder of Death By Audio, hes extended that same spirit through his signal-scrambling effects, empowering artists everywhere to push sound past its limits. Onstage, A Place To Bury Strangers delivers a shamanistic experienceimmersive, feral, and electrifyingwhere real-time experiments and sudden breakthroughs collide.

title: Suicide Note with Fred Camper (Chicago Restoration Premiere)
description:
In 1975, artist and critic Fred Camper’s stepfather leapt from the fifteenth-floor window of the family’s apartment without so much as a note. Haunted by the annihilating void of a wordless suicide, Camper began cataloging the world left behind on rolls of silent Super 8 film. Over the next eight years, he would record and organize diaristic dispatches from New York City: street scenes in Herald Square, a fireworks show over New York Harbor, a record of the first art installation at PS1, lateral views from the World Trade Center. Stitching together overlapping strands of personal, architectural, and ecological concern, Suicide Note would function for Camper as “a portrait of Manhattan’s constricted spaces, and more generally of the way humans occupy space.” The result is a vivid tapestry of a society on the brink. (Fred Camper, USA, 1976-1984, approx. 105 minutes, 16mm)
Restored by Chicago Film Society with the support of the National Film Preservation Foundation and Big Creek Cooperative. Introduction and post-screening discussion with filmmaker, artist, and critic Fred Camper.

title: Mike Wheeler Blues Band w/ Laretha Weathersby
description:
Two 
calibers of singers exist in today’s music industry. There are vocalists and 
then there are entertainers. Laretha Weathersby is both. Her dynamic, effervescent stage presence 
is unparalleled and her sultry, wispy vibrato makes her a Blues natural.
Voted 
2009-2010’s “Chicago Blues Diva of the Year,” she belts out traditional Blues 
classics with passion and poise and delivers riveting renditions of timeless 
R&B, Soul and Top 40 tunes, all while captivating crowds with her jovial 
disposition and dynamic dancing. Known for her rousing stage presence, crowd members rarely 
blink when Laretha hits the stage, fearing they will miss one of her signature 
dance moves or the chance to chant along with the charismatic chanteuse.
Reigning 
from the Southside of Chicago, Laretha’s mother, a former Gospel soloist, 
detected her daughter’s singing abilities and enrolled the toddler in piano classes 
and encouraged her as a teenager to be an active member of the choir at the 
family’s place of worship. But it was not until the 1990s that Laretha began to 
cultivate a personal relationship with Blues music.
Emerging 
as one of the premiere female Blues vocalists in the City of Chicago in the 
late 1990s, Laretha has performed at such legendary Blues hotspots as The 
Kingston Mines, BLUES on Halsted and since 2010 is a spectacular presence here 
at BLUE CHICAGO.
Her 
debut album – Dance the Blues Away – is an eclectic mix of traditional Blues 
infused with remnants of contemporary R&B and Soul. The album reveals 
Laretha’s reverence for conventional Blues music while flaunting her fluent 
transition into contemporary R & B and Soul.
According 
to Ms. Weathersby, “the power of Blues music lies in its ability to relate to 
each and every member of the human race. People of all different backgrounds 
can connect with the universal concepts of love, triumph and tribulation, which 
are the very elements upon which Blues music is based. I consider it an honor 
and joy to incorporate that human element into my live performances and it is 
with passion and humility that I accept the honor and challenge of preserving 
Blues music for future generations.”
www.LarethaWeathersby.com

title: Omni (Deluxe 10 Year Anniversary)
description: Doors: 9PM / Show: 10PM / 21+ Ten years on, Omnis Deluxe is a bit of a paradox; Its an island of a record with a fully formed untethered-to-any-scene unique quality but I hear its influence everywhere in the art punk underground. There are countless bands that have mined inspiration from the LPs cerebral pop cool, single string riffs, syncopated hooks, and crispy mid-fi production style. Perhaps in 2016 when Omni cheekily named the album Deluxe, they knew they had a classic on their hands. The band was poking fun of the streaming era marketing tactic where artists re-enter the algorithm via a deluxe expanded version of an album right after the original is released but ironically, ten years later Omnis debut is a genuine classic and is being re-released with a bonus disc of B-sides, outtakes, and demos. Omni began as a way for Philip Frobos (bass + vocals) and Frankie Broyles (guitars + drums + keys) to practice creative spontaneity in contrast to the slower meticulous methods their then other bands employed. One fateful night in 2013, the then-roommates devised an Eno-inspired creative game: Would it be possible to write an entire song (arrangement + lyrics, etc.) all in one three hour night session? Whereas most bands begin sculpting a riff or progression brought in by one member, Omni revelled at the chance to begin each songwriting session with a true tabula rosa with no goal in mind except trusting the process. These sessions often began with a melodic bass line that was then quickly complemented by syncopated pointillist guitar (Frankie almost never voices full chords on guitar in Omni). Philip would then retreat to a quiet area to write lyrics as quickly as possible while Frankie worked on writing and recording the drum parts. Seeking the definitive by chance, any accidents that happened in the takes became baked into the songs arrangements; An extra measure here or resting a beat too long there forced the band to come up with creative musical solutions.

title: The Cook, The Thief, His Wife, & Her Lover
address: 3519 N Clark St, SUITE C301, Chicago, IL, 60657
description:
Peter Greenaway's 1989 magnum opus THE COOK, THE THIEF, HIS WIFE & HER LOVER is neo-noir for the hungry, devious soul. Released at a time when crime cinema was growing increasingly perverse with the likes of ANGEL HEART (1987), BLUE VELVET (1986), and BODY DOUBLE (1984), Greenaway's film out-shocks the buch by intertwining two of human nature's favorite pastimes: food and sex. Like Marco Ferreri's LA GRAND BOUFFE (1973) and Paul Bartel's EATING RAOUL (1982) before it, food and sex quickly turn into a recipe for something decidedly more sinister and... cannibalistic. Shocking audiences at the time of its release, time has not tamed Greenaway's film at all, and you'll never look at Helen Mirren or Michael Gambon the same way again. (Justin LaLiberty)

title: Spirit Tasting
description:
DIRECTED BY
Chris LaMartina
WRITTEN BY
Chris LaMartina,
Michael Varrati
STARRING
Zoe Angeli,
Helenmary Ball,
John Dimes
Toasting their late friend at a distillery on New Year’s Eve, three former bandmates stumble into a top-shelf tasting where wishes are required for every bottle. But when their dreams become nightmares, they discover that every pour has its price.
Inspired by tales of B-movie maverick Roger Corman filming features like Little Shop of Horrors and The Terror in less than a week, director Chris LaMartina celebrated his 40th birthday by shooting the feature in just four days of principal photography on a total budget of $40K.
Spirit Tasting is a sobering post-punk riff on the seminal horror story "The Monkey’s Paw" that explores “what ifs” of the past and aspirations for the future—with ghastly and gory consequences. The film stars Sean Doherty, Matt Lake, Melissa LaMartina, Trevor Wilhelms, Matt Baughman, Cate Paris, and Tatiana Nya Ford with cameos from Grady Hendrix, Clay McLeod Chapman, Peaches Christ, and Henry Zebrowski.

description:
DIRECTED BY
Ralph Bakshi

Ralph Bakshi,
Frank Frazetta,
Roy Thomas

It began as a once-in-a-lifetime collaboration between two of the greatest icons of the fantasy genre: controversial animator Ralph Bakshi (director of FRITZ THE CAT, WIZARDS and the original THE LORD OF THE RINGS) and legendary illustrator Frank Frazetta (creator of the iconic CONAN THE BARBARIAN, VAMPIRELLA and Edgar Rice Burroughs book covers). It became - and remains - one of the most startling animation epics of all time. Now experience a world unlike any ever seen, where savage warriors, horrific monsters and luscious maidens battle for the soul of a civilization in a time of good and evil, pleasure and pain, and FIRE AND ICE.
Featuring the voice talents of William Ostrander (CHRISTINE), Maggie Roswell (THE SIMPSONS), Steve Sandor (STRYKER), Stephen Mendel (JACK FROST), and the incomparable Susan Tyrrell (CRY-BABY), Blue Underground is proud to present FIRE AND ICE in a brand-new restoration, scanned in 4K 16-bit from the original negative!

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: ASOR-ISAC Teacher Workshop: Bring Archaeology to your Classroom
description:
Join the American Society of Overseas Research (ASOR) and the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures (ISAC) for a hands-on workshop created for K–12 educators.
 Workshop Schedule
 10:00am–11:00 am | Investigating Ancient Artifacts
 Experience ISAC’s Artifact Analysis activity using replica artifacts. Learn strategies for helping students make observations, form inferences, interpret material evidence, and ask meaningful questions about the past. Find out more about ISAC’s Museum in a Box program where you can bring artifact replicas to your own classroom and explore ASOR’s teacher resources and ISAC’s lesson plans on the ancient world!
 11:00am–12:00pm | Archaeology in the Field
 Hear firsthand perspectives from an archaeological field director and a student excavation volunteer. Learn what happens on a dig, how discoveries are interpreted, and what students can gain from participating in archaeological fieldwork. A question-and-answer session will follow.
 Your Registration Includes
 Hands-on artifact-analysis training
 Classroom-ready educational resources
 Information about an upcoming curriculum competition
 Admission to Saturday’s ASOR poster session and afternoon sessions
 Digital certificate of completion
 CPDUs for Illinois Teacher: Up to Five hours available. Saturday Teacher Workshop (2 hours), Poster session attendence (1 hour), ASOR workshop Teaching with the Ancient Near East Today (2 hours)
 Registration Options
 $30 | Saturday Teacher Workshop and Conference Access
 Includes the teacher workshop, poster session where you can talk to presenters about their projects, and Saturday afternoon sessions including ASOR workshop Teaching with the Ancient Near East Today from 2:00–4:05pm. Ancient Near East Today is ASOR’s open-access digital platform for public scholarship, disseminating the latest research, insights, and news about the ancient Near East and beyond.
 $50 | Full ASOR Annual Meeting Access
 Attend the entire conference, from Wednesday evening through Saturday evening, November 18–21.
 No previous background in archaeology or the ancient world is required.
 About ASOR
 For 125 years, ASOR has been a flagship for archaeology, history, and cultural heritage in the Middle East and wider Mediterranean, supporting professional standards for excavations, research, peer review, and conduct. ASOR has a unique ability to bring together scholars from archaeology, history, science and other fields to protect and study cultural heritage and share its importance with the public especially as so many sites are being threatened or destroyed. Learn more at asor.org.

title: Compton Lectures: Angela Olinto “Flying High to Catch Neutrinos and Other Extreme Particles”
description:
Join us for a free public lecture series celebrating 50 Years of Discovery at the Enrico Fermi Institute of UChicago. Attendees can join in person or virtually.
 Prof. Angela Olinto presents: Flying High to Catch Neutrinos and Other Extreme Particles
 What can neutrinos and cosmic rays teach us about the most powerful processes in the universe?
 Researchers are flying ultra-fast cameras on NASA science balloons to help answer that question, observing extremely energetic subatomic particles, including neutrinos and cosmic rays, arriving from the deepest corners of the cosmos.
 Over the past decades, these scientific instruments have evolved to combine different types of observations, allowing researchers to learn more from these particles and better understand the extreme events that produce them.
 In this talk, Angela V. Olinto, (Emeritus Professor Univ of Chicago, Provost and Rutherfurd Professor of Columbia University and a leading astrophysicist), will describe her work related to earlier balloon projects that helped develop this technology, and look ahead to a planned balloon flight in 2028, which promises to deepen our understanding of the powerful processes that shape our universe.

An aggressive documentary filmmaker fights present-day 1970s government censorship as she seeks the truth about bricklayer Matuesz Birkut, a state-manufactured proletariat hero during the Soviet-controlled 1950s. Fourteen years in the making, MAN OF MARBLE is a film-within-a-film that blends documentary, pseudo-documentary, and fictional techniques that inevitably draw comparison to CITIZEN KANE. title: Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? Gallery Hours
description:
Arts + Public Life at the University of Chicago presents Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? a new exhibition by Chicago artist Candace Hunter centered on the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway and the Black communities displaced in its path. Now embedded within Chicago’s physical and social fabric, the Dan Ryan Expressway obscures both the choices that produced it and the lives reorganized around it. The construction disrupted the ordinary intimacies through which a place becomes home: routes traveled, neighbors known, businesses frequented, porches gathered on.
 Through photographic collage, architectural fragments, archival materials, sound, sculptural interventions, and oral histories, Hunter moves between what is documented and what is remembered. The work resists the idea that displacement can be understood solely through statistics.
 The series builds on the Memory Teas Candace hosted during her APL residency, which gathered first-person accounts from Black Chicagoans who remember the Dan Ryan’s construction and the neighborhoods transformed by it. Rather than asking these memories to complete the historical record, Hunter allows them to stay partial, layered, and unresolved.
 While centered on Chicago’s South Side, the history at the heart of Intentionality, 1960 reaches beyond the city. Across the United States, highway construction, redevelopment, and urban renewal reshaped Black communities, often presenting profound social and spatial disruption as necessary progress. Intentionality, 1960 invites audiences to see those histories not as isolated events but as part of a larger American story.
 Intentionality, 1960 will be accompanied by Threshold: Conversations on the Stoop, a series of public dialogues on the front porch within the exhibition between Candace and scholars to dive into topics related to the exhibition. The Threshold conversations are presented with support from the Office of the Provost Diversity and Inclusion team, in partnership with the Chicago Forum for Free Inquiry and Expression.
 Intentionality, 1960: Whose Dreams? will be on view from September 24-December 12 in the Arts + Public Life Gallery Space located in the Arts Incubator at 301 E. Garfield Blvd.
 Gallery Hours: Thursday-Saturday | 1:00 - 5:00pm

The Ruth Page Center for the Arts is proud to present its annual live production of “Ruth Page’s The Nutcracker” featuring original choreography by the legendary Ruth Page and directed by the artistic team: Victor Alexander, Birute Barodicaite, Dori Rothschild, Chrissy Lacny, John Atterberry and Renardo Johnson. 
Originally presented at the Arie Crown Theatre from 1965 until 1997, this production is Chicago’s longest-running Nutcracker tradition, recreating highlights from Ruth Page’s beloved original full-length staging. It features exquisite dancing, world-renowned guest artists, stunning costumes and magical settings in the Land of Snow and Kingdom of Sweets. International and local guest artists are featured alongside the talented dancers of the Ruth Page Professional Dance Training Program and students from Ruth Page School of Dance.   
Chicago’s longest-running “Nutcracker” has delighted tens of thousands of fans and begins this season with a special one-hour version of the celebrated production, “Ruth Page’s The Nutcracker Suite,” at the Beverly Arts Center, 2407 W. 111th St., Saturday, Nov. 21 at 1 and 5 p.m. Tickets, ranging from $17 to $59 (depending on venue), are on sale now at RuthPage.org.
Photo by A. Deran Photography

description:

6500 N Clark Street, 2nd floor
 : When the rest of the world is largely indifferent to the spread of AIDS in New York City, a group of gay men come together to spread awareness and try to save themselves. The play follows Ned Weeks, a polarizing but passionate activist as he fights for money, acceptance, and compassion from the city government, his family, and his gay community. The Normal Heart is an intensely political, semi-autobiographical play based on Larry Kramer’s experiences with the founding of the Gay Men’s Health Crisis and the early days of the AIDS epidemic.

title: The Gradient
description:
The GradientWritten by Steph Del Ross
Presented by Campfire Repertory Theatre Directed by Campfire Rep Associate Artist, Gina Cioffi
What happens when accountability becomes a business? In Steph Del Rosso’s sharp, darkly funny satire, men accused of sexual misconduct enter a futuristic rehabilitation center designed to reform them. When idealistic new employee Tess joins the organization, she quickly discovers that redemption becomes complicated when good intentions collide with technology, corporate ambition, and profit. The Gradient challenges audiences to examine power, forgiveness, and who gets to decide when someone has truly changed.
*Content warning: This play includes themes of sexual assault, sexism and misogyny, and adult language, and is recommended for ages 16-17+.

title: SOL Collective: The Voices In Our Heads
description:
SHOW DESCRIPTION: The Voices in Our Heads is a powerful and thought-provoking storytelling experience from SOL Collective that explores the inner worlds we all carry with us: the doubts, fears, dreams, memories, expectations, and conversations that shape how we see ourselves and the world around us.
Through compelling moments of humor, vulnerability, and reflection, the production gives voice to the thoughts we often leave unspoken. It asks us to consider which voices deserve our attention, which ones hold us back, and what can happen when we finally listen to ourselves.
Raw, relatable, and deeply human, The Voices in Our Heads invites audiences into a shared space of connection and self-discovery—reminding us that although our inner voices may sound different, none of us are alone in hearing them.
ABOUT SOL Collective: Founded in 2020, the SOL Collective was established to uplift and showcase the voices of women of color in the storytelling community and arts scene of Chicago. The name SOL holds significant meaning for us as it symbolizes our identity as women of the Sun, our connection to our ancestral spirits, and our commitment to sharing the Stories of Our Lives.

description:
There are many moments that can define a man’s life and for Pharez Whitted, this is one of them. He’s taken on the new role as Chicago’s Youth Symphony Orchestra (CYSO) Jazz Director and Howard Reich at the Chicago Tribune described Pharez perfectly – “Few Chicago musician-educators are more qualified than Whitted to build the new band, for he commands a richly deserved reputation as a trumpet virtuoso, seasoned educator and irrepressible champion of the music.”
Whitted is humble with his legacy and his deep roots in music go as far back as the 1930’s in Indianapolis where the Hampton Family Band first began performing. His mother Virtue, his uncle Slide Hampton and the other 10 siblings (12 in total) laid the foundation with their self-educated and courageous father, Clarke “Deacon” Hampton at the helm. With that level of determination and talent, Whitted was destined to inherit the gift of music.

An Undying Love For A Burning World is an epic album of colossal hypnotism beautiful, fearsome and utterly compelling in a way that only Neurosis can be. Aaron Turner (Sumac, Isis)joins the band on vocals and guitar, a name whose legacy is intertwined with the bands own and a true kindred spirit.

title: CRAIG FINN & The Band of Forgiveness
description:
FITZGERALDS NIGHTCLUB PRESENTS:
CRAIG FINN & The Band of Forgiveness
$42 general admission seated // $50/seat reserved tables
(Fully Seated Show)
Craig Finn is a Minnesota-bred singer/songwriter based in New York City, best known as the singer of The Hold Steady. Finn spent the ’90's leading Minneapolis indie band Lifter Puller, which released 3 albums and an EP. After relocating to New York, he joined with Lifter Puller member Tad Kubler to form The Hold Steady in 2003. The Hold Steady quickly achieved critical acclaim and a worldwide fanbase with their unique pairing of dense lyrical narratives with big rock guitars. The Hold Steady’s ninth album, The Price Of Progress, was released in March 2023, commemorating the band’s 20th Anniversary.
Craig Finn released his 6th solo album Always Been in 2025. Produced by Adam Granduciel (The War On Drugs), the album features musical performances by Granduciel and members of The War on Drugs, Kathleen Edwards, Sam Fender, and more.
Always Been tells the story of a man who becomes a clergyman despite a lack of faith. The songs detail his rise, fall, and eventual redemption, while also shining a light to sharply reveal the other characters that populate the world he moves through. A limited edition, 92-page companion book Lousy With Ghosts accompanies the album and features 11 works of fiction by Craig Finn. These stories take place in the same universe as the record, giving deeper looks at the characters within.
Finn released his first solo album in 2012 with three additional solo LPs put forth from 2015 – 2019: Faith in the Future, We All Want The Same Things, and 2019's I Need a New War – which coalesced into a sign-of-the-times musical trilogy. Finn’s fifth album, A Legacy of Rentals was released in 2022 and received universal critical acclaim.
In 2025, Finn debuted The Band of Forgiveness – an accomplished group of Minneapolis based musicians who bring a unique musical perspective to Finn’s solo compositions. In early 2026, The Band of Forgiveness toured the UK, culminating in a sold out performance at London’s esteemed Union Chapel.
That’s How I Remember It is Craig Finn’s podcast series, launched in 2022. Co-produced and distributed by Talkhouse, the podcast series examines the connection between memory and creativity. Each episode features a discussion between Finn and one creator – including musicians, authors, filmmakers, and more – about the role memory plays in their art. These exclusive conversations reveal the different ways each creator synthesizes their remembered life experience to tell stories about themselves and the world we live in. Podcast guests have included George Saunders, Fred Armisen, Bill Hader, Lucinda Williams, Johnny Marr, Jason Isbell, Duff McKagan, Adam Duritz, Ben Gibbard, and many more.
Grab dinner before the show at BABYGOLD BARBECUE
Or enjoy full service dining inside the club when doors open.

description:

Since 1994, Subterranean has been a cornerstone of the Wicker Park live music & nightlife scene. Built in the 1890s, the historic structure at 2011 W North Avenue has a storied past, having once served as a brothel, a bathhouse, and as a wire room for gambling during the prohibition era. Owner Robert Gomez has worked hard to preserve the original features of the space that have been in place since the building’s creation and give Subterranean its one of a kind character, including the iconic Tiffany & brass chandelier that hangs above the dance floor. The Subterranean stage has played host to notable and legendary acts including Chappell Roan, Turnstile, Dinosaur Jr, Lizzo, Tame Impala, Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires, Halsey, Pussy Riot, Built To Spill, Brand New, BADBADNOTGOOD, Lee Scratch Perry, Alabama Shakes, Durand Jones & The Indications, Fall Out Boy, and has been home to some of Chicago’s longest running residencies: Thursday nights’ Reggae Gold and the longest-running hip-hop open mic in the nation, the 606 Open Mic.

title: GOOD HEAT
description:
Good Heat is a world created between riddim and blues, between the island diaspora and the cities, like Chicago, Brooklyn, and London, that nurtured imagination and expanded expression globally. November 21, Syx Williams curates a specific feel, thoughtfully bringing together DJ, musical artists and dancers to infuse Chicago with some Good Heat.
Join us for DJ GabSoul’s Chicago debut! The night also features Chicago staple DJ Mochi, Chicago Blues legend Harmonica Hinds, and Dancehall Queen Ms. Mighty. Music will range from island music (ie soca, dancehall, bouyon) to R&B, soul, house, hip-hop, and whatever fits within the feel of the room.
ABOUT THE ARTISTS
Syx Williams | IG: @syxwilliams + @thisisgoodheat
Syx curates experiences around feeling, within music and community. A church-raised contralto with Trini and Bajan parents, growing up between California and South London, and nurtured by Chicago, she merges musical worlds to create unexpected familiarity amongst range. She created and hosts Between Us, an intimate live performance and listening series. She also curated a live D'Angelo tribute at Soho House. Through Good Heat, she brings the same care to a larger stage, introducing audiences to unique and distinct musical experiences in Chicago.
DJ GabSoul | IG: @gabsoul_
GabSoul, also known as "the ILLustrious Eclectic Selecta," is a first-generation Caribbean-American DJ and multi-hyphenate who has carved a unique space for herself with a dynamic fusion of soulful and danceable sounds, specializing in Black music across the diaspora. As a native New Yorker and a product of the city’s vibrant melting pot, her musical journey reflects the rich tapestry of her heritage and the diverse influences of her upbringing. Known for her captivating stage presence and impeccable selections, GabSoul creates unforgettable sets that effortlessly blend timeless classics with contemporary hits and everything in between.
HARMONICA HINDS
Harmonica Hings is a Trinidadian-born Chicago blues singer and musician. He moved from Trinidad to Canada and then settled permanently in Chicago, becoming known in the 1970s when he played in the house band of the famed Theresa's Lounge in Chicago. With a five decade career, he remains active on the Chicago blues scene, including Buddy Guy's Legends and several Chicago Blues Fest appearances.
DJ Mochi | IG: @dj_mochi
DJ Mochi is a Chicago-based DJ, producer, and event curator. Across genres like R&B, Dancehall and House, his selections transport audiences to clubs around the world. For Mochi, music is a universal language that has the unique power to connect people. His mission as a DJ is to build a diverse and forward-thinking community, open to fresh sounds and experiences.
DHQ MS. MIGHTY | IG: @meowlabelle + @bodybymighty
DHQ Ms. Mighty is a Chicago-born Dancehall movement specialist, instructor, and performer of Jamaican descent. She is a certified Dancehall Queen, holding honors as Midwest DHQ champion, and 4th International Dancehall Queen (2023). As the founder of BODY by Mighty, she blends Caribbean culture with fitness and lifestyle. Ms. Mighty’s interdisciplinary work is dedicated to archiving, educating, and preserving dancehall culture.

title: Rockin’ in the Park
description:
Rockin’ in the Park 2026
Rosemont’s Parkway Bank Park Entertainment District is turning up the volume this summer with the return of Rockin’ in the Park, a free outdoor concert series bringing live music, tribute bands, food and drink tents, and fireworks to the great lawn.
The 2026 series kicks off on Sunday, May 24 with a post-show fireworks display. Free concerts continue every Thursday and select Friday evenings from May 28 through September 3, with Thursday night shows ending in a musical fireworks display.
This year’s lineup celebrates the sounds of Rush, Journey, The Who, Bruno Mars, George Michael, Steely Dan, Pink Floyd, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, the Bee Gees, Elton John, and more.
Concerts run from 7–10 PM. Admission is free. Outside food and coolers are prohibited. Parking is available at the Parkway Bank Park parking garage and is free with validation from any Parkway Bank Park venue.
2026 Lineup
Thursday, July 9: New World Men*
A powerful tribute to Rush, bringing the spirit, precision, and intensity of the legendary band’s live shows to the stage.
Thursday, July 16: Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press*
Beloved Chicago party band Rod Tuffcurls & The Bench Press delivers huge harmonies, sharp musicianship, and a wildly fun setlist built for singing, dancing, and staying out later than planned.
Thursday, July 23: Departure*
Departure recreates the look, sound, and feel of Journey, packing their set with high-energy performances of the band’s biggest hits.
Thursday, July 30: Live the Who*
Direct from Detroit, Live the Who pays tribute to The Who’s explosive 1968–1974 era with the sound, look, and raw energy of the iconic rock band.
Friday, July 31: 24K Magic / George Michael Reborn
24K Magic brings the Bruno Mars party with slick choreography, bold style, and hit after hit. George Michael Reborn keeps the night moving with the sound, moves, and charisma of George Michael and Wham!
Thursday, August 6: Brooklyn Charmers*
Brooklyn Charmers bring fresh energy and serious precision to the music of Steely Dan, honoring the band’s smooth hooks, sharp lyrics, and unmistakable sound.
Thursday, August 13: Echoes of Pompeii*
This 10-piece Pink Floyd tribute takes audiences through every era of the band’s catalog, from the early Syd Barrett days to later classics.
Thursday, August 20: Southern Accents*
Southern Accents recreates the music, style, and sound of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers with contagious energy and serious attention to detail.
Thursday, August 27: No Quarter*
No Quarter delivers the full sound, power, and spirit of Led Zeppelin with a tribute show built for fans who want more than just the hits.
Friday, August 28: Bee Gees Gold / The Wayouts
Bee Gees Gold recreates the harmonies, look, and sound of the Bee Gees, from early favorites to disco-era classics. The Wayouts open up the garage with a high-energy tribute to 1960s rock.
Thursday, September 3: Rhythm of the Rocketman*
Rhythm of the Rocketman celebrates Elton John with a high-energy tribute packed with beloved hits like “Rocket Man,” “Tiny Dancer,” “Your Song,” and “Bennie and the Jets.”

title: 25 for 25: ANTONIO GAUDI
description: A Gene Siskel Film Center holiday favorite, we bring back the ever-popular cult film by Hiroshi Teshigahara (WOMAN OF THE DUNES), inspired by the wild, undulating, joyously erupting forms of Barcelona architect Antoni Gaud. Teshigahara's eye for texture, shape, and sensual detail meets Gaud's whimsy in the cinematic exploration of such masterpieces of visionary architecture as the basilica of La Sagrada Famlia. The contemporary of artists such as Picasso and Joan Mir, Gaud drew on Barcelona's medieval Romanesque architecture and ancient Arab culture for his inspiration. This film reveals the intricacy and hallucinatory richness of his concepts through camerawork alone. Forgoing narration, Teshigahara accompanies his images with a brilliantly eclectic selection of music, ranging from baroque harpsichord to glass orchestra. (BS) Screened in December over many years as a Siskel Film Center Holiday tradition, last appearing in 2019

title: The Winter’s Tale
description:
“It is required you do awake your faith.”
Once upon a time in a land called Sicilia, King Leontes is infected by an uncontrollable jealousy over his pregnant wife, Hermione. Shakespeare’s timeless romance takes us on a fairy tale adventure from the darkness of Sicilia to the color and music of Bohemia. Shipwrecks, bears, and magic oracles dance across the stage in this story of betrayal and forgiveness, reunion and reconciliation. Hope and forgiveness sit at the heart of Shakespeare’s most magical of fairy stories with an unforgettable ending driven by the power of redemption.
For the first time in CST’s history, two plays will be performed in repertory by one masterfully talented Chicago Shakespeare Company of actors. Under the creative leadership of CST Artistic Director Edward Hall and taking its inspiration from Shakespeare’s own company and CST’s roots as the Shakespeare Repertory, a company of 14 actors perform both The Winter’s Tale and A Midsummer Night’s Dream, two of Shakespeare’s most beguiling fairy tales. This double header of productions makes for a thrilling theatrical experience, with two beautiful plays exploring the formidable power of love, laughter, and forgiveness.
